lessons.title: What Graph Theory Is
lessons.content:
Imagine you live in an old city built on both banks of a river, with two islands in the middle. Seven bridges join the four pieces of land. Every Sunday people walk around town and ask a fun question: can I take a walk that crosses every bridge exactly once? Nobody could find such a walk, but nobody could prove it was impossible either. The city was Konigsberg, and in 1736 the Swiss mathematician Leonhard Euler finally settled the question. His answer was no, and the way he proved it started a whole new branch of mathematics. That branch is graph theory, and this course is all about it.

Euler's big trick: Euler noticed that the shape of the land, the length of the bridges and the width of the river did not matter at all. Only two things mattered: which pieces of land exist, and which bridges join which pieces. So he shrank every piece of land into a dot and turned every bridge into a line between two dots. Suddenly a messy map became a tiny clean picture of four dots and seven lines. That picture is a graph. Throwing away everything except what is connected to what is the single most important idea in this course.

What a graph is: A graph is a set of dots, called vertices (one vertex, many vertices), together with a set of lines, called edges, where each edge joins two vertices. That's it. The dots can stand for anything: people, cities, web pages, atoms, computers, exam subjects. The edges stand for a relationship between two of them: friends, a road, a link, a chemical bond, a cable, a clash in the timetable. Some books call vertices nodes and edges links or arcs. They mean the same things.

The notation: We write a graph as G = (V, E). V is the vertex set and E is the edge set. For example, take V = {a, b, c, d} and E = {ab, bc, cd, da}. Here ab is a short name for the edge joining a and b. If you draw this, you get a square: a joined to b, b to c, c to d, and d back to a. The number of vertices is called the order of the graph, written n or |V|. The number of edges is called the size, written m or |E|. Our square has order 4 and size 4.

A picture is not the graph: This surprises many students. The drawing is just one way to show the graph. You can draw the square as a square, as a diamond, or as a twisted bow tie where two lines cross, and it is still the same graph, because the same pairs are joined. Where you put the dots and whether lines are straight or curvy does not change anything. A crossing of two lines in a drawing is not a vertex. Only the listed dots are vertices.

Why we bother: Graphs turn very different problems into the same kind of problem. Finding the quickest way from Mirpur to Motijheel, deciding which exams can share a time slot, finding the best friend suggestions on Facebook, planning wires on a circuit board, and checking if a molecule can exist all become questions about dots and lines. Once you solve the dots-and-lines version, you have solved all of them at once. That is why graph theory shows up in computer networks, databases, compilers, artificial intelligence, chemistry, biology and even sports scheduling.

How graph theory differs from graph algorithms: You already met BFS, DFS, Dijkstra and Kruskal in the Algorithms course. Those are recipes a computer follows. Graph theory is the mathematics behind them. It asks questions like: Is this always true? Why does it work? How many are there? What is the smallest possible number? For example, an algorithm finds a spanning tree, but graph theory proves that every spanning tree of a graph with n vertices has exactly n - 1 edges. Theory tells you what is possible before you even write code.

Kinds of questions we will ask: Existence questions: Does this graph have a walk that uses every edge once? Can it be drawn with no crossing lines? Counting questions: How many different trees can you build on 5 labelled vertices? Optimisation questions: What is the fewest number of colours needed so that joined vertices get different colours? Structure questions: When are two graphs really the same graph in disguise? Each lesson of this course answers one family of these questions.

A tiny worked example: Let us model four friends: Rina, Sami, Tuli and Upol. Rina is friends with Sami and Tuli. Sami is friends with Tuli. Upol is friends with Tuli only. Vertices: R, S, T, U. Edges: RS, RT, ST, TU. Order 4, size 4. Now we can ask graph questions. Who has the most friends? Tuli, with 3 friends. Is there a group of three who are all friends with each other? Yes, R, S and T form a triangle. Can a message pass from Upol to Rina? Yes, through Tuli. Three real questions, all answered by looking at a tiny picture.

Directed and weighted, a first look: Sometimes a relationship goes one way only. On Facebook friendship works both ways, but on Instagram you can follow someone who does not follow you back. Then we draw edges as arrows, and the graph is called a directed graph or digraph. Sometimes each edge carries a number, like the distance in kilometres or the bus fare. That is a weighted graph. Lesson 2 will define all these kinds carefully.

Back to Konigsberg: Euler's reasoning, simple version: walk along the route and think about any piece of land that is not the start or end. Every time you enter it by one bridge, you must leave by another bridge. So bridges at that piece get used in pairs: in, out, in, out. That means such a piece needs an even number of bridges. In Konigsberg every one of the four pieces had an odd number of bridges (5, 3, 3 and 3). At most two pieces, the start and the end, are allowed to be odd. Four odd pieces is too many, so the walk is impossible. No trial and error needed, just counting.

The degree idea hiding inside: The number of edges touching a vertex is called its degree. Euler's proof is really about degrees. Count the degrees in Konigsberg: 5 + 3 + 3 + 3 = 14. And 14 is exactly twice the 7 bridges, because every bridge touches two pieces of land. This fact, that the degrees always add up to twice the number of edges, is the handshaking lemma. It is the first theorem of graph theory and we prove it properly in lesson 3.

A short history: After Euler in 1736, graph ideas popped up in many places. In the 1840s and 1850s Gustav Kirchhoff used them to study electrical circuits, and Arthur Cayley later used trees to count chemical molecules. In 1852 Francis Guthrie asked whether four colours are always enough to colour a map, a question that was only settled in 1976 with the help of a computer. The word graph in this sense was introduced by James Joseph Sylvester in 1878. The first textbook fully about graph theory, by Denes Konig, appeared in 1936. Today graph theory is one of the busiest areas of mathematics because computers made it so useful.

Course map, part one: First we learn the language: kinds of graphs, degrees, special families like complete graphs and cycles, subgraphs, matrices, and when two graphs are secretly the same (isomorphism). Then we study movement through a graph: walks, paths, distance, and how well connected a graph is, including cut vertices, bridges and Menger's theorem.

Course map, part two: Next come the famous tours: Euler tours that use every edge once and Hamilton cycles that visit every vertex once. Then trees, the simplest connected graphs, including a beautiful formula that counts them. After that, directed graphs and tournaments, then matchings, which pair things up, like students with projects.

Course map, part three: Finally we study drawing graphs without crossings (planar graphs and Euler's formula V - E + F = 2), colouring graphs (vertex colouring, the four colour theorem, edge colouring), and the surprising Ramsey theory, which says complete disorder is impossible in large enough graphs. The last lesson ties everything together.

Real-life example 1, Dhaka bus routes: Suppose you want to model the city bus network. Each bus stop is a vertex: Gabtoli, Farmgate, Shahbag, Motijheel and so on. Draw an edge between two stops if a bus goes directly from one to the next. Put the travel time in minutes on each edge, so the graph is weighted. Now real questions become graph questions. Is every stop reachable from every other? That is connectivity. What is the fastest route from Gabtoli to Motijheel? That is a shortest path. If the road at one stop is closed for repairs, does the network split into pieces? That is asking whether the stop is a cut vertex. One model, many answers.

Real-life example 2, exam timetable at a school: A school has six subjects. Some students take both Physics and Biology, so those two exams cannot be at the same time. Make each subject a vertex and draw an edge between two subjects that share a student. Now give each vertex a colour that stands for a time slot, with the rule that joined vertices get different colours. The fewest colours you need is the fewest time slots for the exam week. This is graph colouring, which we study in lessons 22 and 23. The head teacher never needs to hear the word graph, but the answer comes from graph theory.

How to study this course: Draw, draw, draw. Every definition becomes clear when you sketch a small example of 4 to 6 vertices. Before trying to prove a statement, test it on small graphs: a triangle, a square, a star, a complete graph on 4 vertices. Many exam questions ask you to check a theorem on a given graph, so practise counting vertices, edges and degrees quickly and carefully.

Common mistakes: Thinking the drawing is the graph, and so believing two different-looking pictures must be different graphs. Treating a crossing point of two lines as a vertex. Mixing up order (number of vertices) and size (number of edges). Forgetting that an edge always has two ends, which is why degrees add up to an even number. In exams, early questions are often: define graph, order and size; model a given situation as a graph; explain the Konigsberg problem and why it has no solution.

Recap: A graph G = (V, E) is a set of vertices plus a set of edges joining pairs of them. It keeps only who is connected to whom and throws away everything else. Euler created the subject in 1736 by solving the Konigsberg bridge problem with a degree argument. Graph theory asks existence, counting, optimisation and structure questions, and its answers power maps, networks, schedules and much more. Next lesson: all the basic words you need, and the different kinds of graphs.
key_points: A graph G = (V, E) is a set of vertices (dots) and a set of edges (lines), each edge joining two vertices.
The order of a graph is its number of vertices n, and the size is its number of edges m.
A drawing is only one picture of a graph; where the dots go and whether lines cross does not change the graph.
Euler solved the Konigsberg bridge problem in 1736: a walk using every bridge once was impossible because all four land pieces had odd degree.
The degree of a vertex is the number of edges touching it, and the degrees always add up to twice the number of edges.
Graph theory asks existence, counting, optimisation and structure questions; graph algorithms are the recipes that compute answers.
Real problems like bus networks, friendships and exam timetables become graph problems once you choose what the vertices and edges mean.
lessons.tip: Keep a rough notebook only for small graphs. Every time you meet a new word in this course, draw one example with 4 to 6 vertices next to it. Pictures you drew yourself are much easier to remember than definitions you read.
lessons.task: Draw the Konigsberg graph: 4 dots for the land pieces and 7 lines for the bridges (one piece has 5 bridges, the other three have 3 each). Write the degree beside each dot, add them up, and check the total is twice 7. Then add one new bridge between two odd pieces and see if a walk using every bridge once becomes possible.

quiz.q: A graph has V = {a, b, c, d, e} and E = {ab, bc, cd}. What are its order and size?
quiz.explain: Order counts vertices (5: a, b, c, d, e) and size counts edges (3: ab, bc, cd). Vertex e simply has no edges.

quiz.q: Two lines cross in the middle of a drawing of a graph. What is the crossing point?
options: Nothing, just part of the picture
quiz.explain: Only the listed vertices are vertices. A crossing in a drawing is not part of the graph itself.

quiz.q: Why was a walk crossing each Konigsberg bridge exactly once impossible?
options: There were exactly 7 bridges, an odd number
All four land pieces had an odd number of bridges, but at most two may be odd
quiz.explain: Middle stops of a walk use bridges in pairs, so they need even degree. Only the start and end may be odd, and Konigsberg had four odd pieces.

quiz.q: In the friends graph with edges RS, RT, ST, TU, which vertex has the largest degree?
quiz.explain: T touches RT, ST and TU, so its degree is 3. R and S have degree 2 and U has degree 1.

quiz.q: Which statement best describes the difference between graph theory and graph algorithms?
options: They are exactly the same thing
Graph theory proves facts about graphs; algorithms are step-by-step recipes for computing answers
Graph theory is only about drawing pictures
quiz.explain: Theory tells us what is true or possible, like every tree on n vertices having n - 1 edges; algorithms like BFS compute answers for a given graph.

lessons.title: Basic Terms and Kinds of Graphs
lessons.content:
When you join a new cricket team, the first week is all about learning words: crease, over, maiden, no-ball, LBW. Until you know the words, you cannot follow the game. Graph theory is the same. Today is vocabulary day. We will learn the words for parts of a graph and for the different kinds of graphs. They are simple words, but every later lesson uses them, so learn them well now and the rest of the course gets much easier.

Ends of an edge: Every edge has two ends, called its endpoints. If edge e joins vertices u and v, we write e = uv or e = {u, v}. We say u and v are adjacent, or neighbours, because an edge joins them directly. We say the edge e is incident to u and incident to v. So adjacency is a relation between two vertices, and incidence is a relation between a vertex and an edge. Two edges that share an endpoint are called adjacent edges.

A small running example: Take V = {a, b, c, d, e} and edges ab, ac, bc, cd. Here a and b are adjacent, but a and d are not, because no single edge joins them, even though you can travel a, c, d. Edge cd is incident to c and d. Edges ac and cd are adjacent edges because they share c. Vertex e has no edges at all. We will use this graph for the next few definitions.

Loops and multiple edges: Sometimes an edge starts and ends at the same vertex. That is a loop. Sometimes two or more edges join the same pair of vertices. Those are called multiple edges or parallel edges. In a road map, two different roads between the same two towns would be parallel edges. A loop might be a circular road that leaves a town and comes back to it.

Simple graphs, multigraphs and pseudographs: A simple graph has no loops and no multiple edges. Most of this course uses simple graphs, and when a book just says graph it usually means simple graph. A multigraph allows multiple edges. Some books also allow loops in a multigraph, while others call a graph with loops and multiple edges a pseudograph. Always check which convention your textbook uses. The Konigsberg graph is a multigraph, because some pairs of land pieces had two bridges between them.

Maximum edges in a simple graph: In a simple graph each pair of vertices has at most one edge. The number of pairs from n vertices is n(n - 1)/2. So a simple graph on n vertices has at most n(n - 1)/2 edges. With 5 vertices that is 5 x 4 / 2 = 10 edges. With 10 vertices it is 45 edges. A multigraph has no such limit, since you can keep adding parallel edges.

Directed graphs: In a directed graph, or digraph, each edge has a direction and is drawn as an arrow. A directed edge is often called an arc and written as an ordered pair (u, v), meaning it goes from u to v. Here u is the tail and v is the head. The arc (u, v) is different from (v, u). One-way streets in old Dhaka, Twitter follows, and which task must finish before which other task are all directed relationships. A graph with no directions is called undirected.

Weighted graphs: A weighted graph gives each edge a number called its weight. The weight can be a distance, a time, a cost, a capacity or anything else measurable. For example, an edge from Dhaka to Chattogram might have weight 250, standing for roughly 250 kilometres by road. Weights do not change which vertices are adjacent. They only add information on top of the graph. Graphs can be both directed and weighted at the same time.

Directed degree words, a preview: In a digraph we split the degree into two parts. The out-degree of v counts arrows leaving v, and the in-degree counts arrows arriving at v. On Instagram, your out-degree is how many accounts you follow and your in-degree is how many followers you have. A vertex with in-degree 0 is called a source, because things only flow out of it, and a vertex with out-degree 0 is called a sink. Lesson 3 shows how these numbers add up, and lesson 17 studies digraphs in detail.

Neighbourhood: The open neighbourhood of a vertex v, written N(v), is the set of all vertices adjacent to v. In our running example, N(c) = {a, b, d}, N(a) = {b, c}, and N(e) is the empty set. The closed neighbourhood N[v] is N(v) plus v itself, so N[c] = {a, b, c, d}. Social media friend lists are exactly neighbourhoods: your friend list is N(you).

Degree: The degree of a vertex v, written deg(v) or d(v), is the number of edges incident to v. In a simple graph this equals the number of neighbours, |N(v)|. In our example: deg(a) = 2, deg(b) = 2, deg(c) = 3, deg(d) = 1, deg(e) = 0. Add them: 2 + 2 + 3 + 1 + 0 = 8, which is twice the 4 edges. That is the handshaking lemma again, coming in lesson 3.

Degree with loops: In a graph with loops, a loop adds 2 to the degree of its vertex, because both ends of the loop touch that vertex. So a vertex with one loop and one ordinary edge has degree 3. This rule keeps the handshaking lemma true for every graph: each edge, loop or not, adds exactly 2 to the total degree.

Isolated and pendant vertices: A vertex of degree 0 is called isolated. It sits alone, like vertex e in our example. A vertex of degree 1 is called pendant, or a leaf, like vertex d. The single edge at a pendant vertex is called a pendant edge. Leaves will be very important when we study trees, because every tree with at least two vertices has at least two leaves.

Minimum and maximum degree: The smallest degree in the graph is written delta(G), with a small Greek delta, and the largest is written Delta(G), with a capital delta. In our example the minimum degree is 0 (vertex e) and the maximum degree is 3 (vertex c). In a simple graph on n vertices, every degree is between 0 and n - 1, since a vertex can be joined to at most all the other n - 1 vertices.

Regular graphs: A graph is k-regular if every vertex has degree exactly k. A triangle is 2-regular, since each corner touches two edges. A cube's skeleton, with 8 corners and 12 edges, is 3-regular. A 3-regular graph is also called cubic. If a k-regular graph has n vertices, then the total degree is nk, so the number of edges is nk/2. That means nk must be even. Example: a 3-regular graph on 5 vertices would need 15/2 edges, which is impossible, so no such graph exists.

Null and trivial graphs: A graph with vertices but no edges at all is called a null graph or empty graph, written N_n or sometimes with a bar over K_n. Every vertex in it is isolated, so it is 0-regular. The graph with exactly one vertex and no edges is called the trivial graph. It sounds silly, but it is the starting case of many induction proofs, like the first domino in a row.

Finite and infinite graphs: In this course every graph is finite, meaning V and E are finite sets. Infinite graphs exist, like the grid of all integer points in the plane with each point joined to its four neighbours, but they need different tools. When a theorem says graph, assume finite unless told otherwise.

Labelled and unlabelled graphs: If the vertices have names that matter, like a, b, c, the graph is labelled. If we only care about the shape, it is unlabelled. On three labelled vertices a, b, c, there are 8 possible simple graphs, because each of the 3 possible edges is either present or absent, giving 2 x 2 x 2 = 8. But up to shape there are only 4: no edges, one edge, two edges forming a path, and the triangle. This difference matters a lot when we count graphs and trees later.

Putting the words together: Describe this graph in full sentences: vertices p, q, r, s, edges pq, pq again, qr, and a loop at s. It is not simple, because pq appears twice (parallel edges) and s has a loop, so it is a pseudograph in the books that use that word. deg(p) = 2, deg(q) = 3, deg(r) = 1, deg(s) = 2 because of the loop. Total 8, which is twice the 4 edges. r is pendant, nothing is isolated, delta = 1 and Delta = 3. Being able to read a graph like this, word by word, is the skill exams check first.

Real-life example 1, a Pathao rider network: Think of riders and restaurants in Dhanmondi. Make each place a vertex and draw an edge when a rider can go directly from one place to the other in under 10 minutes. Add weights equal to the travel time. A restaurant with degree 0 is isolated, which means no rider can quickly reach it, so the company might place an extra rider nearby. A place with very high degree is a hub. The maximum degree tells the busiest hub, and the neighbourhood of a restaurant lists the places reachable within 10 minutes.

Real-life example 2, a class WhatsApp group versus a follower network: In a class group everyone can message everyone, so as a graph every pair of students is joined: a simple, undirected graph where each of n students has degree n - 1. It is (n - 1)-regular. Now think of a YouTube channel network where people subscribe to channels. Subscribing is one-way, so this is a directed graph. A popular Bangladeshi cooking channel might have a huge number of arrows coming in but few going out. Same people, different relationship, different kind of graph.

Common mistakes: Saying two vertices are adjacent just because you can travel between them. Adjacent means joined by one edge directly. Counting a loop as adding 1 to the degree instead of 2. Forgetting that a simple graph has no loops and no parallel edges. Mixing up delta (minimum) and Delta (maximum). Trying to build a k-regular graph with nk odd, which can never work. Exams often give a drawing and ask: list the neighbourhood of a vertex, find all degrees, minimum and maximum degree, identify isolated and pendant vertices, and decide if the graph is simple or regular.

Recap: Adjacent means joined by an edge; incident means an edge touches a vertex. Simple graphs have no loops and no parallel edges, and at most n(n - 1)/2 edges. Digraphs have arrows, weighted graphs have numbers on edges. N(v) is the set of neighbours, deg(v) counts incident edges with loops counted twice, and delta and Delta are the minimum and maximum degree. k-regular means every degree is k, which needs nk even. Next lesson: degrees in depth, the handshaking lemma, and which lists of numbers can be degree lists.
key_points: Two vertices are adjacent if one edge joins them; an edge is incident to its two endpoints.
A simple graph has no loops and no multiple edges and has at most n(n - 1)/2 edges; multigraphs allow parallel edges.
In a digraph each arc (u, v) goes from tail u to head v; in a weighted graph each edge carries a number.
N(v) is the set of neighbours of v, and N[v] also includes v itself.
deg(v) counts edges at v, with a loop counted twice; degree 0 means isolated, degree 1 means pendant (leaf).
delta(G) is the minimum degree and Delta(G) the maximum; in a simple graph every degree lies between 0 and n - 1.
A k-regular graph has every degree equal to k and exactly nk/2 edges, so nk must be even.
On 3 labelled vertices there are 8 simple graphs, but only 4 different shapes.
lessons.tip: Make a one-page glossary with a tiny drawing next to each word: adjacent, incident, loop, parallel edges, simple, digraph, weighted, neighbourhood, degree, isolated, pendant, regular. Revise it before every class this month.
lessons.task: Draw the graph with vertices 1 to 6 and edges 12, 13, 23, 34, 45, 46, 56. Write N(v) and deg(v) for every vertex, find delta and Delta, list any pendant or isolated vertices, and check that the degrees add up to twice the number of edges.

quiz.q: A vertex has one loop and two ordinary edges. What is its degree?
quiz.explain: A loop adds 2 to the degree because both of its ends touch the vertex, so 2 + 1 + 1 = 4.

quiz.q: What is the largest number of edges a simple graph on 6 vertices can have?
quiz.explain: Each pair of vertices can have at most one edge, and there are 6 x 5 / 2 = 15 pairs.

quiz.q: Can a 3-regular graph on 7 vertices exist?
options: Yes, but only as a multigraph
No, because 7 x 3 = 21 is odd and the edge count would be 10.5
quiz.explain: A k-regular graph on n vertices has nk/2 edges, so nk must be even. 21 is odd, so it is impossible.

quiz.q: In a graph with edges ab, ac, bc, cd, what is N(c)?
quiz.explain: The open neighbourhood lists vertices joined to c by an edge: a, b and d. The closed neighbourhood would also include c.

quiz.q: Which statement about the arc (u, v) in a digraph is correct?
options: u is the tail and v is the head; it is different from (v, u)
It is the same as (v, u)
u and v must have equal degree
quiz.explain: Arcs are ordered pairs. (u, v) goes from u to v, and the reverse arc (v, u) is a different arc.

lessons.title: Degrees and Degree Sequences
lessons.content:
At a wedding reception in Dhaka, guests keep shaking hands. Your little cousin, bored, decides to ask every guest: how many hands did you shake? She writes all the numbers on a napkin and adds them up. Here is a prediction you can make without seeing the napkin: the total will be an even number. Always. Not because of luck, but because every handshake has exactly two hands in it. This tiny idea is the first real theorem of graph theory, and today we squeeze a surprising amount out of it.

The handshaking lemma: In any graph, the sum of all the degrees equals twice the number of edges. In symbols: the sum of deg(v) over all vertices v equals 2m, where m is the number of edges. It works for simple graphs, multigraphs and graphs with loops, as long as each loop counts 2 toward the degree of its vertex.

Proof by double counting: Count the edge-ends. Each edge has exactly two ends, so the total number of edge-ends is 2m. Now count the same edge-ends a different way: go vertex by vertex and count how many edge-ends sit at each vertex. That number is exactly deg(v). Adding over all vertices gives the sum of degrees. We counted the same set of things twice, so the two answers must be equal. This style of argument, counting one thing in two ways, is called double counting, and it is one of the most useful tools in the whole course.

Quick checks with the lemma: A graph has degrees 3, 3, 2, 2, 1, 1. The sum is 12, so it has 12 / 2 = 6 edges. A 4-regular graph on 10 vertices has total degree 40, so 20 edges. If someone tells you a graph has degrees 3, 3, 3, 2, 2, the sum is 13, which is odd, so they made a mistake: no such graph exists. The lemma is the fastest error check in graph theory.

Corollary, odd vertices come in pairs: Call a vertex odd if its degree is odd and even if its degree is even. In every graph, the number of odd vertices is even. Proof: the total degree is even (it is 2m). The even vertices contribute an even amount. So the odd vertices must also add up to an even number. A sum of odd numbers is even only when there is an even count of them. So there are 0, 2, 4, ... odd vertices, never 1 or 3 or 5. At the wedding, the number of guests who shook an odd number of hands is even.

Edges from regularity: If a graph is k-regular with n vertices, then nk = 2m, so m = nk/2. The Petersen graph, which we meet next lesson, is 3-regular on 10 vertices, so it has 15 edges. A cubic graph must have an even number of vertices, since 3n must be even. These small facts come straight from the lemma.

Digraph version: In a directed graph each arc has one tail and one head. Each arc adds 1 to the out-degree of its tail and 1 to the in-degree of its head. So the sum of all out-degrees equals the number of arcs m, and so does the sum of all in-degrees. Example: three arcs a to b, b to c, a to c. Out-degrees: a 2, b 1, c 0, total 3. In-degrees: a 0, b 1, c 2, total 3. Both equal m = 3.

Average degree: The average degree of a graph is (sum of degrees) / n = 2m / n. So a graph with 10 vertices and 15 edges has average degree 3. Since the average lies between the smallest and largest value, delta is at most 2m/n, which is at most Delta. If a graph has more edges than vertices, the average degree is above 2, so some vertex has degree at least 3. Facts like this are used inside many proofs later.

Degree sequence: The degree sequence of a graph is the list of its degrees, usually written in non-increasing order (biggest first). The square a, b, c, d has degree sequence (2, 2, 2, 2). The star with one centre and four leaves has (4, 1, 1, 1, 1). Different graphs can share the same degree sequence. For example a 6-cycle and two separate triangles both have (2, 2, 2, 2, 2, 2), yet one is connected and the other is not. So the degree sequence does not determine the graph.

Graphic sequences: A list of non-negative whole numbers is called graphic if some simple graph has exactly that list as its degree sequence. Two easy necessary conditions: the sum must be even (handshaking), and no number may exceed n - 1, where n is the length of the list. But these two are not enough. Look at (3, 3, 3, 1). The sum is 10, even, and no entry is bigger than 3. Yet it is not graphic: three vertices of degree 3 in a 4-vertex simple graph must each be joined to all three other vertices, which would give the fourth vertex degree 3, not 1.

The Havel-Hakimi idea: Havel (1955) and Hakimi (1962) gave a simple test. Take the largest degree d1. Remove it, and subtract 1 from the next d1 largest entries. The original list is graphic exactly when the new, shorter list is graphic. Repeat. If you ever get a negative number, or there are not enough entries to subtract from, the list is not graphic. If you reach all zeros, it is graphic. The idea behind it: the vertex with the largest degree can always be joined to the vertices with the next largest degrees.

Havel-Hakimi worked example 1: Test (3, 3, 2, 2, 2). Remove 3 and subtract 1 from the next three: (2, 1, 1, 2). Re-sort: (2, 2, 1, 1). Remove 2 and subtract from the next two: (1, 0, 1). Re-sort: (1, 1, 0). Remove 1 and subtract from the next one: (0, 0). All zeros, so the list is graphic. Remember to re-sort after each step, or the test can go wrong.

Building the graph from the steps: You can run Havel-Hakimi backwards to actually draw a graph. For (3, 3, 2, 2, 2) name the vertices A(3), B(3), C(2), D(2), E(2). Step 1 joined A to B, C, D. Then B, needing 2 more, was joined to the next two biggest, E and C. Finally D, needing 1 more, was joined to E. Edges: AB, AC, AD, BE, BC, DE. Check degrees: A 3, B 3, C 2, D 2, E 2. Six edges, sum 12. It works.

Havel-Hakimi worked example 2: Test (4, 4, 4, 1, 1). Sum 14, even, and no entry exceeds 4. Remove 4 and subtract from the next four: (3, 3, 0, 0). Remove 3 and subtract from the next three: (2, -1, -1). A negative number appears, so the list is not graphic. Intuition: three vertices need degree 4 in a 5-vertex graph, so each must touch everyone, which would force the last two vertices to have degree at least 3.

The Erdos-Gallai theorem: A second test, proved by Paul Erdos and Tibor Gallai in 1960. A non-increasing list d1, d2, ..., dn with an even sum is graphic if and only if, for every k from 1 to n, the sum of the first k entries is at most k(k - 1) plus the sum of min(di, k) over the remaining entries. Meaning: the k biggest vertices can use at most k(k - 1) degree among themselves, and each other vertex can help them by at most min(its degree, k). For exams, Havel-Hakimi is usually easier to apply by hand.

Multigraphs are easier: If parallel edges are allowed but not loops, a list is a degree sequence exactly when the sum is even and the largest entry is at most the sum of all the others. If loops are allowed too, an even sum is the only condition. So (3, 3, 3, 1) is impossible as a simple graph but fine as a multigraph.

The party puzzle: In any group of two or more people, at least two people have the same number of friends inside the group. Proof: with n people, each friend count is between 0 and n - 1, which is n possible values. But 0 and n - 1 cannot both appear: if someone is friends with everybody, nobody has zero friends. So the n people really share at most n - 1 values, and by the pigeonhole principle two of them share a value. In graph words: every simple graph with at least 2 vertices has two vertices of equal degree.

Real-life example 1, checking a survey: A university club surveys 7 members: how many other members do you study with? Answers: 4, 3, 3, 2, 2, 1, 2. The sum is 17, which is odd. Since studying together is a two-way relationship, the sum must be even, so at least one answer is wrong. The club secretary can spot the error without asking anyone again. Data analysts use exactly this kind of consistency check on network data.

Real-life example 2, a mobile network design: A telecom engineer in Sylhet wants 6 towers where each tower links directly to exactly 3 others, for backup. Is it possible? Total degree 18, so 9 links. The list (3, 3, 3, 3, 3, 3) passes Havel-Hakimi: remove 3, get (2, 2, 2, 3, 3), re-sort (3, 3, 2, 2, 2), which we showed is graphic. One such design is the triangular prism: two triangles with matching corners joined. With 7 towers each linked to exactly 3 others, the total would be 21, odd, so the engineer knows instantly it cannot be done.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Forgetting that each loop adds 2. Forgetting to re-sort in Havel-Hakimi. Believing that even sum plus max at most n - 1 is enough for graphic. Thinking a degree sequence fixes the graph. Exams ask: prove the handshaking lemma; prove the number of odd vertices is even; find the number of edges from given degrees; test sequences with Havel-Hakimi and draw a graph if graphic; prove the party puzzle.

Recap: The degrees always add up to 2m, because each edge has two ends. So odd-degree vertices come in an even number, a k-regular graph has nk/2 edges, and in a digraph in-degrees and out-degrees each add up to m. A degree sequence lists degrees biggest first; it is graphic if a simple graph realises it. Test with Havel-Hakimi (remove the biggest, subtract, re-sort, repeat) or Erdos-Gallai. Every simple graph with 2 or more vertices has two vertices of equal degree. Next lesson: the special families of graphs that show up everywhere.
key_points: Handshaking lemma: the sum of all degrees equals 2m, proved by counting edge-ends in two ways.
Every graph has an even number of odd-degree vertices.
In a digraph the sum of in-degrees and the sum of out-degrees both equal the number of arcs.
Average degree is 2m/n, so delta <= 2m/n <= Delta.
A degree sequence is graphic if some simple graph has it; even sum and max <= n - 1 are necessary but not sufficient.
Havel-Hakimi: remove the largest d, subtract 1 from the next d entries, re-sort, repeat; a negative entry means not graphic, all zeros means graphic.
Erdos-Gallai gives an exact inequality test; for multigraphs without loops the test is even sum and largest <= sum of the rest.
Every simple graph with at least two vertices has two vertices of the same degree (pigeonhole).
lessons.tip: Whenever a question gives you degrees, add them first. If the sum is odd, the answer is already 'impossible' and you save time. If it is even, divide by 2 to get the edge count and keep it as a check for your drawing.
lessons.task: Use Havel-Hakimi on (4, 3, 3, 2, 2, 2) and on (5, 5, 4, 3, 2, 1). For each one that is graphic, draw a simple graph with that degree sequence and count its edges to check against the handshaking lemma.

quiz.q: A graph has degree sequence (4, 3, 3, 2, 2). How many edges does it have?
quiz.explain: The sum of degrees is 14, and by the handshaking lemma that is 2m, so m = 7.

quiz.q: Which number of odd-degree vertices is impossible in a graph?
quiz.explain: The number of odd-degree vertices is always even, because the total degree 2m is even.

quiz.q: Why is (3, 3, 3, 1) not graphic, even though its sum is even?
options: Three vertices of degree 3 among 4 vertices must touch everyone, forcing the last vertex to degree 3
quiz.explain: In a simple 4-vertex graph degree 3 means joined to all others, so the fourth vertex would have degree 3, not 1. Havel-Hakimi gives (2, 2, 0) then a negative entry.

quiz.q: In a digraph with 9 arcs, what is the sum of all in-degrees?
quiz.explain: Each arc adds exactly 1 to the in-degree of its head, so in-degrees add up to the number of arcs, 9.

quiz.q: What does the party puzzle say for any simple graph with at least 2 vertices?
options: Two vertices have the same degree
quiz.explain: Degrees lie in 0..n-1 but 0 and n-1 cannot both occur, so n vertices share at most n-1 values and two must match.

lessons.title: Special Graph Families
lessons.content:
In a zoo, you don't learn every animal from scratch. You first learn families: cats, birds, snakes. Once you know the cat family, a tiger or a leopard is easy to understand. Graph theory also has families of graphs that keep showing up again and again: paths, cycles, complete graphs, wheels, stars, complete bipartite graphs, cubes, and one famous troublemaker called the Petersen graph. Today we meet each family, learn its name, draw it, and count its vertices, edges and degrees. These are the test cases you will use to check every theorem in the rest of the course.

Path graphs: The path P_n is n vertices in a row, each joined to the next: v1 - v2 - v3 - ... - vn. It has n vertices and n - 1 edges. The two end vertices have degree 1 and all inner vertices have degree 2. P_4 looks like a short line of four dots. Warning: some books name a path by its number of edges instead, so their P_3 has 4 vertices. Always check how your teacher defines it. In this course P_n has n vertices.

Cycle graphs: The cycle C_n, for n at least 3, is a path whose two ends are also joined, closing a ring: v1 - v2 - ... - vn - v1. It has n vertices and n edges, and it is 2-regular. C_3 is a triangle, C_4 is a square, C_5 is a pentagon. We need n at least 3 because in a simple graph you cannot make a ring with only two dots. A cycle is called odd or even by its length, and this will matter a lot in lesson 11, where odd cycles are exactly what stop a graph from being bipartite.

Complete graphs: The complete graph K_n has n vertices with every pair joined by an edge. Each vertex is joined to all n - 1 others, so K_n is (n - 1)-regular. By handshaking it has n(n - 1)/2 edges, which is the largest possible number for a simple graph. K_1 is a single dot, K_2 is one edge, K_3 is a triangle, K_4 looks like a square with both diagonals, and K_5 is a pentagon with a five-pointed star inside. Counting: K_10 has 45 edges, K_20 has 190 edges.

K_n as handshakes: If n people at a meeting all shake hands once with each other, the number of handshakes is n(n - 1)/2, exactly the edges of K_n. Eleven players in a cricket team high-fiving each other once give 11 x 10 / 2 = 55 high-fives. Whenever a problem says every pair, think of K_n.

Null graphs, the opposite: The null graph on n vertices has no edges. It is the complement of K_n: what you get if you remove every edge of K_n. We will define complements properly in lesson 5, but the idea is simple: K_n has everything, the null graph has nothing.

Wheel graphs: Take a cycle and add one new vertex in the middle, called the hub, joined to every vertex on the cycle. That is a wheel, like a bicycle wheel with spokes. With a rim of n vertices, the wheel has n + 1 vertices and 2n edges: n rim edges plus n spokes. The hub has degree n and every rim vertex has degree 3. Books differ: some call this W_n and others call it W_(n+1), counting all vertices. Example: a rim of 5 gives 6 vertices and 10 edges.

Bipartite graphs, a first look: A graph is bipartite if its vertices can be split into two groups, say X and Y, so that every edge goes between X and Y and no edge stays inside one group. Think of a graph of students and clubs, with an edge when a student joins a club. A student never joins a student, and a club never joins a club. Lesson 11 studies bipartite graphs deeply.

Complete bipartite graphs: K_(m,n) has a group X of m vertices and a group Y of n vertices, with every vertex of X joined to every vertex of Y, and no edges inside X or inside Y. It has m + n vertices and m x n edges. Vertices in X have degree n and vertices in Y have degree m. K_(3,3) has 6 vertices and 9 edges, and it is the famous utility graph from the puzzle of joining three houses to gas, water and electricity without crossing pipes. We prove in lesson 20 that it cannot be done.

Star graphs: The star K_(1,n) is a complete bipartite graph with one centre joined to n leaves. It has n + 1 vertices and n edges. The centre has degree n and the leaves have degree 1. A star is what a network looks like when every computer connects only to one central switch. It is also a tree, because it is connected with no cycles.

Hypercube graphs: The n-dimensional cube Q_n has one vertex for each binary string of length n, and two vertices are adjacent when their strings differ in exactly one bit. Q_1 is one edge, 0 - 1. Q_2 is a square: 00, 01, 11, 10. Q_3 is the skeleton of an ordinary cube with corners 000 to 111. Q_n has 2^n vertices. Each string has n bits you could flip, so Q_n is n-regular, and by handshaking it has n x 2^n / 2 = n x 2^(n - 1) edges. Q_3 has 8 vertices and 12 edges, Q_4 has 16 vertices and 32 edges.

Building cubes from smaller cubes: Q_n can be built from two copies of Q_(n-1). Put a 0 in front of every label in the first copy and a 1 in front of every label in the second, then join each vertex to its twin in the other copy. For Q_3: one square with labels 000, 001, 011, 010 and another with 100, 101, 111, 110, plus four edges joining twins. This recursive picture is how some parallel computers and network designs connect processors, since any two processors are at most n steps apart.

Hypercubes are bipartite: Split the strings into those with an even number of 1s and those with an odd number of 1s. Flipping one bit always changes the count of 1s by one, so every edge joins an even string to an odd string. So Q_n is bipartite with two equal groups of 2^(n - 1) vertices.

The Petersen graph: Draw an outer pentagon (a 5-cycle) and an inner five-pointed star (another 5-cycle drawn as a pentagram). Join each outer corner to the matching inner point. The result has 10 vertices and 15 edges and is 3-regular. It is named after the Danish mathematician Julius Petersen, who described it in 1898. Its shortest cycle has length 5, it is not planar, and it has no Hamilton cycle. Whenever someone guesses a general rule about graphs, people test it on the Petersen graph first, because it breaks so many guesses. You will meet it again in several lessons.

Grid graphs: The grid graph has vertices at the points of an r by c grid, with edges between horizontal and vertical neighbours. A 3 by 3 grid has 9 vertices and 12 edges: each of the 3 rows has 2 horizontal edges, which is 6, and each of the 3 columns has 2 vertical edges, another 6. Grids model city blocks, chessboards and pixels in an image.

Prisms and ladders: Take two copies of the cycle C_n and join each vertex to its twin in the other copy. The result is the prism graph, the skeleton of a prism shape. It has 2n vertices, n + n + n = 3n edges, and it is 3-regular. The triangular prism (n = 3) has 6 vertices and 9 edges, and the prism with n = 4 is exactly the cube Q_3. If you use two paths instead of two cycles, you get a ladder graph, which looks just like a real ladder: two rails and rungs between them. A ladder made from two copies of P_n has 2n vertices and 3n - 2 edges.

A counting table to remember: P_n: n vertices, n - 1 edges. C_n: n vertices, n edges, 2-regular. K_n: n vertices, n(n - 1)/2 edges, (n - 1)-regular. K_(m,n): m + n vertices, mn edges. Star K_(1,n): n + 1 vertices, n edges. Wheel with rim n: n + 1 vertices, 2n edges. Q_n: 2^n vertices, n x 2^(n - 1) edges, n-regular. Petersen: 10 vertices, 15 edges, 3-regular. You can check each line with the handshaking lemma: for example K_(m,n) has total degree m x n + n x m = 2mn, and 2mn / 2 = mn.

Families hiding inside each other: Many families overlap, and noticing it saves work. K_3 and C_3 are the same graph, the triangle. K_(1,1) is just K_2, a single edge. K_(2,2) is the same as C_4, a square, which is also Q_2. A wheel with a rim of 3 is K_4, since the hub and the three rim vertices are all joined. A star K_(1,n) is a tree, and every path is a tree too. When an exam asks whether some graph is regular, bipartite or complete, first check whether it is secretly a member of a family you already know.

Real-life example 1, Dhaka Metro and rail lines: A single metro line with stations in a row is a path graph: each middle station joins the one before and the one after. A circular line, like a ring road with bus stops all around it, is a cycle. If the city adds a central interchange connected to every ring stop, the network becomes a wheel, and the interchange's degree equals the number of ring stops. City planners use these shapes as building blocks when they design transport.

Real-life example 2, a cricket tournament: In a single round-robin tournament every team plays every other team once. With 10 teams, the matches are the edges of K_10, so there are 45 matches. In a series between two countries' squads where each of 4 Bangladeshi bowlers bowls to each of 5 visiting batsmen in the nets, the pairings form K_(4,5), giving 20 bowler-batsman pairs. Same counting ideas, two familiar settings.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Mixing up the path naming (vertices vs edges) and wheel naming conventions. Forgetting C_n needs n at least 3. Writing K_(m,n) edges as m + n instead of mn. Thinking Q_n has n vertices instead of 2^n. Exams ask you to draw K_5, K_(2,3), W_5, Q_3 and the Petersen graph; to compute vertices, edges and degrees for each family; to prove the edge formula for K_n or Q_n with the handshaking lemma; and to say which families are regular or bipartite.

Recap: Paths and cycles are the simplest families, complete graphs K_n have every possible edge, complete bipartite graphs K_(m,n) join two groups completely, stars are K_(1,n), wheels add a hub to a cycle, hypercubes Q_n join binary strings that differ in one bit, and the Petersen graph is the classic counterexample. Their edge counts all follow from the handshaking lemma. Next lesson: how to cut pieces out of graphs and glue graphs together.
key_points: P_n has n vertices and n - 1 edges; C_n (n >= 3) has n vertices and n edges and is 2-regular.
K_n joins every pair, is (n - 1)-regular, and has n(n - 1)/2 edges, the maximum for a simple graph.
K_(m,n) has m + n vertices and mn edges; the star K_(1,n) is the special case with one centre.
A wheel with a rim of n vertices has n + 1 vertices and 2n edges; naming conventions differ between books.
Q_n has 2^n vertices (binary strings), is n-regular, has n x 2^(n - 1) edges, and is bipartite by parity of 1s.
The Petersen graph has 10 vertices, 15 edges, is 3-regular, has shortest cycle 5, is non-planar and non-Hamiltonian.
Every edge formula can be checked with the handshaking lemma.
lessons.tip: Draw each family in the same corner of your notes every time you revise: P_5, C_5, K_5, K_(2,3), a wheel with rim 5, Q_3 and the Petersen graph. After a week you can draw all seven in two minutes, and they become your personal test kit for every theorem.
lessons.task: Draw Q_3 with all 8 binary labels. Check that every vertex has degree 3 and count the 12 edges. Then colour vertices with an even number of 1s red and the rest blue, and confirm every edge joins a red vertex to a blue one.

quiz.q: How many edges does K_8 have?
quiz.explain: K_n has n(n - 1)/2 edges, so 8 x 7 / 2 = 28.

quiz.q: How many vertices and edges does Q_4 have?
quiz.explain: Q_n has 2^n vertices and n x 2^(n - 1) edges: 16 vertices and 4 x 8 = 32 edges.

quiz.q: How many edges does K_(4,6) have?
quiz.explain: Every one of the 4 vertices in one group is joined to every one of the 6 in the other, giving 4 x 6 = 24 edges.

quiz.q: Which statement about the Petersen graph is true?
options: It is 3-regular with 10 vertices and 15 edges
quiz.explain: The Petersen graph has 10 vertices, each of degree 3, so 10 x 3 / 2 = 15 edges. It has many cycles, so it is not a tree.

quiz.q: A wheel has a rim (cycle) of 7 vertices plus a hub. How many edges does it have?
quiz.explain: There are 7 rim edges and 7 spokes from the hub, giving 2 x 7 = 14 edges.

lessons.title: Subgraphs and Graph Operations
lessons.content:
Think of a big Lego city. You can pull out one house and study it alone. You can remove one road and see what breaks. You can snap two small towns together into a bigger one. Graphs work the same way. Today we learn how to take pieces out of a graph (subgraphs), how to remove vertices and edges, how to flip a graph inside out (the complement), and how to glue graphs together in several clever ways (union, join, product, line graph). These operations are the toolbox for almost every proof later in the course.

Subgraph: A graph H is a subgraph of G if every vertex of H is a vertex of G and every edge of H is an edge of G. We write H is contained in G. One rule: you may only keep an edge if you also keep both of its endpoints, because an edge without ends makes no sense. Example: G is the square a, b, c, d with edges ab, bc, cd, da. Then H with vertices a, b, c and edges ab, bc is a subgraph. So is the single vertex d with no edges. So is G itself.

Spanning subgraph: A subgraph that keeps all the vertices of G, but maybe fewer edges, is called a spanning subgraph. From the square, keeping all four vertices but only edges ab, bc, cd gives a spanning subgraph that is a path. Since each edge can be kept or dropped independently, a graph with m edges has exactly 2^m spanning subgraphs. The square has 2^4 = 16. Spanning trees, a special kind of spanning subgraph, get their own lessons later.

Induced subgraph: Choose a set S of vertices and keep every edge of G that has both ends in S. The result is the subgraph induced by S, written G[S]. You do not get to choose the edges; they come automatically. In the square, G[{a, b, c}] has edges ab and bc. There is no edge ac in G, so none in G[S]. In K_5, every induced subgraph on k vertices is K_k, because all pairs are joined. Induced means 'take these people and all the friendships among them'.

The difference in one example: In the square, the subgraph with vertices a, b, c and only the edge ab is a subgraph but not an induced subgraph, because it left out the edge bc even though both b and c were kept. Every induced subgraph is a subgraph, but not every subgraph is induced. Exam questions love this difference.

Deleting a vertex: G - v means remove vertex v and every edge incident to it. In the square, G - a leaves b, c, d with edges bc and cd, a path. Deleting a vertex of degree d removes exactly d edges. G - v is the same as the induced subgraph on all vertices except v. Deleting a set S of vertices, G - S, removes them all with their edges.

Deleting an edge: G - e means remove just the edge e and keep all vertices, including both endpoints. In the square, G - ab gives the path a - d - c - b. Vertex deletion and edge deletion behave very differently: removing an edge never removes a vertex, but removing a vertex can remove many edges at once. When we study connectivity in lessons 9 and 10, we will ask which deletions break a graph into pieces.

Adding edges: G + e means add a new edge e between two existing vertices that were not adjacent. Adding edges is used in proofs like Ore's theorem in lesson 13, where we imagine adding edges one by one to a graph until it becomes complete, and watch what stays true.

Complement: The complement of a simple graph G, written G-bar, has the same vertices as G, and two vertices are adjacent in G-bar exactly when they are not adjacent in G. You flip every pair: edges become non-edges and non-edges become edges. If G has n vertices and m edges, then G-bar has n(n - 1)/2 - m edges, because together they make K_n. Each vertex v has degree n - 1 - deg(v) in the complement.

Complement examples: The complement of K_n is the null graph. The complement of K_(m,n) is two separate complete graphs K_m and K_n, because inside each group nothing was joined, and between groups everything was. The complement of the square C_4 is two separate edges: a was joined to b and d, so in the complement a is joined only to c, and similarly b to d.

Self-complementary graphs: Some graphs are isomorphic to their own complement; they have the same shape after flipping. The path P_4 is one: a - b - c - d has complement with edges ac, bd, ad, which forms the path c - a - d - b. The 5-cycle C_5 is another: its complement is also a 5-cycle, the star pentagram inside the pentagon. A self-complementary graph on n vertices must have exactly half of the n(n - 1)/2 possible edges, so n(n - 1)/4 must be a whole number. That happens only when n leaves remainder 0 or 1 when divided by 4. So there is no self-complementary graph on 6 or 7 vertices.

Union and intersection: For graphs G1 and G2, the union G1 union G2 has all vertices and all edges from both. The intersection keeps only the vertices and edges they share. If G1 and G2 have no vertices in common, their union is called a disjoint union and simply puts them side by side. Two triangles side by side are the disjoint union of two copies of K_3, written 2K_3. A graph that is not connected is the disjoint union of its pieces.

Join: The join G1 + G2 takes the disjoint union of G1 and G2 and then adds every edge between a vertex of G1 and a vertex of G2. Joining two null graphs with m and n vertices gives the complete bipartite graph K_(m,n). Joining a cycle C_n with a single vertex K_1 gives the wheel. Joining K_m and K_n gives K_(m+n). So many families from lesson 4 are just joins of simpler pieces.

Cartesian product: The product G box H has one vertex for every pair (g, h), with g from G and h from H. Two pairs are adjacent if they agree in one coordinate and are adjacent in the other: same g and h adjacent to h', or same h and g adjacent to g'. Picture it as placing a copy of H at every vertex of G and joining matching vertices of neighbouring copies. The grid graph is P_r box P_c. The prism is C_n box K_2. The hypercube Q_n is Q_(n-1) box K_2, matching the two-copies construction from lesson 4.

Counting in a product: If G has n1 vertices and m1 edges and H has n2 vertices and m2 edges, then G box H has n1 x n2 vertices and n1 x m2 + n2 x m1 edges. Check with Q_3 = C_4 box K_2: vertices 4 x 2 = 8, edges 4 x 1 + 2 x 4 = 12. Correct. For the 3 by 3 grid P_3 box P_3: vertices 9, edges 3 x 2 + 3 x 2 = 12, matching our count from lesson 4.

Line graph: The line graph L(G) has one vertex for each edge of G, and two of these are adjacent when the original edges share an endpoint. It turns edges into vertices. L(P_4) is P_3, because P_4 has 3 edges in a row. L(C_n) is C_n again. L(K_(1,3)), a star with 3 edges all meeting at the centre, is K_3, because all three edges touch each other. Line graphs are useful because problems about edges, like edge colouring in lesson 24, become problems about vertices of L(G).

Counting edges of a line graph: Every vertex v of G with degree d has d edges meeting at it, and each pair of them gives one edge in L(G). So L(G) has the sum over all v of d(d - 1)/2 edges. For K_4, every vertex has degree 3, giving 3 pairs each, so L(K_4) has 4 x 3 = 12 edges on 6 vertices. It is 4-regular.

Edge contraction: Contracting an edge e = uv, written G / e, merges u and v into a single new vertex that is adjacent to everything u or v was adjacent to. Any loop is removed, and in simple graphs duplicate edges are merged into one. Contracting one edge of a triangle gives a single edge. Contracting an edge of C_5 gives C_4. Contraction is the key tool for graph minors in lesson 21 and for the chromatic polynomial in lesson 23.

Real-life example 1, your class on Facebook: Facebook's whole friendship network is a huge graph G. Pick the set S of the 40 students in your section. The induced subgraph G[S] is the friendship network inside your class, every friendship between two classmates and nothing else. Its complement inside S shows which pairs of classmates are not yet friends, which is exactly the set of pairs Facebook might suggest to each other. Teachers who plan group projects could use the complement to mix students who have not worked together before.

Real-life example 2, a road closure in Chattogram: Model the city's roads as a graph with junctions as vertices. A flyover under repair is an edge deletion G - e: the junctions remain, only that road is gone. A flooded junction during monsoon is a vertex deletion G - v: the junction and every road through it disappear. Traffic planners compare these subgraphs to see whether every area can still be reached, which leads straight into connectivity in lesson 9.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Keeping an edge in a subgraph after deleting one of its endpoints. Choosing edges freely in an induced subgraph. Forgetting the edge count of the complement is n(n - 1)/2 - m. Mixing up join and union. Drawing L(G) with vertices for G's vertices instead of G's edges. Exams ask: list induced subgraphs, draw the complement and check self-complementarity, prove n is 0 or 1 mod 4 for self-complementary graphs, draw line graphs and products, and count their vertices and edges.

Recap: A subgraph keeps some vertices and edges; spanning keeps all vertices; induced keeps all edges among chosen vertices. G - v removes a vertex with its edges, G - e removes one edge. The complement flips edges and non-edges and has n(n - 1)/2 - m edges. Union, join, Cartesian product, line graph and contraction build new graphs from old ones, and many famous families are built this way. Next lesson: storing graphs in matrices and lists, and what matrix algebra can tell us.
key_points: H is a subgraph of G if its vertices and edges come from G; an edge can be kept only with both endpoints.
A spanning subgraph keeps all vertices; a graph with m edges has 2^m spanning subgraphs.
The induced subgraph G[S] keeps every edge of G with both ends in S.
G - v deletes v and all its edges; G - e deletes only the edge e.
The complement has n(n - 1)/2 - m edges; self-complementary graphs exist only when n is 0 or 1 mod 4 (examples P_4 and C_5).
The join G1 + G2 adds all edges between the two graphs; K_(m,n) and wheels are joins.
The Cartesian product G box H has n1 n2 vertices and n1 m2 + n2 m1 edges; grids, prisms and hypercubes are products.
The line graph L(G) turns edges into vertices and has the sum of d(d - 1)/2 edges; contraction G / e merges two adjacent vertices.
lessons.tip: For each operation, practise on the same small graph, like the square with one diagonal. Doing every operation on one familiar graph shows you the differences much more clearly than new examples each time.
lessons.task: Take the house graph: a square a, b, c, d with a roof vertex r joined to a and b. Draw G - r, G - ab (edge), the induced subgraph on {a, b, c}, the complement, and the line graph. For each one count vertices and edges, and check the complement has 10 - 6 = 4 edges.

quiz.q: G is the square with edges ab, bc, cd, da. Which subgraph is induced by {a, b, c}?
options: Vertices a, b, c with edges ab, bc, ac
Vertices a, b, c with edges ab and bc
Vertices a, b, c with edge ab only
Vertices a, b, c with no edges
quiz.explain: An induced subgraph keeps every edge of G between the chosen vertices. G has ab and bc among them, and no ac.

quiz.q: A simple graph has 8 vertices and 10 edges. How many edges does its complement have?
quiz.explain: Together G and its complement form K_8 with 28 edges, so the complement has 28 - 10 = 18.

quiz.q: For which number of vertices can a self-complementary graph exist?
quiz.explain: n(n - 1)/4 must be a whole number, which needs n to be 0 or 1 mod 4. 9 gives 9 x 8 / 4 = 18; 6, 7 and 10 do not work.

quiz.q: What is the line graph of the star K_(1,4)?
quiz.explain: All four edges of the star meet at the centre, so every pair of them is adjacent in the line graph, giving K_4.

quiz.q: How many edges does the Cartesian product C_5 box K_2 (the pentagonal prism) have?
quiz.explain: n1 m2 + n2 m1 = 5 x 1 + 2 x 5 = 15. It has 10 vertices and is 3-regular, matching 10 x 3 / 2 = 15.

lessons.title: Representing Graphs with Matrices and Lists
lessons.content:
A drawing is great for your eyes, but a computer cannot look at a drawing. It needs numbers in memory. So how do we hand a graph to a computer? There are a few standard ways: a table of zeros and ones called the adjacency matrix, another table called the incidence matrix, and lists that record each vertex's neighbours. Each choice has strengths and weaknesses. And here is the fun part: once a graph is a matrix, ordinary matrix multiplication starts answering graph questions, like how many mutual friends two people have on Facebook.

The adjacency matrix: Number the vertices 1 to n. The adjacency matrix A is an n by n table where the entry in row i, column j is 1 if vertices i and j are adjacent, and 0 if they are not. Example: the path a - b - c. Row a is (0, 1, 0), row b is (1, 0, 1), row c is (0, 1, 0). Each row says who that vertex is joined to.

Properties for simple graphs: For a simple undirected graph, A has zeros on the main diagonal, because there are no loops. A is symmetric: the entry at (i, j) equals the entry at (j, i), since an edge from i to j is also an edge from j to i. The sum of row i is deg(i), the number of 1s in that row. Adding all entries gives the sum of degrees, which is 2m. So the handshaking lemma appears again: every edge shows up twice in A, once above the diagonal and once below.

Multigraphs and loops: For a multigraph, the entry is the number of edges between i and j, so it can be 2 or 3. For loops, conventions differ: some books write 1 for a loop on the diagonal, others write 2 so that row sums still equal degrees. Check your textbook before an exam. For a weighted graph we often store the weight instead of 1, and use 0 or infinity to mean no edge, depending on the algorithm.

Directed graphs: For a digraph, the entry at row i, column j is 1 if there is an arc from i to j. Now A is usually not symmetric, since an arc i to j does not mean an arc j to i. The sum of row i is the out-degree of i, and the sum of column i is the in-degree of i. Example: arcs a to b, b to c, c to a. Row a: (0, 1, 0), row b: (0, 0, 1), row c: (1, 0, 0). Each row and each column has one 1, matching out-degree 1 and in-degree 1 for every vertex.

The incidence matrix: Number the vertices 1 to n and the edges 1 to m. The incidence matrix M is an n by m table where the entry at row v, column e is 1 if vertex v is an endpoint of edge e, and 0 otherwise. For the path a - b - c with edges e1 = ab and e2 = bc: row a is (1, 0), row b is (1, 1), row c is (0, 1). Every column has exactly two 1s, because every edge has two ends. Row sums are again the degrees. Adding all entries counts edge-ends, which is 2m. Same lemma, new picture.

Incidence matrix for digraphs: For directed graphs, a common convention puts +1 where the arc leaves a vertex and -1 where it enters (some books use the opposite signs). Then every column adds up to 0. This signed matrix is the one Kirchhoff used for electrical circuits, where current leaving and entering a junction must balance.

Adjacency lists: An adjacency list stores, for each vertex, a list of its neighbours. For the path a - b - c: a: [b], b: [a, c], c: [b]. For an undirected graph each edge appears twice, once in each endpoint's list, so the lists hold 2m entries in total. For a digraph we usually store out-neighbours, and each arc appears once. Most real programs, from Google Maps style routing to social networks, use adjacency lists.

Edge lists: The simplest storage of all: just list the edges as pairs, like (a, b), (b, c). This is how graphs are often saved in files and how Kruskal's algorithm likes its input, sorted by weight. It takes space proportional to m, but checking whether two vertices are adjacent means scanning the whole list.

Space trade-offs: The adjacency matrix always uses n x n cells, no matter how many edges exist. The adjacency list uses space proportional to n + m. A graph is called dense if m is close to n squared and sparse if m is much smaller. Road networks are sparse: a junction meets maybe 3 or 4 roads, not thousands. For a road graph with a million junctions, a matrix would need a million times a million cells, a trillion, almost all zero. Lists need only a few million entries. That is why sparse graphs use lists.

Speed trade-offs: Is u adjacent to v? With a matrix, look at one cell, constant time. With a list, scan u's list, which takes time up to deg(u). Visit all neighbours of u? With a list, exactly deg(u) steps. With a matrix, you must scan the whole row of n cells. Algorithms like BFS and DFS visit every neighbour of every vertex, so with lists they take time proportional to n + m, but with a matrix they take n squared. Choose the structure that makes your most common question cheap.

Powers of A count walks: Here is the magic. A walk of length k is a sequence of k edges where each edge starts where the previous one ended, and repeats are allowed (lesson 8 defines it carefully). Theorem: the entry in row i, column j of A^k equals the number of walks of length k from i to j. The reason for k = 2: (A^2) at (i, j) is the sum over all vertices x of A(i, x) times A(x, j). That product is 1 exactly when i is joined to x and x is joined to j, which is a walk i - x - j. So the sum counts all such walks.

A squared, worked: For the path a - b - c, A^2 has rows a: (1, 0, 1), b: (0, 2, 0), c: (1, 0, 1). Check: from a to c in 2 steps there is one walk, a - b - c. From b back to b there are two, b - a - b and b - c - b. From a to b in exactly 2 steps there are none, since a must go to b first and then away from b. The diagonal of A^2 always equals the degrees, because a closed walk of length 2 from v just goes to a neighbour and back.

Counting triangles with A cubed: The diagonal entry (A^3) at (v, v) counts closed walks of length 3 from v, which are exactly trips around a triangle through v. Each triangle gives 6 such walks overall: 3 starting vertices times 2 directions. So the number of triangles in a graph equals trace(A^3) / 6, where the trace is the sum of the diagonal. For K_3, each diagonal entry of A^3 is 2, the trace is 6, and 6 / 6 = 1 triangle. Correct.

The Laplacian matrix: Let D be the diagonal matrix with the degrees on its diagonal and zeros elsewhere. The Laplacian is L = D - A. For the path a - b - c: row a is (1, -1, 0), row b is (-1, 2, -1), row c is (0, -1, 1). Every row adds up to 0. The Laplacian is used in spectral graph theory, in physics, and in clustering data. A known fact: the number of connected pieces of a graph equals the number of times 0 appears as an eigenvalue of L. In lesson 15 we will use L to count spanning trees with the matrix-tree theorem.

Relabelling and matrices: If you renumber the vertices, the adjacency matrix changes by swapping rows and the same columns. The graph is the same, so the two matrices describe isomorphic graphs. This is why simply comparing two matrices cell by cell cannot tell you whether two graphs are the same shape; lesson 7 deals with that.

Bipartite graphs and odd powers: Here is one more neat fact. In a bipartite graph, every walk switches sides at each step, so a closed walk must have even length. That means every diagonal entry of A^k is 0 whenever k is odd. For the square a - b - c - d - a, A^3 has an all-zero diagonal, which also confirms the square has no triangles. Matrix powers can therefore give quick evidence about the structure of a graph without drawing it at all.

Real-life example 1, mutual friends: Facebook shows 'You have 12 mutual friends' with someone. If A is the friendship adjacency matrix, then for two different people i and j, the entry of A^2 at (i, j) is the number of walks i - x - j, which is the number of people x who are friends with both. That is exactly the mutual friends count. Friend-suggestion systems at many social networks use counts like this: the more mutual friends you share with a stranger, the more likely you know them.

Real-life example 2, a small office network in Khulna: An office has 5 computers and a printer, and the IT person writes a 6 by 6 adjacency matrix in a spreadsheet, with 1 where a cable directly joins two machines. Row sums show which machine has the most cables, which is the riskiest single point. For the whole of Bangladesh's road network, though, the government mapping team would never use a matrix, because tens of thousands of junctions would make a huge table of mostly zeros. They would store an adjacency list or an edge list instead.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Forgetting that the adjacency matrix of an undirected graph is symmetric. Mixing up row sum and column sum for digraphs. Thinking each column of an incidence matrix can have one 1 or three 1s; for ordinary edges it is always two. Using a matrix for a huge sparse graph. Exams ask: write A and M for a given graph, read degrees from them, draw a graph from a given matrix, compute A^2 and interpret its entries, count triangles with trace(A^3) / 6, and compare matrix and list storage for sparse and dense graphs.

Recap: The adjacency matrix records which pairs are joined; for simple undirected graphs it is symmetric with zero diagonal and row sums equal degrees. The incidence matrix records which vertex touches which edge, with two 1s per column. Adjacency lists use space n + m and suit sparse graphs; matrices use n squared and give instant adjacency checks. Entries of A^k count walks of length k, the diagonal of A^2 gives degrees, trace(A^3) / 6 counts triangles, and the Laplacian L = D - A will help count spanning trees. Next lesson: when are two graphs really the same?
key_points: The adjacency matrix A has a 1 at (i, j) when i and j are adjacent; for simple undirected graphs it is symmetric with a zero diagonal.
Row sums of A give degrees; for a digraph, row sums give out-degrees and column sums give in-degrees.
The incidence matrix is n by m with exactly two 1s in each column, and its row sums are the degrees.
Adjacency lists use space proportional to n + m and suit sparse graphs; matrices use n^2 space but answer 'is u adjacent to v?' instantly.
The (i, j) entry of A^k counts walks of length k from i to j; the diagonal of A^2 gives degrees.
The number of triangles equals trace(A^3) / 6.
The Laplacian L = D - A has rows summing to 0 and is used later to count spanning trees.
lessons.tip: When you compute A^2 by hand, check your answer by listing the walks on the drawing for one or two entries. If the matrix says 3 walks and you can only find 2, you have caught an arithmetic slip before the examiner does.
lessons.task: Write the adjacency matrix of the square a - b - c - d - a. Compute A^2 by hand. Check that the diagonal shows the degrees, and explain why the entry for (a, c) is 2 while the entry for (a, b) is 0. Then write the adjacency list and count its entries (it should be 2m = 8).

quiz.q: In the adjacency matrix of a simple undirected graph, what does the sum of row v equal?
options: The number of edges in the graph
quiz.explain: Each 1 in row v marks one neighbour of v, so the row sum is the number of neighbours, which is deg(v).

quiz.q: How many 1s does each column of the incidence matrix of a simple graph contain?
quiz.explain: Each column is one edge, and every edge has exactly two endpoints.

quiz.q: For two different vertices i and j, what does the (i, j) entry of A^2 count?
options: Paths of any length between i and j
Common neighbours of i and j
quiz.explain: It counts walks i - x - j of length 2, one for each vertex x adjacent to both, which are the common neighbours (mutual friends).

quiz.q: A graph has trace(A^3) = 24. How many triangles does it contain?
quiz.explain: Each triangle gives 6 closed walks of length 3 (3 starting points x 2 directions), so 24 / 6 = 4 triangles.

quiz.q: Why do road-map programs store road networks as adjacency lists rather than matrices?
options: Road networks are sparse, so a matrix would waste n^2 space on zeros
Lists answer 'is u adjacent to v?' faster than matrices
Road networks are always complete graphs
quiz.explain: Each junction has only a few roads, so m is far smaller than n^2. Lists use space n + m, while a matrix would be almost entirely zeros.

lessons.title: Graph Isomorphism
lessons.content:
Two students are asked to draw the friendship network of the same five people. One draws a neat pentagon. The other draws a messy star shape with lines crossing everywhere, and uses nicknames instead of real names. Are their two graphs the same? If every friendship in one picture matches a friendship in the other once you work out who is who, then yes, they are the same graph wearing different clothes. Graph theorists call this isomorphism, from Greek words meaning same shape. Today we learn how to prove two graphs are the same shape, and, just as important, how to prove they are not.

The definition: Two graphs G and H are isomorphic if there is a one-to-one matching f between the vertices of G and the vertices of H such that u and v are adjacent in G exactly when f(u) and f(v) are adjacent in H. The matching f is called an isomorphism. One-to-one and onto (a bijection) means every vertex of G gets a different partner in H and nobody in H is left out. The 'exactly when' part means edges go to edges and non-edges go to non-edges. We write G is isomorphic to H with a wavy equals sign.

What it means in plain words: An isomorphism is a renaming. If you take G, erase all the vertex names, and write new names using f, you get H exactly, edge for edge. Position on the page, crossing lines, and curvy edges never matter. That is why when we said in lesson 2 that there are 4 graphs on 3 vertices up to shape, we really meant 4 isomorphism classes.

A worked yes example: G has vertices 1, 2, 3, 4 with edges 12, 23, 34, 41, a square. H has vertices w, x, y, z with edges wy, yx, xz, zw, which might be drawn as a bow tie with crossing lines. Try f: 1 to w, 2 to y, 3 to x, 4 to z. Check every edge of G: 12 becomes wy, an edge of H. 23 becomes yx, an edge. 34 becomes xz, an edge. 41 becomes zw, an edge. Both graphs have 4 edges, so all edges match and no extra edges exist in H. So G and H are isomorphic. To prove a yes, you must show the mapping and check every edge.

The pentagon and the pentagram: Draw C_5 as a pentagon with corners 1, 2, 3, 4, 5. Now draw a five-pointed star by joining 1 to 3, 3 to 5, 5 to 2, 2 to 4, and 4 to 1. The star is also a single cycle of length 5 that visits every vertex: 1 - 3 - 5 - 2 - 4 - 1. So the star is isomorphic to the pentagon, using the mapping 1 to 1, 2 to 3, 3 to 5, 4 to 2, 5 to 4. Two pictures that look completely different, one graph.

Why proving 'no' needs a different tool: With n vertices there are n! possible matchings. For 10 vertices that is 3,628,800. You cannot try them all by hand. Instead, we find a property that isomorphic graphs must share, and show the two graphs differ in that property. Such a property is called an invariant.

Invariants you should check first: If G and H are isomorphic then they have the same number of vertices, the same number of edges, and the same degree sequence. They have the same number of connected pieces. They have the same number of triangles, and more generally the same number of cycles of each length. One is bipartite exactly when the other is. Their complements are also isomorphic. If any one of these differs, the graphs are not isomorphic, and that single difference is a full proof.

Invariants are necessary, not sufficient: The danger goes the other way. Two graphs can agree on many invariants and still be different. The cycle C_6 and two separate triangles both have 6 vertices, 6 edges and degree sequence (2, 2, 2, 2, 2, 2). But C_6 is connected and the triangles are not, and the triangles contain triangles while C_6 does not. So they are not isomorphic. Matching numbers alone never prove a yes. Only a mapping does.

A trickier no example: Take C_6 with vertices 1 to 6 in order. G adds the chord 1 - 4, joining opposite vertices. H adds the chord 1 - 3, joining vertices two apart. Both have 6 vertices, 7 edges and degree sequence (3, 3, 2, 2, 2, 2). Both are connected. But H has the triangle 1 - 2 - 3, while G has no triangle: its cycles through the chord are 1 - 2 - 3 - 4 - 1 and 1 - 4 - 5 - 6 - 1, both of length 4. Different number of triangles, so not isomorphic.

Looking at degrees of neighbours: Another useful invariant: for each vertex, the list of its neighbours' degrees. An isomorphism maps a degree-3 vertex to a degree-3 vertex, and its neighbours to neighbours, so the neighbour-degree lists must match too. If in G the two degree-3 vertices are adjacent but in H they are not, the graphs cannot be isomorphic. Using the degrees also cuts down the search for a mapping: high degree vertices can only map to vertices with the same degree.

A practical method for 'yes' questions: Step 1: compare vertices, edges, degree sequences. If they differ, stop: no. Step 2: look for special vertices, like the only degree-4 vertex or the only vertex on a triangle, and map them first, since they have only one possible partner. Step 3: extend the mapping to neighbours, keeping degrees equal. Step 4: check every edge. If you get stuck, backtrack and try another choice, or look for an invariant that proves no.

Isomorphism with matrices: G and H are isomorphic exactly when you can reorder the rows and columns of H's adjacency matrix, using the same order for both, to get G's adjacency matrix. In matrix language, A_H = P A_G P^T for some permutation matrix P. This is why two different-looking adjacency matrices can belong to the same graph.

Isomorphism is an equivalence relation: Every graph is isomorphic to itself (use the identity mapping). If G is isomorphic to H, then H is isomorphic to G (use the reverse mapping). If G is isomorphic to H and H to K, then G is isomorphic to K (do one mapping after the other). So isomorphism splits all graphs into classes of same-shaped graphs, called isomorphism classes. When we count 'graphs on n vertices' without labels, we are really counting these classes.

Automorphisms, the symmetries of a graph: An isomorphism from a graph to itself is called an automorphism. It is a symmetry: a relabelling that leaves the edge set unchanged.
