The identity, which changes nothing, always counts. The path P_3, a - b - c, has 2 automorphisms: do nothing, or swap a and c. The cycle C_n has 2n: n rotations and n reflections. K_n has n! automorphisms, since any reordering keeps all edges. The Petersen graph has 120 automorphisms, which is why it looks so balanced.

How many different graphs exist: On n labelled vertices there are 2^(n(n - 1)/2) simple graphs, since each of the n(n - 1)/2 pairs is either an edge or not. On 4 labelled vertices that is 2^6 = 64. But up to isomorphism, the number of different shapes is much smaller: 1 graph on 1 vertex, 2 on 2 vertices, 4 on 3 vertices, 11 on 4 vertices, and 34 on 5 vertices. The 11 on 4 vertices are a good exercise: list them by number of edges, from 0 to 6, and you get 1, 1, 2, 3, 2, 1, 1, which adds up to 11.

Why it is a famous hard problem: Deciding whether two big graphs are isomorphic is called the graph isomorphism problem. Nobody knows a polynomial-time algorithm for it, and nobody has proved it NP-complete either, which makes it an unusual problem in complexity theory. In 2015 Laszlo Babai announced an algorithm that runs in quasi-polynomial time, a major breakthrough. In practice, programs such as nauty solve most real instances quickly by using invariants cleverly.

Directed and weighted versions: For digraphs, an isomorphism must also keep the direction: an arc from u to v must map to an arc from f(u) to f(v), not the other way. So now in-degrees and out-degrees become invariants too. The directed triangle a to b to c to a and the graph with arcs a to b, a to c, b to c have the same underlying triangle, but they are not isomorphic, because the first has every out-degree equal to 1 while the second has out-degrees 2, 1 and 0. For weighted graphs we usually also require each edge to keep its weight.

Real-life example 1, chemistry isomers: Butane and isobutane both have the formula C4H10, four carbon atoms and ten hydrogens. Look only at the carbon skeleton. In butane the four carbons form a chain, the path P_4. In isobutane one carbon is joined to the other three, the star K_(1,3). P_4 has degree sequence (2, 2, 1, 1) and K_(1,3) has (3, 1, 1, 1), so the skeletons are not isomorphic, and that is exactly why chemists treat them as two different compounds with different boiling points. Cayley used this idea in the 1870s to count possible molecules.

Real-life example 2, two maps of one campus: Two first-year students at Dhaka University each sketch the walking paths between the Arts Building, Curzon Hall, TSC, the Central Library and Shahid Minar. Their sketches look nothing alike, and one uses short nicknames. To check whether they describe the same network, the class rep matches buildings by their number of paths, then checks every path. If every path matches, the two sketches are isomorphic: same network, different drawings. If one student has a path from TSC to the library that the other lacks, the edge counts differ and the maps disagree.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Concluding 'isomorphic' because the degree sequences match. Giving a mapping without checking every edge. Forgetting that non-edges must also map to non-edges, which is automatic only if the edge counts are equal. Exams ask: decide if two given graphs are isomorphic and justify; give an explicit isomorphism; list invariants; find all non-isomorphic graphs with 4 vertices or with a given degree sequence; count automorphisms of small graphs; show a graph is self-complementary by giving an isomorphism to its complement.

Recap: Two graphs are isomorphic if a bijection between their vertices maps edges to edges and non-edges to non-edges. To prove yes, give the mapping and check every edge. To prove no, find an invariant that differs: vertices, edges, degree sequence, components, triangles, cycle lengths, bipartiteness. Matching invariants never prove yes. Automorphisms are a graph's symmetries. There are 11 graphs on 4 vertices up to isomorphism, and deciding isomorphism for big graphs is a famous open problem. Next lesson: walks, paths, cycles and distance.
key_points: G and H are isomorphic if a bijection f maps every edge to an edge and every non-edge to a non-edge.
To prove isomorphic, give the mapping explicitly and check every edge.
To prove not isomorphic, find one invariant that differs: order, size, degree sequence, components, number of triangles, cycle lengths, bipartiteness.
Equal invariants are necessary but never enough: C_6 and two triangles share the same degree sequence but differ.
Map special vertices first (unique degrees, triangles) to cut down the search.
An automorphism is an isomorphism from a graph to itself: C_n has 2n, K_n has n!, the Petersen graph has 120.
Up to isomorphism there are 1, 2, 4, 11, 34 simple graphs on 1 to 5 vertices; on 4 labelled vertices there are 64.
No polynomial-time algorithm is known for graph isomorphism, and it is not known to be NP-complete.
lessons.tip: When an exam asks 'are these isomorphic?', spend the first 30 seconds counting vertices, edges and degrees, then count triangles. Most 'no' answers fall out right there. Only start building a mapping when every invariant you check agrees.
lessons.task: Draw all 11 non-isomorphic simple graphs on 4 vertices, grouped by number of edges (0 to 6 edges: 1, 1, 2, 3, 2, 1, 1 graphs). For each pair in the same group, write one invariant that tells them apart.

quiz.q: Two graphs have the same number of vertices, edges and the same degree sequence. What can you conclude?
options: Nothing yet; they may or may not be isomorphic
quiz.explain: Matching invariants are necessary but not sufficient. C_6 and two triangles agree on all three but are different graphs.

quiz.q: C_6 plus the chord 1-4 and C_6 plus the chord 1-3 have the same degree sequence. Which invariant shows they are not isomorphic?
quiz.explain: The chord 1-3 creates the triangle 1-2-3, while the chord 1-4 only creates 4-cycles. Triangles must be preserved by an isomorphism.

quiz.q: How many automorphisms does the cycle C_8 have?
quiz.explain: C_n has 2n automorphisms: n rotations and n reflections, so 2 x 8 = 16.

quiz.q: How many simple graphs are there on 4 vertices up to isomorphism?
quiz.explain: There are 64 labelled graphs on 4 vertices, but they fall into 11 different shapes.

quiz.q: Why are butane (chain of 4 carbons) and isobutane (one carbon joined to 3 others) different molecules in graph terms?
options: They have different numbers of carbon atoms
Their carbon skeletons P_4 and K_(1,3) are not isomorphic, since their degree sequences differ
One of them has a cycle
They have different numbers of carbon-carbon bonds
quiz.explain: Both skeletons have 4 vertices and 3 edges, but P_4 has degrees (2, 2, 1, 1) and K_(1,3) has (3, 1, 1, 1), so they are different shapes.

lessons.title: Walks, Trails, Paths, Cycles and Distance
lessons.content:
Imagine a rickshaw puller in Old Dhaka moving through the lanes all day. Sometimes he passes the same corner twice. Sometimes he goes down the same lane twice. Sometimes he takes a clean route from one place to another without ever repeating anything. Graph theory has a separate word for each kind of trip, and mixing them up is one of the most common mistakes students make. Today we sort them out: walks, trails, paths, circuits and cycles. Then we measure how far apart vertices are, and learn the words radius, diameter, centre and girth.

Walk: A walk is a sequence v0, e1, v1, e2, v2, ..., ek, vk where each edge ei joins v(i-1) to vi. In a simple graph we can just list the vertices, like a - b - c - b - d. The length of a walk is its number of edges, k, not its number of vertices. A walk may repeat vertices and edges as much as it likes. It goes from v0 to vk, and it is closed if v0 = vk, otherwise open. A single vertex with no edges counts as a walk of length 0.

Trail: A trail is a walk that never uses the same edge twice. Vertices may repeat. The figure-eight trip a - b - c - a - d - e - a around two triangles that share vertex a is a trail: every edge is used once, but a is visited three times. Euler tours, which we study in lesson 12, are trails that use every edge.

Path: A path is a walk that never visits the same vertex twice. If no vertex repeats, no edge can repeat either, so every path is a trail, and every trail is a walk. Paths are the clean routes. The path from a to d in the square a - b - c - d - a can be a - b - c - d or a - d. Note that the word path is used both for this kind of walk and for the path graph P_n from lesson 4. A path in G is really a subgraph of G that is a path graph.

Circuit and cycle: A closed trail is called a circuit: it returns to the start and never repeats an edge. A cycle is a closed walk with at least one edge where no vertex repeats except that the first equals the last. In a simple graph a cycle has length at least 3. The square a - b - c - d - a is a cycle of length 4. The figure-eight a - b - c - a - d - e - a is a circuit but not a cycle, because a appears in the middle too.

A quick comparison: Walk: anything goes. Trail: no repeated edges. Path: no repeated vertices. Circuit: closed trail. Cycle: closed path. Be careful, because some textbooks use different words, for example 'simple path' for path or 'tour' for circuit. In exams, always write the definition you are using in one line before answering.

Worked example of the differences: In the graph with edges ab, bc, ca, cd: a - b - c - a - b is a walk of length 4, but not a trail, since ab is used twice. a - b - c - a is a cycle of length 3. a - b - c - d is a path of length 3. d - c - a - b - c is a trail of length 4 (edges dc, ca, ab, bc are all different), but not a path, since c repeats.

Every walk contains a path: Lemma: if there is a u - v walk, then there is a u - v path. Proof idea: if the walk visits some vertex x twice, cut out everything between the first and the last visit of x. What remains is still a walk from u to v, and it is shorter. Keep cutting until no vertex repeats; the process must end because the length keeps dropping. Example: u - a - b - a - v becomes u - a - v. This is why, when we only care whether two vertices can be reached, walks and paths give the same answer.

Odd closed walks contain odd cycles: A second useful lemma: every closed walk of odd length contains a cycle of odd length. The idea is similar: if the closed walk repeats a vertex, split it into two shorter closed walks at that vertex. Their lengths add up to the odd total, so one of them is odd. Keep splitting the odd part until no vertex repeats, and you are left with an odd cycle. This lemma is the key step in proving that bipartite graphs are exactly the graphs with no odd cycles, in lesson 11.

Minimum degree forces paths and cycles: If every vertex has degree at least delta, with delta at least 1, then the graph has a path of length at least delta. If delta is at least 2, the graph contains a cycle, in fact one of length at least delta + 1. Proof idea: take a longest path, ending at vertex x. Every neighbour of x must already be on the path, otherwise we could extend it. x has at least delta neighbours on the path, so the path has at least delta more vertices before x. If delta is at least 2, joining x to its neighbour farthest back on the path closes a cycle of length at least delta + 1. The longest path trick appears in many proofs.

Distance: The distance d(u, v) between two vertices is the length of a shortest u - v path. If no path exists, we say the distance is infinite. A shortest path is also called a geodesic. In an unweighted graph BFS finds distances, as you saw in Algorithms. In the square a - b - c - d - a: d(a, b) = 1 and d(a, c) = 2. Distance behaves like a real distance: d(u, v) is at least 0, equals 0 only when u = v, d(u, v) = d(v, u), and it obeys the triangle inequality d(u, w) at most d(u, v) + d(v, w).

Eccentricity: The eccentricity e(v) of a vertex in a connected graph is the distance from v to the vertex farthest from it. It tells you how far out v has to reach to touch everyone. For the path a - b - c - d - e: e(a) = 4, e(b) = 3, e(c) = 2, e(d) = 3, e(e) = 4.

Radius, diameter and centre: The radius rad(G) is the smallest eccentricity, and the diameter diam(G) is the largest eccentricity, which is also the largest distance between any two vertices. The centre of G is the set of vertices whose eccentricity equals the radius. For the path above: radius 2, diameter 4, centre {c}. In every connected graph, rad(G) is at most diam(G), which is at most 2 rad(G). The second inequality holds because any two vertices can reach each other through a central vertex using at most rad + rad steps.

Distances in famous families: K_n has diameter 1 because everybody is adjacent. C_n has diameter n/2 rounded down, and every vertex is central because the cycle looks the same from everywhere. A star has radius 1 and diameter 2, with the centre as its centre. The Petersen graph has diameter 2: any two vertices are adjacent or share a neighbour. The hypercube Q_n has diameter n, since two binary strings differ in at most n bits, and you fix one bit per step.

Girth and circumference: The girth of a graph is the length of its shortest cycle, and the circumference is the length of its longest cycle. A graph with no cycles has infinite girth by convention. K_n for n at least 3 has girth 3. K_(m,n) with m and n at least 2 has girth 4, since bipartite graphs have no triangles. Q_n for n at least 2 has girth 4. The Petersen graph has girth 5 and circumference 9: it has cycles of length 9 but none of length 10, which is the same as saying it has no Hamilton cycle.

Distance in digraphs: In a digraph, a directed walk must follow the arrows, and the distance from u to v can differ from the distance from v to u. On a one-way street grid, getting from the mosque to the market might take 2 blocks, while getting back takes 4. So directed distance is not symmetric.

Real-life example 1, bus transfers in Dhaka: Make each bus route a vertex and join two routes if they share a stop where you can switch. Then the distance between two routes is the number of switches you need. The eccentricity of a route tells how many switches the worst trip from it needs, and the centre of this graph is the set of best routes to live near if you want to reach anywhere with few changes. A city planner who wants every trip to need at most two changes wants this graph to have diameter at most 2.

Real-life example 2, the small-world idea: In big social networks, the diameter is surprisingly small compared to the number of people. Even though millions of people use a network, most pairs are joined by short chains of friends. The famous phrase 'six degrees of separation' comes from experiments in the 1960s by the psychologist Stanley Milgram, who asked people to pass letters through acquaintances to a stranger and found that successful chains were usually short. In graph language, social networks have small average distance, which is why a viral video from Sylhet can reach the whole country within hours.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Measuring length by vertices instead of edges. Calling a trail with a repeated vertex a path. Calling a circuit that passes through a vertex twice a cycle. Forgetting that distance is infinite between different components, so eccentricity and diameter are usually defined only for connected graphs. Exams ask: classify given sequences as walk, trail, path, circuit or cycle; prove every walk contains a path; compute distances, eccentricities, radius, diameter, centre and girth for a given graph; prove rad is at most diam which is at most 2 rad.

Recap: Walks may repeat anything, trails never repeat edges, paths never repeat vertices; circuits are closed trails and cycles are closed paths. Length counts edges. Every walk contains a path, and every odd closed walk contains an odd cycle. Minimum degree at least 2 forces a cycle. Distance is the length of a shortest path; eccentricity, radius, diameter and centre describe how spread out a graph is; girth is the shortest cycle length. Next lesson: when is a graph connected, and which single vertices or edges hold it together?
key_points: A walk can repeat vertices and edges; a trail repeats no edge; a path repeats no vertex.
A circuit is a closed trail; a cycle is a closed path, of length at least 3 in a simple graph.
Length always counts edges, not vertices.
Every u - v walk contains a u - v path, and every odd closed walk contains an odd cycle.
If the minimum degree is at least 2, the graph contains a cycle (longest path argument).
d(u, v) is the length of a shortest path; it is symmetric and obeys the triangle inequality in undirected graphs.
Eccentricity is the farthest distance from a vertex; radius is the minimum, diameter the maximum, and rad <= diam <= 2 rad.
Girth is the shortest cycle length: 3 for K_n, 4 for K_(m,n) and Q_n, 5 for the Petersen graph.
lessons.tip: Write the five words walk, trail, path, circuit, cycle on a card with one short rule each: anything, no repeated edge, no repeated vertex, closed trail, closed path. Look at the card before every exam; this is where easy marks are lost.
lessons.task: Draw the wheel with a hub h and rim a - b - c - d - e - f - a. Compute the eccentricity of every vertex, then the radius, diameter and centre. Find the girth and the circumference. Then write one walk, one trail that is not a path, and one cycle of length 5.

quiz.q: In the graph with edges ab, bc, ca, cd, what is d - c - a - b - c?
options: A trail but not a path
quiz.explain: Its edges dc, ca, ab, bc are all different, so it is a trail, but c appears twice, so it is not a path.

quiz.q: What is the length of the walk a - b - c - b - d?
quiz.explain: Length counts edges: ab, bc, cb, bd, which is 4 edges, even though there are 5 vertex entries.

quiz.q: For the path a - b - c - d - e, what are the radius and diameter?
quiz.explain: Eccentricities are 4, 3, 2, 3, 4. The smallest is 2 (radius, at c) and the largest is 4 (diameter).

quiz.q: What is the girth of K_(3,4)?
quiz.explain: A bipartite graph has no odd cycles, so no triangles. K_(3,4) has 4-cycles like x1 - y1 - x2 - y2 - x1, so the girth is 4.

quiz.q: Why is diam(G) at most 2 rad(G) in a connected graph?
options: Because any two vertices can reach each other through a central vertex in at most rad + rad steps
Because every graph is a tree
quiz.explain: Take a central vertex c with eccentricity rad. For any u and v, d(u, v) <= d(u, c) + d(c, v) <= rad + rad by the triangle inequality.

lessons.title: Connectivity: Components, Cut Vertices and Bridges
lessons.content:
During a heavy monsoon, one low road in a district floods, and suddenly a whole group of villages cannot be reached by car. Nothing else broke, just one road. Other times, a single crossroads market is closed for a festival, and traffic from the north side can no longer reach the south side. In graph language, the flooded road was a bridge and the closed crossroads was a cut vertex. Today we study what it means for a graph to be in one piece, how to count its pieces, and how to find the weak spots whose loss breaks it apart.

Connected graphs: A graph is connected if there is a path between every pair of vertices. Otherwise it is disconnected. The square is connected. Two separate triangles drawn side by side form one disconnected graph. A single vertex is connected, trivially. Remember from lesson 8 that if there is any walk between two vertices then there is a path, so 'reachable' can be tested either way.

Components: Say u is related to v if there is a path from u to v. This relation is reflexive (a vertex reaches itself), symmetric (reverse the path) and transitive (join two paths into a walk, which contains a path). So it is an equivalence relation, and its classes split the vertices into groups. The subgraph induced by each group is called a connected component, or just a component. A component is a maximal connected subgraph: connected, and you cannot add any more vertices while staying connected. We write k(G) or omega(G) for the number of components. A graph is connected exactly when it has one component.

A worked example: Vertices 1 to 8 with edges 12, 23, 31, 45, 67. Components: {1, 2, 3} (a triangle), {4, 5} (one edge), {6, 7} (one edge) and {8} (isolated). So k = 4. An isolated vertex is a component all by itself. BFS or DFS from any unvisited vertex finds one whole component, so running them repeatedly counts the components in time proportional to n + m.

At least n - k edges: A graph with n vertices and k components has at least n - k edges. Proof idea: start with n isolated vertices, which is n components. Add the edges one at a time. Each new edge either joins two different components into one, lowering the count by exactly one, or lies inside one component and changes nothing. To get down from n components to k, you need at least n - k edges. Corollary: a connected graph on n vertices has at least n - 1 edges. Trees, which have exactly n - 1 edges, are the most economical connected graphs.

At most this many edges: In the other direction, a simple graph with n vertices and k components has at most (n - k)(n - k + 1)/2 edges. The extreme case is one big complete graph on n - k + 1 vertices plus k - 1 isolated vertices. A useful corollary: a simple graph with n vertices and more than (n - 1)(n - 2)/2 edges must be connected. With 6 vertices, more than 10 edges forces connection.

High minimum degree forces connection: If every vertex of a simple graph on n vertices has degree at least (n - 1)/2, then the graph is connected, and in fact any two vertices are at distance at most 2. Proof: take two non-adjacent vertices u and v. Each has at least (n - 1)/2 neighbours, all among the other n - 2 vertices. Together that is at least n - 1 neighbour slots in only n - 2 places, so by pigeonhole they share a neighbour. Example: on 7 vertices, minimum degree 3 guarantees connection.

A graph or its complement: For any graph G, at least one of G and its complement is connected. Proof idea: suppose G is disconnected. Take any two vertices u and v. If they are in different components of G, they are not adjacent in G, so they are adjacent in the complement. If they are in the same component, pick a vertex w in a different component; then u - w - v is a path in the complement. Either way, u and v are joined in the complement, so it is connected.

Adding and removing edges, the effect on components: Removing an edge from a graph can raise the component count by at most 1, and adding an edge can lower it by at most 1. So if you start with a connected graph and delete edges one at a time, the count climbs slowly, one step at a time. This simple 'at most one' fact is behind the n - k bound above, and it is also why deleting a single edge is called the gentlest way to damage a network.

Cut vertices: A vertex v is a cut vertex (or articulation point) if deleting it increases the number of components. In the path a - b - c, b is a cut vertex: deleting it leaves a and c apart. The centre of a star is a cut vertex. A cycle has no cut vertices: delete any vertex and a path remains, still connected. Equivalent description for a connected graph: v is a cut vertex exactly when there are two other vertices u and w such that every u - w path passes through v.

Bridges: An edge e is a bridge (or cut edge) if deleting it increases the number of components. Every edge of a tree is a bridge. No edge of a cycle is a bridge. Deleting one edge can raise the number of components by at most one, because the edge only held its two endpoints together. Deleting one vertex, on the other hand, can create many components: removing the centre of a star with 5 leaves creates 5 components.

The bridge theorem: An edge is a bridge if and only if it lies on no cycle. Proof, first direction: if e = uv lies on a cycle, then after deleting e you can still go from u to v the long way around the cycle, so nothing gets disconnected and e is not a bridge. Second direction: if e is not a bridge, then after deleting it there is still some path from u to v. Adding e back closes that path into a cycle containing e. So 'not a bridge' and 'on a cycle' mean the same thing.

Bridges and cut vertices together: If e = uv is a bridge and u has degree at least 2, then u is a cut vertex: deleting u also removes e and separates u's other neighbours from v's side. The converse fails: a graph can have cut vertices and no bridges. Two triangles sharing one vertex (a bow tie) have a cut vertex in the middle, but every edge lies on a triangle, so there are no bridges.

Every connected graph has two safe vertices: Every connected graph with at least 2 vertices has at least two vertices that are not cut vertices. Proof idea: take a longest path. Its two ends cannot be cut vertices, because every neighbour of an end lies on the path, and the rest of the path keeps everything together after the end is removed. This fact is handy in induction proofs: you can always remove a non-cut vertex and keep the graph connected.

Blocks: A block of a graph is a maximal connected subgraph that has no cut vertex of its own. Each block is either a single bridge with its two ends, or a 2-connected piece where you cannot disconnect it by removing one vertex. The bow tie has two blocks, the two triangles, sharing the cut vertex. Any two blocks share at most one vertex, and that shared vertex is a cut vertex. If you draw one node for each block and one for each cut vertex, joining a cut vertex to the blocks containing it, you always get a tree, called the block-cutpoint tree. It shows the weak structure of the graph at a glance.

Connectivity in digraphs: A digraph is strongly connected if for every pair u, v there is a directed path from u to v and also from v to u. It is weakly connected if it becomes connected when you ignore directions. A one-way ring road is strongly connected; a one-way street that leads out of town and never back is only weakly connected. The strongly connected components split the vertices into groups, and shrinking each group to one vertex gives a graph with no directed cycles, called the condensation. Algorithms like Kosaraju's, from the Algorithms course, find these components in linear time.

Finding cut vertices with a simple test: For a small graph you can find cut vertices by brute force: for each vertex v, delete it, run BFS on what is left, and see if everything is still reached. That costs n separate searches. Tarjan's algorithm does the whole job in a single DFS by recording, for each vertex, the earliest discovered vertex its subtree can reach through a back edge. If some child's subtree cannot climb above v, then v is a cut vertex. You do not need the details here; just know that cut vertices and bridges can be found in linear time.

Real-life example 1, a village link: Imagine a char island village in a river, joined to the mainland only by one bamboo bridge, plus a road network on each side. In the graph of places, that bamboo bridge is a graph bridge: it lies on no cycle, so if a flood washes it away the island becomes its own component. The fix suggested by graph theory is simple: build a second crossing anywhere between the two sides, so the original link now lies on a cycle and stops being a bridge. Engineers call this redundancy.

Real-life example 2, an office network in Rajshahi: Twenty computers are connected through switches. One switch sits between the accounts floor and the server room, and every cable from accounts goes through it. That switch is a cut vertex. If it fails, accounts is cut off. A network administrator can run a DFS-based algorithm (Tarjan's method for articulation points) on the network map to find every cut vertex and every bridge, and then add backup links exactly there.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Thinking a cut vertex must have high degree; even a degree-2 vertex in a path is a cut vertex. Thinking every graph with a cut vertex has a bridge. Forgetting that isolated vertices count as components. Mixing up strongly and weakly connected. Exams ask: find components, cut vertices, bridges and blocks of a given graph; prove the bridge theorem; prove m is at least n - k; prove G or its complement is connected; prove minimum degree at least (n - 1)/2 implies connected.

Recap: Connected means a path joins every pair. Components are the maximal connected pieces, and a graph with k components needs at least n - k edges. A cut vertex or a bridge is a single vertex or edge whose removal increases the number of components. An edge is a bridge exactly when it lies on no cycle. Blocks are the pieces without cut vertices, arranged like a tree. Digraphs can be strongly or weakly connected. Next lesson: measuring how many vertices or edges must go before a graph breaks.
key_points: A graph is connected if every pair of vertices is joined by a path; components are the maximal connected subgraphs.
A graph with n vertices and k components has at least n - k edges, so a connected graph has at least n - 1.
A simple graph with more than (n - 1)(n - 2)/2 edges, or with minimum degree at least (n - 1)/2, is connected.
For every graph, G or its complement is connected.
A cut vertex or bridge is a vertex or edge whose deletion increases the number of components.
An edge is a bridge if and only if it lies on no cycle; every edge of a tree is a bridge.
Every connected graph with at least 2 vertices has at least two non-cut vertices.
Blocks are maximal pieces with no cut vertex; blocks and cut vertices form a tree. Digraphs can be strongly or weakly connected.
lessons.tip: To find bridges by hand, look for edges that are not on any cycle. Trace each edge with your pencil and try to come back to its start another way. If you can, it is not a bridge. This is quicker and safer than deleting edges one by one.
lessons.task: Draw the graph with vertices 1 to 9 and edges 12, 23, 31, 34, 45, 56, 64, 47, 78, 89. List its cut vertices, its bridges and its blocks, then draw its block-cutpoint tree. Check that each bridge lies on no cycle.

quiz.q: A graph has 10 vertices and 3 components. What is the smallest number of edges it can have?
quiz.explain: A graph with n vertices and k components has at least n - k edges, so 10 - 3 = 7.

quiz.q: Which statement about a bridge is true?
options: An edge is a bridge if and only if it lies on no cycle
Every bridge joins two vertices of degree 1
A cycle always contains at least one bridge
Deleting a bridge can create 3 new components
quiz.explain: If an edge is on a cycle, the rest of the cycle reconnects its ends, so it is not a bridge, and conversely. Deleting one edge raises the component count by at most 1.

quiz.q: Two triangles share exactly one vertex (a bow tie). What does the graph have?
options: Two bridges and no cut vertex
No cut vertex and no bridge
One cut vertex and no bridge
quiz.explain: Removing the shared vertex separates the triangles, so it is a cut vertex, but every edge lies on a triangle, so there are no bridges.

quiz.q: On 9 vertices, what minimum degree guarantees a simple graph is connected by the (n - 1)/2 rule?
quiz.explain: (9 - 1)/2 = 4. Any two non-adjacent vertices then have at least 8 neighbour slots among 7 other vertices, so they share a neighbour.

quiz.q: A digraph becomes connected if arrow directions are ignored, but there is no directed path from u back to v for some pair. It is:
options: Weakly connected but not strongly connected
quiz.explain: Weakly connected means connected as an undirected graph; strongly connected would need directed paths both ways for every pair.

lessons.title: Vertex and Edge Connectivity, and Menger's Theorem
lessons.content:
Last lesson asked a yes or no question: does removing this one vertex or edge break the graph? Today we ask a how-much question: how many vertices, or how many edges, must an enemy remove before the graph falls apart? A spider web with many threads survives a few cuts; a single rope does not. Network engineers care about this number every day, because it tells them how many failures their system can survive. We will define two numbers, vertex connectivity and edge connectivity, prove a neat inequality linking them, and meet Menger's theorem, which says the number of cuts needed equals the number of separate routes available.

Vertex cuts: A vertex cut (or separating set) of a connected graph G is a set S of vertices such that G - S is disconnected. In the path a - b - c, S = {b} is a vertex cut. In the cycle C_6, no single vertex is a cut, but any two non-adjacent vertices together form a vertex cut, splitting the ring into two arcs. A complete graph has no vertex cut at all: whatever you delete, the rest is still complete and connected.

Vertex connectivity kappa: The vertex connectivity kappa(G) is the smallest number of vertices whose removal leaves a disconnected graph or a single vertex. The 'single vertex' part handles complete graphs: kappa(K_n) = n - 1, because you must delete n - 1 vertices to reduce it to one vertex. A disconnected graph has kappa = 0. A connected graph with a cut vertex has kappa = 1. Examples: kappa(P_n) = 1 for n at least 3, kappa(C_n) = 2, kappa(K_(m,n)) = the smaller of m and n, kappa(Q_n) = n, and the Petersen graph has kappa = 3.

Computing kappa for K_(3,4): Call the sides X with 3 vertices and Y with 4. If you delete all 3 vertices of X, the 4 vertices of Y are left with no edges at all, so the graph is disconnected: kappa is at most 3. Can 2 deletions do it? After deleting any 2 vertices, at least one vertex of X and at least two of Y remain, and every remaining X vertex is joined to every remaining Y vertex, so everything is still connected. So kappa(K_(3,4)) = 3, the smaller side, matching the rule.

k-connected graphs: A graph is k-connected if kappa(G) is at least k. So connected means 1-connected, and 2-connected means connected with no cut vertex (and at least 3 vertices). A 3-connected graph survives the loss of any 2 vertices. Note that k-connected means at least k, so every 3-connected graph is also 2-connected.

Edge cuts and lambda: An edge cut is a set F of edges such that G - F is disconnected. The edge connectivity lambda(G) is the smallest size of an edge cut, or 0 if G is already disconnected. A bridge is an edge cut of size 1, so a graph with a bridge has lambda = 1. Examples: lambda(tree) = 1, lambda(C_n) = 2, lambda(K_n) = n - 1, lambda(K_(m,n)) = the smaller of m and n, lambda(Q_n) = n. A graph is k-edge-connected if lambda(G) is at least k.

Whitney's inequality: For every graph, kappa(G) is at most lambda(G), which is at most delta(G), the minimum degree. Hassler Whitney proved this in 1932. The second part is easy: pick a vertex v of minimum degree delta and delete all delta edges at v. Then v is cut off from the rest, so lambda is at most delta. The first part, kappa at most lambda, says breaking by vertices is never harder than breaking by edges. Idea: take a smallest edge cut; for each of its edges, delete one suitable endpoint instead. That removes at most lambda vertices and still separates the graph (or leaves too few vertices), so kappa is at most lambda.

The inequality can be strict: Take two copies of K_4 that share exactly one vertex. Minimum degree is 3. Deleting the shared vertex disconnects the graph, so kappa = 1. But to separate it with edges you must cut 3 edges, either around one vertex or between the shared vertex and one side, so lambda = 3. So kappa = 1 is smaller than lambda = 3, which equals delta = 3. Now take two copies of K_4 joined by a single edge: kappa = 1, lambda = 1, delta = 3. All three numbers can differ, but the order kappa at most lambda at most delta never breaks.

Why the minimum degree is only an upper bound: A graph can have high minimum degree yet be easy to break, like the two K_4 copies joined by one edge above. High degree everywhere is no guarantee of strength; what matters is whether there are bottlenecks. That is why engineers measure connectivity directly instead of just counting links per node.

Whitney's theorem for 2-connected graphs: A graph with at least 3 vertices is 2-connected if and only if every two vertices lie on a common cycle. Equivalently, every two vertices are joined by two paths that share no vertex except their ends. Such paths are called internally disjoint. For example, in C_6 any two vertices split the ring into two arcs, which are exactly two internally disjoint paths. In a path graph, the two end vertices have only one path between them, and indeed the path has cut vertices.

Ear decompositions: Whitney also showed that a graph is 2-connected exactly when it can be built like this: start with a cycle, then repeatedly add an ear, which is a path whose two ends are already in the graph but whose inner vertices are new. The square plus a path from a to c through a new vertex x gives a 2-connected graph. Ears explain why 2-connected graphs have no weak point: each addition creates a second route around every part.

Menger's theorem, vertex version: Let u and v be two non-adjacent vertices. The smallest number of vertices whose removal separates u from v equals the largest number of internally disjoint u - v paths. Karl Menger proved this in 1927. One direction is easy: if there are k internally disjoint paths, any separating set must contain at least one inner vertex from each path, so it has at least k vertices. The deep part is the other direction: if you cannot separate them with fewer than k vertices, then k disjoint paths really exist.

Menger's theorem, edge version: For any two different vertices u and v, the smallest number of edges whose removal separates u from v equals the largest number of edge-disjoint u - v paths, meaning paths that share no edge. This is the same idea as the max-flow min-cut theorem from the Algorithms course: give every edge capacity 1, and the maximum flow from u to v counts edge-disjoint paths while the minimum cut counts separating edges.

Global version: Combining Menger with the definitions gives a lovely description. A graph is k-connected if and only if every pair of vertices is joined by at least k internally disjoint paths (this form is due to Whitney). Similarly, it is k-edge-connected if and only if every pair is joined by at least k edge-disjoint paths. So connectivity is not just about cuts; it is about the number of independent routes.

Menger worked on the cube: In Q_3, take u = 000 and v = 111, which are not adjacent. Three internally disjoint paths: 000 - 100 - 110 - 111, 000 - 010 - 011 - 111, and 000 - 001 - 101 - 111. No two share an inner vertex. And the set {100, 010, 001}, all neighbours of 000, separates u from v with 3 vertices. So the minimum cut and the maximum number of disjoint paths are both 3, exactly as Menger promises, and kappa(Q_3) = 3.

How few edges can a k-connected graph have: Since kappa is at most delta, every vertex of a k-connected graph has degree at least k, so by handshaking it has at least kn/2 edges, rounded up. Frank Harary showed in 1962 that this is achievable: for every k less than n there is a k-connected graph on n vertices with exactly that many edges. For k = 2 the cycle C_n is the example, with n edges. These Harary graphs are the cheapest designs for a given level of reliability.

A three-number checklist: Whenever you meet a new graph in an exam, write delta first, since it is the easiest to read off. Then look for a single cut vertex or bridge: if you find one, kappa or lambda is 1. If not, try pairs. Because kappa is at most lambda which is at most delta, you never need to test cuts bigger than delta. For small graphs this checklist finishes in a minute or two.

Real-life example 1, Bangladesh and the internet: International internet traffic from Bangladesh travels over submarine cables, with landing stations at Cox's Bazar and Kuakata, plus land links through neighbouring countries. If the country had only one cable, that cable would be a bridge in the network graph, and a single cut would isolate the country. With several separate routes, the edge connectivity between Bangladesh and the rest of the world is higher, so one damaged cable slows things down instead of cutting everyone off. Menger's theorem is the precise way to say it: k edge-disjoint routes means k cuts are needed to isolate.

Real-life example 2, a bank's data centres: A mobile banking company keeps its main servers in Dhaka and a backup in another city. Engineers want the network between them to be 2-connected: no single router failure should cut the link. By Whitney's theorem, that is the same as having two internally disjoint routes between every pair of important routers. They check it by finding two such routes, or by running an algorithm that computes kappa, which is built on max-flow just like Menger's proof.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Forgetting the special rule kappa(K_n) = n - 1. Thinking kappa = lambda always. Mixing up internally disjoint (no shared inner vertices) and edge-disjoint (no shared edges). Using Menger's vertex version for adjacent vertices, where it does not apply directly. Exams ask: compute kappa, lambda and delta for given graphs; give an example with kappa less than lambda less than delta; prove lambda at most delta; state Whitney's and Menger's theorems; find disjoint paths and matching separating sets.

Recap: kappa(G) is the fewest vertices and lambda(G) the fewest edges whose removal disconnects G, and Whitney's inequality says kappa at most lambda at most delta. A graph is 2-connected exactly when every two vertices share a cycle. Menger's theorem says the minimum number of separating vertices (or edges) equals the maximum number of internally disjoint (or edge-disjoint) paths. A k-connected graph needs at least kn/2 edges. Next lesson: bipartite graphs and the odd cycle test.
key_points: kappa(G) is the minimum number of vertices whose removal disconnects G or leaves one vertex; kappa(K_n) = n - 1.
lambda(G) is the minimum number of edges whose removal disconnects G.
Whitney's inequality: kappa(G) <= lambda(G) <= delta(G), and each inequality can be strict.
Examples: kappa = lambda = 2 for C_n, n - 1 for K_n, min(m, n) for K_(m,n), n for Q_n, 3 for Petersen.
A graph with at least 3 vertices is 2-connected iff every two vertices lie on a common cycle.
Menger: the minimum u-v separating set equals the maximum number of internally disjoint u-v paths (edge version: edge cuts and edge-disjoint paths).
G is k-connected iff every pair of vertices has k internally disjoint paths.
A k-connected graph on n vertices needs at least kn/2 edges (rounded up), and Harary graphs achieve this.
lessons.tip: When asked for kappa or lambda, give two things: a cut of that size (showing the value is at most that) and the same number of disjoint paths between a well-chosen pair (showing it is at least that). Menger guarantees both exist, and together they make a complete answer.
lessons.task: For K_(2,3) and for the wheel with a rim of 5 vertices, find kappa, lambda and delta. For each, show a smallest vertex cut and a smallest edge cut, and draw the matching number of internally disjoint paths between two vertices on opposite sides of the cut.

quiz.q: What are kappa, lambda and delta for two copies of K_4 sharing exactly one vertex?
quiz.explain: Removing the shared vertex disconnects it, so kappa = 1. Separating with edges needs 3 edges, so lambda = 3, and the minimum degree is 3.

quiz.q: Which inequality always holds (Whitney, 1932)?
quiz.explain: Breaking by vertices is never harder than by edges, and deleting all edges at a minimum-degree vertex shows lambda <= delta.

quiz.q: What is the vertex connectivity of the hypercube Q_4?
quiz.explain: kappa(Q_n) = n. Q_4 is 4-regular, and between opposite corners there are 4 internally disjoint paths.

quiz.q: What does Menger's theorem (vertex version) say for non-adjacent u and v?
options: The fewest vertices separating u and v equals the most internally disjoint u-v paths
Every u-v path has the same length
u and v always have a common neighbour
The number of edges equals the number of paths
quiz.explain: Menger (1927): minimum separating set size = maximum number of internally disjoint paths.

quiz.q: A graph has at least 3 vertices and every two vertices lie on a common cycle. What can you conclude?
quiz.explain: By Whitney's theorem, this property is exactly equivalent to being 2-connected (no cut vertex).

lessons.title: Bipartite Graphs and the Odd Cycle Test
lessons.content:
At a school sports day, the teacher wants to split the class into two teams, Red and Blue, so that no two best friends end up on the same team, because best friends chat instead of playing. Sometimes this works perfectly. But if Anik, Bina and Chitra are all best friends with each other, it is hopeless: put Anik in Red, then Bina must be Blue, then Chitra must be different from both, and there is no third team. A triangle of friends ruins the plan. Today we learn exactly which graphs can be split into two teams like this. The answer is beautiful and short: the graphs with no odd cycles.

Definition: A graph is bipartite if its vertex set can be split into two disjoint sets X and Y so that every edge has one end in X and the other end in Y. No edge stays inside X and no edge stays inside Y. The pair (X, Y) is called a bipartition, and X and Y are called the parts or sides. A graph with no edges is bipartite in a trivial way.

The colouring view: Splitting into X and Y is the same as colouring every vertex red or blue so that each edge joins a red vertex to a blue one. So bipartite means 2-colourable. In the colouring language of lesson 22, a graph with at least one edge is bipartite exactly when its chromatic number is 2. This view is useful because colouring is easy to do step by step.

Examples of bipartite graphs: K_(m,n) is bipartite by its very definition. Every even cycle is bipartite: colour around the ring red, blue, red, blue, and the last vertex is blue, which fits next to the first red one. Every path and every tree is bipartite. The hypercube Q_n is bipartite, splitting by even and odd numbers of 1s, as we saw in lesson 4. Grid graphs are bipartite: colour them like a chessboard.

Non-examples: The triangle K_3 is not bipartite, as the sports day showed. More generally no odd cycle is bipartite: going around C_5 with alternating colours, the fifth vertex gets the same colour as the first, and they are adjacent. Any graph that contains an odd cycle as a subgraph is therefore not bipartite. K_n for n at least 3 contains triangles, so it is not bipartite. The Petersen graph contains 5-cycles, so it is not bipartite either.

Konig's theorem: A graph is bipartite if and only if it contains no odd cycle. Denes Konig published this in his 1936 book, the first textbook of graph theory. It turns a search problem (find a split) into a pattern problem (look for odd cycles). Let us prove both directions.

Proof, bipartite means no odd cycle: Walk around any cycle in a bipartite graph. Every edge switches sides, from X to Y or from Y to X. To return to the starting vertex, you must switch sides an even number of times. So every cycle has an even number of edges. That is the easy direction.

Proof, no odd cycle means bipartite: It is enough to handle one connected component at a time. Pick any vertex r in the component. Put a vertex in X if its distance from r is even and in Y if its distance is odd. Now suppose some edge uv joins two vertices in the same set, so d(r, u) and d(r, v) have the same parity. Then go from r to u along a shortest path, cross the edge uv, and come back from v to r along a shortest path. This closed walk has length d(r, u) + 1 + d(r, v), which is odd because the two distances have the same parity. By the lemma from lesson 8, an odd closed walk contains an odd cycle. That contradicts our assumption. So every edge joins X to Y, and the graph is bipartite.

The BFS test: The proof is also an algorithm. Run breadth-first search from a vertex r. BFS puts vertices in layers by distance: layer 0 is r, layer 1 its neighbours, and so on. Colour even layers red and odd layers blue. Then check every edge. If some edge joins two vertices of the same colour, the graph contains an odd cycle and is not bipartite. Otherwise the colouring is a bipartition. Repeat for each component. The whole test takes time proportional to n + m.

BFS test, worked: Vertices 1 to 6, edges 12, 23, 34, 45, 56, 61 and the chord 14. BFS from 1: layer 0 is {1}, layer 1 is {2, 4, 6}, layer 2 is {3, 5}. Even layers: {1, 3, 5}. Odd layer: {2, 4, 6}. Check each edge: 12, 23, 34, 45, 56, 61 and 14 all join an odd-numbered vertex to an even-numbered one. So the graph is bipartite with X = {1, 3, 5} and Y = {2, 4, 6}. Now add the edge 13. BFS from 1 now puts 3 into layer 1 together with 2, and the edge 23 joins two vertices in the same layer. The odd cycle 1 - 2 - 3 - 1 is the proof that the new graph is not bipartite.

Testing by hand without BFS: For small graphs you can do the same thing with a pencil. Colour any vertex red. Colour all its neighbours blue. Colour all their uncoloured neighbours red, and keep spreading. If you ever need to give a vertex a colour that clashes with a neighbour, stop and trace back: the two clashing vertices, together with the paths that coloured them, contain an odd cycle. If the spreading finishes with no clash, you have your two sides. This is just BFS done by hand, but it is the method most students use in exams.

The split is unique for connected graphs: If a bipartite graph is connected, its bipartition is unique, except that you can swap the names X and Y. Once you colour one vertex red, every vertex's colour is forced by its distance from it. If the graph has c components, each component can be flipped independently, so there are 2^c ways to 2-colour it. A graph of three separate edges has 2^3 = 8 red-blue colourings.

Degrees on both sides: In a bipartite graph, every edge has exactly one end in X. So the sum of the degrees of the vertices in X equals the number of edges m, and the same is true for Y. A nice consequence: if a bipartite graph is k-regular with k at least 1, then k times |X| = m = k times |Y|, so |X| = |Y|. Both sides have the same size. We will use this in lesson 18 to show every such graph has a perfect matching.

How many edges can a bipartite graph have: If the sides have sizes a and b with a + b = n, the most edges possible is a times b, reached by K_(a,b). The product a times b is largest when a and b are as equal as possible, giving at most n squared / 4 edges, rounded down. For n = 10 that is 25 edges, from K_(5,5). So a graph on 10 vertices with 26 edges cannot be bipartite and must contain an odd cycle. In lesson 25 Mantel's theorem will show something stronger: it must contain a triangle.

Subgraphs and bipartite graphs: Every subgraph of a bipartite graph is bipartite, since you can keep the same colours. So being bipartite is easy to destroy, by adding one wrong edge, and impossible to create by deleting vertices of a non-bipartite graph unless you break all its odd cycles. Finding the fewest vertices to delete to make a graph bipartite is a hard problem in general, which shows how special bipartite graphs are.

The chessboard puzzle: Remove two opposite corner squares from an 8 by 8 chessboard. Can the remaining 62 squares be covered exactly by 31 dominoes, each covering two neighbouring squares? Think of the squares as vertices of the grid graph, which is bipartite with black and white sides. Each domino covers one black and one white square. Opposite corners have the same colour, so after removing them there are 32 squares of one colour and 30 of the other. 31 dominoes would need 31 of each, so it is impossible. A two-line proof, thanks to bipartiteness.

The adjacency matrix of a bipartite graph: If you list the vertices of X first and then the vertices of Y, the adjacency matrix has a special block shape: zeros in the X by X block and in the Y by Y block, and all the 1s in the two off-diagonal blocks, which are transposes of each other. The smaller off-diagonal block, with one row per X vertex and one column per Y vertex, is called the biadjacency matrix. It holds all the information about the graph and is how bipartite data, like customers and products, is usually stored.

Real-life example 1, an online shop: On Daraz, think of customers on one side and products on the other, with an edge whenever a customer bought a product. Customers never buy customers, and products never buy products, so the graph is bipartite. Recommendation systems work on such graphs: if you and another shopper bought many of the same products, then products the other shopper bought are good suggestions for you. Two steps across the bipartite graph (you to a product to another shopper) and then one more step (to a new product) is exactly how many simple recommendation ideas move.

Real-life example 2, a coaching centre timetable: A coaching centre in Mymensingh has teachers on one side and subjects on the other, with an edge if a teacher can teach that subject. This graph is bipartite by nature. The question 'can every subject get its own teacher at the same time?' is a matching question on a bipartite graph, which lesson 18 answers with Hall's theorem. Many real assignment problems, like jobs and workers or students and hostel rooms, are bipartite in the same way.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Thinking a graph with an even number of vertices must be bipartite. Forgetting that a single odd cycle anywhere ruins bipartiteness. Assuming a bipartite graph must have equal sides; only regular ones must. Running the BFS test on only one component of a disconnected graph. Exams ask: decide whether given graphs are bipartite, giving a bipartition or an odd cycle; prove Konig's theorem; prove a k-regular bipartite graph has equal sides; find the maximum edges of a bipartite graph on n vertices; solve chessboard-colouring puzzles.

Recap: A graph is bipartite if its vertices split into two sides with every edge going across, which is the same as being 2-colourable. Konig's theorem: bipartite exactly when there is no odd cycle, proved by colouring vertices by even or odd distance from a root. BFS tests it in linear time. Connected bipartite graphs have a unique split; each side's degrees add up to m; regular bipartite graphs have equal sides; and there are at most n squared / 4 edges. Next lesson: Euler's famous tours that use every edge exactly once.
key_points: A graph is bipartite if its vertices split into X and Y with every edge joining X to Y; equivalently, it is 2-colourable.
Konig's theorem (1936): a graph is bipartite if and only if it has no odd cycle.
Proof idea: colour vertices by even or odd distance from a root; a same-colour edge would create an odd closed walk, hence an odd cycle.
BFS layering tests bipartiteness in time proportional to n + m and either gives a bipartition or finds an odd cycle.
Trees, even cycles, K_(m,n), grids and Q_n are bipartite; odd cycles, K_n (n >= 3) and the Petersen graph are not.
A connected bipartite graph has a unique bipartition up to swapping; with c components there are 2^c 2-colourings.
In a bipartite graph the degrees in X add up to m, and so do the degrees in Y; a k-regular bipartite graph has |X| = |Y|.
A bipartite graph on n vertices has at most n^2/4 edges (rounded down), reached by the balanced K_(n/2, n/2).
lessons.tip: To show a graph is not bipartite, you only need one odd cycle, and you should write it out vertex by vertex. To show it is bipartite, write X and Y explicitly. An answer with just 'yes' or 'no' loses most of the marks.
lessons.task: Run the BFS bipartite test by hand on the graph with vertices 1 to 8 and edges 12, 23, 34, 41, 15, 26, 37, 48, 56, 67, 78, 85 (this is the cube Q_3). Write the layers and the two sides. Then add the edge 13 and find the odd cycle the test reveals.

quiz.q: Which of these graphs is NOT bipartite?
quiz.explain: C_7 is an odd cycle, so it cannot be 2-coloured. Even cycles, trees and complete bipartite graphs are all bipartite.

quiz.q: What does Konig's theorem state?
options: A graph is bipartite iff it has an even number of vertices
A graph is bipartite iff it contains no odd cycle
A graph is bipartite iff it is a tree
A graph is bipartite iff all degrees are even
quiz.explain: Bipartite graphs are exactly the graphs without odd cycles; the parity of vertex count or degrees does not decide it.

quiz.q: A bipartite graph is 4-regular and one side has 7 vertices. How many vertices does the other side have?
quiz.explain: The degrees on each side add up to m, so 4 x 7 = m = 4 x |Y|, giving |Y| = 7.

quiz.q: What is the maximum number of edges in a bipartite simple graph on 12 vertices?
quiz.explain: The maximum is n^2/4 = 144/4 = 36, reached by K_(6,6).

quiz.q: In the BFS test, which finding proves the graph is not bipartite?
options: Some layer has more than 3 vertices
An edge joins two vertices in the same layer
The graph has a vertex of degree 1
quiz.explain: Two vertices in the same layer have equal distance from the root, so the edge between them closes an odd closed walk, which contains an odd cycle.

lessons.title: Eulerian Graphs: Using Every Edge Once
lessons.content:
Here is a classic puzzle many of us played on the back of an exercise book: draw a little house with a square, both diagonals and a roof, without lifting your pen and without going over any line twice. Some people manage it, some get stuck forever. Is there a trick? Yes, and it is the same trick Euler used for the Konigsberg bridges in 1736. Today we turn that trick into a full theorem, prove it, and learn two algorithms that actually find the route. Then we see why postmen, garbage trucks and even DNA scientists care.

Definitions: An Euler trail in a graph is a trail that uses every edge exactly once. An Euler circuit (or Euler tour) is a closed Euler trail: it uses every edge exactly once and ends where it started. A graph with an Euler circuit is called Eulerian. A graph that has an Euler trail but no Euler circuit is sometimes called semi-Eulerian. Remember from lesson 8 that a trail may repeat vertices; only edges must not repeat. Isolated vertices do not matter here, because they have no edges to use.

The main theorem: A connected graph has an Euler circuit if and only if every vertex has even degree. Euler showed in 1736 that even degrees are necessary. The fact that they are also sufficient was proved carefully by Carl Hierholzer, published in 1873. The theorem also works for multigraphs, which matters, because Konigsberg itself was a multigraph.

Proof that even degrees are needed: Follow an Euler circuit around. Every time it passes through a vertex, it arrives on one edge and leaves on another, using two edges at that vertex. The starting vertex is also left at the very beginning and entered at the very end, which again is a pair. Since every edge is used exactly once, the edges at each vertex are used up in pairs, so every degree is even.

Proof that even degrees are enough, part 1: Start at any vertex v and walk, never reusing an edge, until you get stuck. Where can you get stuck? Each time you enter a vertex other than v, you have used an odd number of its edges so far, and since its degree is even, there is at least one unused edge to leave by. So you can only get stuck at v. That means the walk you made is a closed trail, call it C.

Proof that even degrees are enough, part 2: If C uses every edge, we are done. If not, remove the edges of C. Every vertex loses an even number of edges, so all degrees stay even. Because the graph is connected, some vertex u on C still has an unused edge. Start at u and build another closed trail C' from the leftover edges in the same way. Now splice: travel along C until you reach u, take the whole detour C', come back to u, and finish C. You get a longer closed trail. Repeat until every edge is used. This splicing idea is exactly Hierholzer's algorithm.

Euler trails: A connected graph has an Euler trail (not necessarily closed) if and only if it has either zero or exactly two vertices of odd degree. If it has exactly two odd vertices, every Euler trail starts at one of them and ends at the other. Proof idea: if u and v are the two odd vertices, add an extra edge between them. Now every degree is even, so there is an Euler circuit. Delete the extra edge from the circuit, and what remains is an Euler trail from u to v.

Konigsberg settled: The four land pieces had degrees 5, 3, 3 and 3. All four are odd, which is more than two, so there is neither an Euler circuit nor an Euler trail. If the citizens had built one more bridge between two of the odd pieces, two odd vertices would remain and an Euler trail would exist. Two more bridges in the right places would make all degrees even and give an Euler circuit.

The little house: Label the square A and B at the bottom, D and C at the top, with diagonals AC and BD and a roof vertex E joined to C and D. Degrees: A has 3 (AB, AD, AC), B has 3 (AB, BC, BD), C has 4 (BC, CD, AC, CE), D has 4 (AD, CD, BD, DE), E has 2. Exactly two odd vertices, A and B. So you can draw the house in one stroke, but only if you start at A or B. One route: A - B - C - D - A - C - E - D - B. Count: 8 edges, all different. Start at C and you will always get stuck.

How many strokes in general: If a connected graph has 2k odd vertices with k at least 1, its edges can be split into exactly k trails, and no fewer. Each trail can absorb at most two odd vertices as its ends. So a figure with 6 odd vertices needs at least 3 pen strokes. This tells you instantly how many times you must lift the pen.

Families that are Eulerian: K_n has every degree equal to n - 1, so K_n has an Euler circuit exactly when n is odd: K_5 yes, K_4 no. Every cycle C_n is Eulerian, of course. K_(m,n) has degrees m and n, so it is Eulerian exactly when both m and n are even. The hypercube Q_n is n-regular, so it is Eulerian when n is even. The Petersen graph is 3-regular, with ten odd vertices, so it has neither an Euler circuit nor an Euler trail, and drawing it needs 5 pen strokes.

Fleury's algorithm: A careful step-by-step method. Start at an odd vertex if there is one, otherwise anywhere. At each step, choose an unused edge from the current vertex, but never cross a bridge of the remaining graph unless you have no other choice. Then delete the edge you crossed. The rule 'don't burn your bridges' guarantees you never strand edges in a part you cannot return to. Fleury's method is easy to do by hand but slow for computers, because it keeps checking for bridges.

Hierholzer's algorithm, worked: Take the bow tie: triangles a - b - c - a and a - d - e - a sharing vertex a. Degrees: a has 4, the rest have 2, all even, so an Euler circuit exists. Start at b. Walk b - c - a - b. We are stuck at b, since both its edges are used. The circuit so far is b - c - a - b. Vertex a still has unused edges ad and ae. From a, walk a - d - e - a. Splice it in where a appears: b - c - a - d - e - a - b. That uses all 6 edges, done. Computers implement this with a stack and finish in time proportional to the number of edges.

Fleury, worked on the little house: Start at A (odd). From A the edges are AB, AD and AC; none is a bridge at the start, so take AB. From B take BC. From C take CD. From D take DA. From A the only unused edge is AC, so take it. From C, the edges left are CE; take it. From E take ED. From D take DB, the last edge, ending at the other odd vertex B. At no point were we forced to cross a bridge early, so Fleury succeeded with the route A - B - C - D - A - C - E - D - B.

Directed graphs: A directed graph has an Euler circuit if and only if it is connected (ignoring directions, and ignoring isolated vertices) and every vertex has in-degree equal to out-degree. It has an Euler trail if and only if it is connected and either all vertices are balanced, or exactly one vertex has out-degree one more than in-degree (the start), exactly one has in-degree one more than out-degree (the end), and all others are balanced. Think of one-way streets: every street must be driven exactly once, in its own direction.

The Chinese postman problem: A postman must walk along every street of his area at least once and return to the post office, walking as little as possible. If the street graph is Eulerian, the answer is just an Euler circuit, and every street is walked exactly once. If not, some streets must be walked twice. The trick is to pair up the odd vertices and repeat the shortest paths between the pairs, choosing the pairing with the smallest total extra length. Then all degrees become even and an Euler circuit of the enlarged graph is the best route. The problem was posed by the Chinese mathematician Kwan Mei-Ko in the early 1960s, which is where its name comes from, and Jack Edmonds and Ellis Johnson gave an efficient algorithm for it in 1973.

Real-life example 1, waste collection in Dhaka: A city corporation truck must pass along every lane in a ward to collect garbage and return to the depot. Each lane is an edge, each crossing a vertex, and lane lengths are weights. If the ward's crossings all have even degree, the driver can do it with zero repeated lanes. If there are, say, four odd crossings, the planner pairs them into two pairs with the shortest connecting paths, and only those lanes get driven twice. This is the Chinese postman solution, and it saves fuel and time every day. The same idea is used for street sweeping, meter reading and road inspection.

Real-life example 2, reading DNA: Machines cannot read a whole genome in one go; they read millions of short overlapping pieces. One successful way to put them back together builds a de Bruijn graph, where short overlapping strings become edges, and then looks for an Eulerian path through it. Every piece is used once, in an order that agrees with the overlaps. So a puzzle from 1736 about bridges helps modern biologists assemble genomes, including research labs studying crops and diseases in Bangladesh.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Forgetting the connectivity condition: two separate triangles have all degrees even but no Euler circuit. Starting an Euler trail at an even vertex when there are two odd ones. Mixing up Euler (every edge once) with Hamilton (every vertex once, next lesson). In Fleury's algorithm, crossing a bridge when another edge was available. Exams ask: decide if a graph has an Euler circuit or trail; prove Euler's theorem; run Fleury's or Hierholzer's algorithm and write the route; find the minimum number of strokes; solve a small Chinese postman problem; state the directed version.

Recap: A connected graph has an Euler circuit exactly when all degrees are even, and an Euler trail exactly when it has 0 or 2 odd vertices, starting and ending at the odd ones. The proof walks until stuck, which can only happen at the start, then splices extra closed trails, which is Hierholzer's algorithm. Fleury's algorithm avoids bridges. With 2k odd vertices you need k strokes. Digraphs need in-degree equal to out-degree. The Chinese postman problem duplicates shortest paths between paired odd vertices. Next lesson: Hamilton cycles, which visit every vertex once, and why they are much harder.
key_points: An Euler trail uses every edge exactly once; an Euler circuit is a closed Euler trail.
A connected graph has an Euler circuit if and only if every vertex has even degree (Euler 1736, Hierholzer 1873).
A connected graph has an Euler trail iff it has 0 or 2 odd vertices; with 2, the trail starts at one odd vertex and ends at the other.
Proof idea: walk until stuck (only possible at the start), then splice in extra closed trails; this is Hierholzer's algorithm.
Fleury's algorithm: never cross a bridge of the remaining graph unless there is no other choice.
A connected graph with 2k odd vertices (k >= 1) needs exactly k trails (pen strokes) to cover all edges.
A digraph has an Euler circuit iff it is connected and every vertex has in-degree equal to out-degree.
Chinese postman: pair the odd vertices and repeat the shortest connecting paths with the least total length, then take an Euler circuit.
lessons.tip: Before trying to trace a route, write the degree of every vertex and count the odd ones. That single count tells you whether a circuit, a trail or neither exists, and where to start. Only then pick up the pencil.
lessons.task: Draw the graph with vertices 1 to 6 and edges 12, 13, 23, 24, 35, 45, 46, 56, 34. Count the odd-degree vertices, decide whether an Euler circuit or Euler trail exists, and then find one using Hierholzer's splicing method. Write every step.

quiz.q: A connected graph has degrees 4, 4, 2, 2, 2, 2. What does it have?
options: An Euler trail but no circuit
quiz.explain: It is connected and every degree is even, so by Euler's theorem it has an Euler circuit.

quiz.q: A connected graph has exactly two odd vertices, u and v. Where must an Euler trail start?
options: At a vertex of the largest degree
It cannot have an Euler trail
quiz.explain: With exactly two odd vertices, every Euler trail begins at one of them and ends at the other.

quiz.q: A connected figure has 8 odd-degree vertices. What is the fewest number of pen strokes needed to draw it, using each line exactly once?
quiz.explain: Each stroke (trail) can have at most two odd vertices as its ends, so 2k = 8 odd vertices need k = 4 strokes.

quiz.q: What is the key rule of Fleury's algorithm?
options: Do not cross a bridge of the remaining graph unless there is no other choice
Always return to the start after 3 steps
quiz.explain: Crossing a bridge too early can strand unused edges on the far side, so Fleury only crosses a bridge when forced.

quiz.q: Two separate triangles have all degrees equal to 2. Why is there no Euler circuit?
options: Because the graph is not connected
quiz.explain: Euler's theorem needs a connected graph (apart from isolated vertices). A single closed trail cannot jump between the two triangles.

lessons.title: Hamiltonian Graphs: Visiting Every Vertex Once
lessons.content:
A Foodpanda rider in Uttara has six orders to deliver. She wants to start at the restaurant, visit every customer exactly once, and come back, without passing any customer's house twice. That is a different puzzle from last lesson. Euler cared about using every edge (road) once. Now we care about visiting every vertex (place) once, and we do not mind skipping roads. It sounds like a tiny change, but it turns an easy problem into one of the hardest problems in computer science. Today we meet Hamilton paths and cycles, learn the best-known conditions that guarantee them, and learn tests that prove they cannot exist.

Definitions: A Hamilton path is a path that visits every vertex of the graph exactly once. A Hamilton cycle is a cycle that visits every vertex exactly once and returns to the start. A graph with a Hamilton cycle is called Hamiltonian. A Hamilton cycle in a graph with n vertices has exactly n edges, and a Hamilton path has n - 1 edges. If a graph has a Hamilton cycle, removing any one edge of that cycle gives a Hamilton path, but a Hamilton path does not always close into a cycle.

Where the name comes from: In 1857 the Irish mathematician William Rowan Hamilton invented a puzzle called the Icosian game. The board was the skeleton of a dodecahedron, a solid with 12 pentagon faces, 20 corners and 30 edges. The challenge was to travel along the edges visiting every corner exactly once and return home. In graph words: find a Hamilton cycle in the dodecahedron graph. It can be done, and Hamilton's name stuck to the whole idea, even though others had studied similar questions earlier.

The big difference from Euler: For Euler circuits we have a perfect, fast test: connected and all degrees even. For Hamilton cycles, nobody knows any test that is both exact and fast. Deciding whether a graph has a Hamilton cycle is NP-complete; it was on Richard Karp's famous 1972 list of 21 NP-complete problems. So unless P = NP, there is no fast algorithm that works for every graph. What we do have are sufficient conditions (if this holds, a Hamilton cycle exists) and necessary conditions (if this fails, no Hamilton cycle exists).

Families that are Hamiltonian: Every cycle C_n is Hamiltonian, trivially. K_n for n at least 3 is Hamiltonian: visit the vertices in any order and you can always jump to the next one. The wheel is Hamiltonian: go around the rim, but detour through the hub once. The hypercube Q_n for n at least 2 is Hamiltonian, as the Gray code below shows. An r by c grid graph with r and c at least 2 has a Hamilton cycle exactly when r times c is even.

Families that are not: A tree with at least 2 vertices has no cycles at all, so it is not Hamiltonian. A graph with a cut vertex is not Hamiltonian: a Hamilton cycle stays connected when any one vertex is removed (it becomes a path), so removing the cut vertex could not disconnect the graph. K_(m,n) is Hamiltonian only when m = n and m is at least 2, because a cycle in a bipartite graph alternates sides and so uses equally many vertices from each side. The Petersen graph is not Hamiltonian, although it does have a Hamilton path.

A necessary condition, the component test: If G is Hamiltonian, then for every non-empty set S of vertices, deleting S leaves at most |S| components. Reason: the Hamilton cycle itself, after removing the vertices of S, breaks into at most |S| pieces of path, and those pieces already connect everything that remains. So if you can find a set S whose removal leaves more than |S| components, G is not Hamiltonian. Example: in K_(2,3), delete the two vertices of the small side. Three isolated vertices remain, and 3 is more than 2, so K_(2,3) has no Hamilton cycle.

Using the test carefully: The test only proves 'no'. Passing it does not prove 'yes'. The Petersen graph passes it, since removing any set S never leaves more than |S| pieces, yet it has no Hamilton cycle. Still, the test is a quick first check in exams: look for cut vertices, look for a small set whose removal leaves many isolated vertices, and check bipartite graphs for unequal sides.

Dirac's theorem: Let G be a simple graph with n at least 3 vertices. If every vertex has degree at least n/2, then G is Hamiltonian. Gabriel Dirac proved this in 1952. Example: a graph on 10 vertices where everyone has at least 5 neighbours must have a Hamilton cycle, no matter how the edges are arranged. The condition is sufficient but not necessary: C_10 is Hamiltonian even though its minimum degree is only 2.

Ore's theorem: Let G be a simple graph with n at least 3 vertices. If deg(u) + deg(v) is at least n for every pair of non-adjacent vertices u and v, then G is Hamiltonian. Oystein Ore proved this in 1960. It is stronger than Dirac's theorem: if every degree is at least n/2, then any two degrees add up to at least n, so Dirac's condition implies Ore's. But Ore can apply when Dirac does not, because it allows a few low-degree vertices as long as they are adjacent to the other low ones.

Why Ore's theorem is true, the idea: Suppose a graph satisfies Ore's condition but is not Hamiltonian. Keep adding edges as long as the graph stays non-Hamiltonian; the condition stays true because degrees only grow. Eventually adding any one more edge, say uv, would create a Hamilton cycle. So the graph already has a Hamilton path from u to v: u = x1, x2, ..., xn = v. Now look at neighbours. If u is adjacent to x(i+1) and v is adjacent to xi for some i, then u - x(i+1) - ... - v - xi - ... - x1 = u is a Hamilton cycle, a contradiction. Count how many i are blocked: u has deg(u) neighbours and v has deg(v), and the sum is at least n, but there are only n - 1 positions, so by pigeonhole some i works. Contradiction, so the graph was Hamiltonian after all.

The closure idea: The proof suggests a tool. If u and v are non-adjacent and deg(u) + deg(v) is at least n, then G is Hamiltonian exactly when G plus the edge uv is Hamiltonian. Keep adding such edges until none can be added; the result is called the closure of G. Bondy and Chvatal showed in 1976 that G is Hamiltonian if and only if its closure is. If the closure turns out to be complete, G is Hamiltonian.

Gray codes and the hypercube: A Gray code lists all binary strings of length n so that consecutive strings differ in exactly one bit, and the last differs from the first in one bit too. That is precisely a Hamilton cycle in Q_n. For n = 3: 000, 001, 011, 010, 110, 111, 101, 100, and back to 000. Build longer ones by reflection: list the code for n - 1 with a 0 in front, then the same list in reverse order with a 1 in front. Gray codes are used in rotary encoders, which measure the angle of a turning shaft, because changing only one bit at a time avoids reading errors.

Knight's tours: Can a chess knight visit every square of the board exactly once? Make each square a vertex and join squares a knight's move apart. A knight's tour is a Hamilton path in this graph, and a closed tour is a Hamilton cycle. On the standard 8 by 8 board closed tours exist. A knight always jumps between a light and a dark square, so the knight's graph is bipartite. On a 5 by 5 board there are 25 squares, an odd number, so a closed tour is impossible, because a cycle in a bipartite graph has an even number of vertices.

The travelling salesman problem: In a weighted complete graph, the travelling salesman problem (TSP) asks for the Hamilton cycle with the smallest total weight. With n cities there are (n - 1)!/2 different Hamilton cycles in K_n, since you can fix the start and a cycle and its reverse are the same. For 5 cities that is 12, easy. For 20 cities it is more than 6 x 10^16, far too many to check one by one. TSP is NP-hard, so in practice people use clever exact methods for medium sizes and heuristics for large ones, as you saw in the Algorithms course.

Real-life example 1, the delivery rider: The rider's restaurant plus 5 customers form 6 places, so the number of different round trips is 5!/2 = 60. She can compare all 60 on a phone in a blink. But a delivery company planning routes for a whole day, with hundreds of stops, cannot try every Hamilton cycle. Companies use approximation and heuristic methods that find very good routes quickly, even if not provably the best. The graph theory tells them why: the exact problem is NP-hard.

Real-life example 2, seating at a wedding: A host wants to seat 12 guests at a round table so that each guest sits between two people they know. Make a graph of who knows whom. A good seating is exactly a Hamilton cycle. If every guest knows at least 6 of the other 11, Dirac's theorem with n = 12 guarantees a good seating exists, no matter who knows whom. If one guest knows only one person, that guest has degree 1 and cannot be on any cycle, so no good seating exists.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Mixing up Euler (every edge) and Hamilton (every vertex). Thinking Dirac's or Ore's condition is necessary, when it is only sufficient. Using the component test to 'prove' a graph is Hamiltonian. Forgetting n at least 3 in Dirac and Ore. Exams ask: find a Hamilton cycle or prove none exists; apply Dirac and Ore; prove a graph with a cut vertex is not Hamiltonian; show K_(m,n) with m different from n is not Hamiltonian; write a Gray code; explain why Hamilton cycle is NP-complete while Euler circuit is easy.

Recap: A Hamilton cycle visits every vertex once. Deciding Hamiltonicity is NP-complete, so we rely on conditions.
