Necessary: no cut vertex, equal sides in bipartite graphs, and removing any S leaves at most |S| components. Sufficient: Dirac (every degree at least n/2) and Ore (every non-adjacent pair has degree sum at least n), and the Bondy-Chvatal closure. Gray codes give Hamilton cycles in Q_n, knight's tours are Hamilton paths, and TSP looks for the cheapest Hamilton cycle. Next lesson: trees, the simplest connected graphs.
key_points: A Hamilton path visits every vertex exactly once; a Hamilton cycle also returns to the start; such graphs are Hamiltonian.
Unlike Euler circuits, deciding whether a Hamilton cycle exists is NP-complete (on Karp's 1972 list).
Necessary condition: if G is Hamiltonian, deleting any set S leaves at most |S| components; so graphs with cut vertices are not Hamiltonian.
K_(m,n) is Hamiltonian only when m = n >= 2; trees and the Petersen graph are not Hamiltonian.
Dirac (1952): n >= 3 and every degree >= n/2 implies Hamiltonian.
Ore (1960): n >= 3 and deg(u) + deg(v) >= n for all non-adjacent u, v implies Hamiltonian; Ore's condition includes Dirac's.
Bondy-Chvatal: G is Hamiltonian iff its closure (adding edges between non-adjacent pairs with degree sum >= n) is Hamiltonian.
Gray codes are Hamilton cycles in Q_n; knight's tours are Hamilton paths; TSP seeks the cheapest Hamilton cycle among (n - 1)!/2 in K_n.
lessons.tip: When asked whether a graph is Hamiltonian, first try the quick 'no' tests (cut vertex, bipartite with unequal sides, a set S whose removal leaves more than |S| pieces), then the quick 'yes' tests (Dirac, Ore). Only if both fail, search for a cycle by hand, starting from the lowest-degree vertices because their edges are forced.
lessons.task: Write the Gray code for n = 4 using the reflection method and check it is a Hamilton cycle in Q_4 (16 strings, each differing from the next in one bit). Then show that K_(3,4) has no Hamilton cycle using the component test with S = the side of size 3.

quiz.q: What is the key difference between Euler circuits and Hamilton cycles?
options: Euler uses every vertex once; Hamilton uses every edge once
There is a simple fast test for Euler circuits, but deciding Hamilton cycles is NP-complete
Hamilton cycles exist only in trees
quiz.explain: Euler circuits exist exactly when the graph is connected with even degrees, while the Hamilton cycle problem is NP-complete.

quiz.q: A simple graph has 14 vertices and minimum degree 7. What does Dirac's theorem say?
quiz.explain: Dirac: n >= 3 and every degree >= n/2 = 7 guarantees a Hamilton cycle.

quiz.q: Why is K_(2,3) not Hamiltonian?
options: Deleting the 2-vertex side leaves 3 components, more than 2
It has too few edges to be connected
quiz.explain: A Hamilton cycle would allow at most |S| = 2 components after deleting S, but 3 isolated vertices remain. Also a bipartite cycle needs equal sides.

quiz.q: How many different Hamilton cycles does K_6 have (a cycle and its reverse counted once)?
Why can a knight not make a closed tour of a 5 by 5 board?
options: The board is too small for any path
The knight's graph has a cut vertex
The knight's graph is bipartite and 25 is odd, but cycles in bipartite graphs have even length
quiz.explain: Each knight move switches square colour, so the graph is bipartite. A closed tour would be a Hamilton cycle of odd length 25, which is impossible.

lessons.title: Trees I: What Makes a Tree
lessons.content:
Look at a family tree on the wall of your grandparents' house. At the top is great-grandfather, below him his children, below them their children, and so on. There are no loops: nobody is their own grandparent. And everybody is connected to everybody else through some chain of parents and children. Graph theory takes exactly these two properties, connected and no cycles, and calls the result a tree. Trees are the simplest connected graphs, and they show up everywhere: folders on your computer, the Bangladesh administrative map, knockout tournaments, molecules and the spanning trees that algorithms build. Today we learn the six different ways to recognise a tree and why they are all the same thing.

Definitions: A tree is a connected graph with no cycles. A forest is a graph with no cycles; it does not need to be connected, so it is a collection of trees side by side. Every tree is a forest with one component. A single vertex is a tree, the trivial tree. A path P_n and a star K_(1,n) are trees. C_n is not a tree because it is a cycle, and two separate edges form a forest that is not a tree.

Leaves: In a tree, a vertex of degree 1 is called a leaf. Lemma: every tree with at least 2 vertices has at least 2 leaves. Proof: take a longest path in the tree, from u to v. If u had a neighbour other than the next vertex on the path, that neighbour is either on the path, which would create a cycle, or off the path, which would make a longer path. Both are impossible, so u has degree 1. The same holds for v. So u and v are two leaves.

Why leaves matter: Removing a leaf and its edge from a tree leaves a smaller tree: still connected, since the leaf was hanging at the end, and still without cycles. So trees can be taken apart one leaf at a time, and built up one leaf at a time. That makes induction proofs about trees very natural: prove the fact for a single vertex, then show adding a leaf keeps it true.

The edge count: Every tree with n vertices has exactly n - 1 edges. Proof by induction: a single vertex has 0 edges. For a tree with n vertices, remove a leaf; the remaining tree has n - 1 vertices and, by induction, n - 2 edges. Put the leaf back with its one edge: n - 1 edges. So a tree with 10 vertices has 9 edges, and a tree with 1000 vertices has 999 edges.

The big equivalence theorem: For a graph G with n vertices, these six statements are equivalent; if one is true, all are true. (1) G is connected and has no cycles. (2) G is connected and has n - 1 edges. (3) G has no cycles and has n - 1 edges. (4) There is exactly one path between every pair of vertices. (5) G is connected, but removing any edge disconnects it; every edge is a bridge. (6) G has no cycles, but adding any new edge creates exactly one cycle. Any one of them can be used as the definition of a tree.

Why unique paths: If there were two different paths from u to v, follow them from u until they first separate, then continue until they first meet again. The two pieces between the separation and the meeting form a cycle. So no cycles means at most one path, and connected means at least one. Hence exactly one. Conversely, if every pair has exactly one path, a cycle is impossible, because any two vertices on a cycle would have two paths around it.

Why every edge is a bridge: From lesson 9, an edge is a bridge exactly when it lies on no cycle. A tree has no cycles, so every edge is a bridge. That is why trees are called minimally connected: they have just enough edges to stay connected, and losing any one of them breaks the graph. Adding an edge uv to a tree, on the other hand, creates exactly one cycle: the new edge plus the unique old path from u to v. That is why trees are maximally acyclic.

Counting edges both ways, a check: Statements (2) and (3) show that for a graph with n vertices and n - 1 edges, connected and acyclic always come together. So if someone gives you a connected graph with 7 vertices and 6 edges, you know without looking that it has no cycles. And a graph with 7 vertices, 6 edges and a cycle must be disconnected.

Forests: A forest with n vertices and k components (k trees) has exactly n - k edges, because each tree with n_i vertices has n_i - 1 edges and adding them up gives n - k. So a forest with 20 vertices and 3 trees has 17 edges. This also gives a quick way to count components of a forest: k = n - m.

How many leaves, exactly: The degrees of a tree add up to 2(n - 1) = 2n - 2. Subtract 2 from every degree: the total becomes -2. Leaves contribute -1 each, degree-2 vertices contribute 0, and a vertex of degree d at least 3 contributes d - 2. So the number of leaves equals 2 plus the sum of (d - 2) over all vertices of degree at least 3. Example: a tree has one vertex of degree 4, two of degree 3, and the rest have degree 1 or 2. Then it has 2 + 2 + 1 + 1 = 6 leaves, no matter how it is drawn.

The centre of a tree: Recall the centre is the set of vertices with the smallest eccentricity. Camille Jordan showed in 1869 that the centre of a tree is always either one vertex or two adjacent vertices. Here is a hands-on way to find it: delete all the leaves at once. The remaining graph is still a tree, and every vertex's eccentricity drops by exactly 1, so the centre stays the same. Repeat until one or two vertices remain. They are the centre. In the path a - b - c - d - e, peel a and e, then b and d, leaving c. In a - b - c - d, peel a and d, leaving b and c, two adjacent centre vertices.

Trees are bipartite and sparse: A tree has no cycles at all, so in particular no odd cycles, and by Konig's theorem from lesson 11 every tree is bipartite: colour vertices by even or odd depth from any vertex. Trees are also the sparsest connected graphs: with n - 1 edges, their average degree is 2(n - 1)/n, which is just under 2. Any connected graph with average degree at least 2 must therefore contain a cycle.

Rooted trees: Often we pick one vertex as the root and hang the tree from it, like a family tree. Then every other vertex has a unique parent, the next vertex on the path toward the root. The vertices below a vertex are its children. Vertices with the same parent are siblings. Ancestors are on the path up to the root, and descendants are everything below. A vertex with no children is a leaf, and a vertex with children is internal. The depth or level of a vertex is its distance from the root, and the height of the tree is the largest depth.

m-ary trees: A rooted tree is m-ary if every internal vertex has at most m children, and full m-ary if every internal vertex has exactly m children. Binary trees are 2-ary. A full m-ary tree with i internal vertices has n = m times i + 1 vertices, since every vertex except the root is a child of exactly one internal vertex, and it has (m - 1) times i + 1 leaves. A binary tree of height h has at most 2^h leaves. These counts are the basis of many analyses in Data Structures and Algorithms.

A chemistry example, alkanes: An alkane molecule has formula C_n H_(2n+2): n carbon atoms of degree 4 and 2n + 2 hydrogen atoms of degree 1, with single bonds as edges. Count: vertices n + 2n + 2 = 3n + 2. Degree sum 4n + 2n + 2 = 6n + 2, so edges = 3n + 1, which is exactly (number of vertices) - 1. A connected molecule with that edge count has no cycles: every alkane is a tree. This was one of Arthur Cayley's starting points for counting trees in the 1870s.

Real-life example 1, Bangladesh's administrative map: The country is divided into 8 divisions, the divisions into 64 districts, the districts into upazilas, and upazilas into unions. Put Bangladesh at the root, divisions at level 1, districts at level 2, and so on. Every district belongs to exactly one division, so it has exactly one parent. There are no cycles. This rooted tree is how government databases organise records, and the number of edges is always one less than the number of units, exactly as the theorem says.

Real-life example 2, a knockout tournament: In a knockout cricket or football tournament with n teams, each match eliminates exactly one team, and the tournament ends when one champion remains. So there are exactly n - 1 matches. Draw the bracket: the teams are leaves, the matches are internal vertices, and the final is the root. When n is a power of 2, it is a full binary tree with n leaves and n - 1 internal vertices, matching the formula with m = 2. A 16-team tournament always has 15 matches.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Forgetting that a tree must be connected (a forest is not necessarily a tree). Assuming n - 1 edges alone makes a tree; you also need connected or acyclic. Forgetting the trivial tree. Confusing height and depth. Exams ask: prove every tree has at least 2 leaves; prove a tree has n - 1 edges; prove the equivalence of definitions; find the number of leaves from degree information; find the centre by peeling leaves; apply the full m-ary tree formulas.

Recap: A tree is a connected graph without cycles; a forest is a graph without cycles. Every tree on n vertices has n - 1 edges and, if n is at least 2, at least two leaves. Six equivalent descriptions: connected and acyclic, connected with n - 1 edges, acyclic with n - 1 edges, unique paths, minimally connected, maximally acyclic. Forests have n - k edges. The centre of a tree is one vertex or two adjacent ones. Rooted and m-ary trees add the vocabulary of parents, children and levels. Next lesson: how many trees are there? Cayley's formula and Prufer codes.
key_points: A tree is a connected graph with no cycles; a forest is a graph with no cycles (its components are trees).
Every tree with at least 2 vertices has at least 2 leaves (ends of a longest path).
Every tree with n vertices has exactly n - 1 edges, provable by removing a leaf and using induction.
Equivalent definitions: connected + acyclic; connected + n - 1 edges; acyclic + n - 1 edges; unique paths; every edge a bridge; adding any edge makes exactly one cycle.
A forest with n vertices and k trees has n - k edges.
Number of leaves = 2 + sum of (d - 2) over vertices of degree d >= 3.
The centre of a tree is one vertex or two adjacent vertices (Jordan, 1869); find it by peeling leaves.
A full m-ary tree with i internal vertices has mi + 1 vertices and (m - 1)i + 1 leaves; a knockout tournament with n teams has n - 1 matches.
lessons.tip: In tree proofs, the two moves you need almost every time are 'take a longest path' and 'remove a leaf and use induction'. When you are stuck on a tree question, try one of those two first.
lessons.task: Draw any tree with 10 vertices that has exactly one vertex of degree 4 and one of degree 3, with all others of degree 1 or 2. Predict the number of leaves with the formula, then count them on your drawing. Then find the centre by peeling leaves step by step.

quiz.q: A forest has 30 vertices and 26 edges. How many trees (components) does it have?
quiz.explain: A forest with n vertices and k components has n - k edges, so k = n - m = 30 - 26 = 4.

quiz.q: A connected graph has 12 vertices and 11 edges. What can you conclude?
quiz.explain: A connected graph with n - 1 edges is a tree; this is one of the equivalent definitions.

quiz.q: A tree has two vertices of degree 5 and all others have degree 1 or 2. How many leaves does it have?
quiz.explain: Leaves = 2 + sum of (d - 2) over vertices with d >= 3 = 2 + 3 + 3 = 8.

quiz.q: What can the centre of a tree be?
options: Exactly one vertex, or two adjacent vertices
quiz.explain: Jordan (1869): peeling leaves repeatedly ends with one vertex or two adjacent vertices, which form the centre.

quiz.q: A knockout tournament has 32 teams. How many matches are played?
quiz.explain: Each match eliminates one team and 31 teams must be eliminated, so 31 matches, the internal vertices of the bracket tree.

lessons.title: Trees II: Counting Trees
lessons.content:
Five villages in a char area want electricity. The engineer wants to connect them with as little wire as possible, so the wiring plan must be a tree on the five villages: connected, with no wasteful loops. How many different plans are there to choose from? Try to list them and you will quickly lose track. The answer is exactly 125, and there is a beautiful formula behind it. Today we learn how to count trees: Cayley's formula, the clever Prufer code that proves it, and the matrix-tree theorem that counts spanning trees of any graph using a determinant.

Labelled versus unlabelled: When we count trees we must be clear about labels. A labelled tree has named vertices, like villages 1 to 5, and two trees count as different if they have different edge sets, even if they have the same shape. An unlabelled tree only cares about shape, which means counting isomorphism classes. On 3 vertices there is only one shape, the path, but there are 3 labelled trees, since any of the 3 vertices can be in the middle.

Small cases: n = 1: 1 tree. n = 2: 1 tree, a single edge. n = 3: 3 labelled trees. n = 4: there are two shapes, the star K_(1,3) and the path P_4. Labelled stars: choose the centre, 4 ways. Labelled paths: a path is an ordering of the 4 vertices, 4! = 24 orderings, but each path is counted twice (forwards and backwards), so 12. Total 4 + 12 = 16. Look at the pattern: 1, 1, 3, 16. Next comes 125.

Cayley's formula: The number of labelled trees on n vertices is n^(n - 2). Check: 3^1 = 3, 4^2 = 16, 5^3 = 125, and 10^8 = 100 million for 10 vertices. The formula carries Arthur Cayley's name from his 1889 paper, though Carl Borchardt had found an equivalent result earlier, in 1860. There are many proofs; the most famous is a bijection found by Heinz Prufer in 1918.

The Prufer code idea: Prufer found a way to turn every labelled tree on vertices 1 to n into a sequence of length n - 2, where each entry is a number from 1 to n, and to turn every such sequence back into exactly one tree. Since there are n choices for each of the n - 2 positions, there are n^(n - 2) sequences, and so n^(n - 2) trees. Counting trees becomes counting sequences, which is easy.

Encoding a tree: Repeat n - 2 times: find the leaf with the smallest label, write down its only neighbour, and delete that leaf. When two vertices remain, stop. The list you wrote is the Prufer code.

Encoding, worked: Tree on 6 vertices with edges 1-4, 2-4, 3-4, 4-5, 5-6. Leaves are 1, 2, 3 and 6. Smallest leaf is 1, its neighbour is 4: write 4, delete 1. Leaves now 2, 3, 6: smallest is 2, write 4, delete 2. Smallest is 3, write 4, delete 3. Now vertex 4 has only neighbour 5, so it is a leaf; leaves are 4 and 6, smallest is 4, write 5, delete 4. Two vertices, 5 and 6, remain, so stop. The Prufer code is (4, 4, 4, 5), of length 4 = 6 - 2.

A useful property: Every vertex v appears in the Prufer code exactly deg(v) - 1 times. In our example vertex 4 has degree 4 and appears 3 times; vertex 5 has degree 2 and appears once; the leaves 1, 2, 3 and 6 never appear. So the leaves of a tree are exactly the labels missing from its code. This property is the key to decoding.

Decoding a sequence: Start with the code S and the list L = 1, 2, ..., n. Repeat: find the smallest number in L that does not appear in S. Join it by an edge to the first entry of S. Remove that number from L and remove the first entry from S. When S is empty, two numbers remain in L; join them with an edge. You have rebuilt the tree.

Decoding, worked: S = (4, 4, 4, 5), L = 1 to 6. Smallest in L not in S is 1: edge 1-4. Now S = (4, 4, 5), L = 2 to 6. Smallest not in S is 2: edge 2-4. S = (4, 5), L = 3, 4, 5, 6. Smallest not in S is 3: edge 3-4. S = (5), L = 4, 5, 6. Smallest not in S is 4: edge 4-5. S is empty, L = 5, 6: edge 5-6. Edges 1-4, 2-4, 3-4, 4-5, 5-6: exactly the tree we started with. Encoding and decoding undo each other, which proves the bijection.

Trees with given degrees: The property 'v appears deg(v) - 1 times' gives a bonus formula. The number of labelled trees on vertices 1 to n where vertex i has degree d_i (with the d_i adding up to 2n - 2) equals (n - 2)! divided by the product of (d_i - 1)! over all i. Example: on 6 vertices, how many trees have vertex 4 of degree 4, vertex 5 of degree 2 and all others leaves? The code has four 4s minus one, so three 4s and one 5: 4!/(3! times 1!) = 4 trees. Check: vertex 5 joins 4 and one of the other four vertices, and there are 4 choices. Correct.

Unlabelled trees: Counting shapes is much harder, and there is no simple closed formula. The numbers of unlabelled trees on 1 to 7 vertices are 1, 1, 1, 2, 3, 6, 11. On 5 vertices the three shapes are the path P_5, the star K_(1,4), and the 'chair' shape where one vertex of degree 3 has a path of length 2 hanging from it. Listing them by maximum degree is a good way to make sure you have them all.

Spanning trees: A spanning tree of a connected graph G is a subgraph that is a tree and contains every vertex of G. Every connected graph has at least one, because you can keep deleting edges that lie on cycles until none remain. We write tau(G) for the number of spanning trees. Cayley's formula says tau(K_n) = n^(n - 2), since every labelled tree on n vertices is a spanning tree of K_n. A tree has tau = 1, and the cycle C_n has tau = n, because removing any one of its n edges leaves a spanning path. For complete bipartite graphs, tau(K_(m,n)) = m^(n - 1) times n^(m - 1).

The Laplacian again: Recall from lesson 6 that the Laplacian of G is L = D - A: degrees on the diagonal, -1 for each edge, 0 elsewhere. Every row adds up to 0, so the determinant of L itself is always 0. But if you delete any one row and the matching column, the determinant of what remains is special.

Kirchhoff's matrix-tree theorem: For any connected graph G, the number of spanning trees tau(G) equals the determinant of the matrix you get from the Laplacian L by deleting row i and column i, for any i you like. Gustav Kirchhoff found this in 1847 while studying electrical circuits. It turns a counting problem into a determinant, which computers can calculate quickly even for large graphs.

Matrix-tree, worked on the square: C_4 with vertices 1, 2, 3, 4 in order. Each degree is 2. Delete row 1 and column 1 of L. What remains is the 3 by 3 matrix with rows (2, -1, 0), (-1, 2, -1), (0, -1, 2). Its determinant is 2 times (2 x 2 - (-1)(-1)) minus (-1) times ((-1) x 2 - (-1) x 0) plus 0 = 2 x 3 - 2 = 4. So C_4 has 4 spanning trees, matching tau(C_n) = n.

Matrix-tree, worked on K_4: Every degree is 3 and every off-diagonal entry is -1. Delete one row and column to get rows (3, -1, -1), (-1, 3, -1), (-1, -1, 3). Determinant: 3 times (9 - 1) minus (-1) times (-3 - 1) plus (-1) times (1 + 3) = 24 - 4 - 4 = 16. That is 4^2 = 16, matching Cayley's formula. Two completely different methods, the same answer.

Deletion and contraction: There is also a recursive way to count. For any edge e that is not a loop, tau(G) = tau(G - e) + tau(G / e). Spanning trees either avoid e, and then they are spanning trees of G - e, or use e, and then contracting e turns them into spanning trees of G / e. Here G / e must keep parallel edges. Example: the triangle. G - e is a path with 1 spanning tree. G / e is two vertices joined by two parallel edges, with 2 spanning trees. Total 3, correct.

Real-life example 1, the village wiring: For the five villages, every possible minimal wiring plan is a labelled tree on 5 vertices, so there are 5^3 = 125 plans. If some pairs of villages cannot be joined directly, because a river channel is in the way, the possible links form a graph G instead of K_5, and the number of plans is tau(G), which the engineer can compute with the matrix-tree theorem on a laptop. Picking the cheapest among them is the minimum spanning tree problem from lesson 16 and the Algorithms course.

Real-life example 2, network reliability: A graph with many spanning trees has many different ways to stay connected, so it is more robust when links fail at random. Network designers sometimes compare two designs with the same number of links by computing tau for each: the one with more spanning trees usually survives random failures better. Electrical engineers use the same matrix in circuit analysis, which is exactly where Kirchhoff started.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Forgetting that Cayley's formula counts labelled trees, not shapes. Writing a Prufer code of length n instead of n - 2. In encoding, removing the smallest vertex instead of the smallest leaf. In decoding, forgetting to skip numbers still in the remaining sequence. Taking the determinant of the whole Laplacian, which is always 0. Exams ask: encode and decode Prufer codes; prove Cayley's formula; count trees with given degrees; list unlabelled trees on 5 or 6 vertices; compute tau with the matrix-tree theorem or deletion-contraction.

Recap: There are n^(n - 2) labelled trees on n vertices (Cayley's formula). Prufer codes give a bijection between these trees and sequences of length n - 2 from 1 to n: encode by repeatedly removing the smallest leaf and writing its neighbour, decode by repeatedly joining the smallest label not in the sequence. Each vertex appears deg - 1 times. Unlabelled trees have no simple formula: 1, 1, 1, 2, 3, 6, 11. Kirchhoff's matrix-tree theorem counts spanning trees of any graph with a determinant of the Laplacian with one row and column removed. Next lesson: spanning trees, cycles, cuts and minimum spanning trees.
key_points: Labelled trees count different edge sets; unlabelled trees count shapes (isomorphism classes).
Cayley's formula: there are n^(n - 2) labelled trees on n vertices (3, 16, 125 for n = 3, 4, 5).
Prufer encoding: repeatedly delete the smallest leaf and write its neighbour, giving a sequence of length n - 2.
Prufer decoding: repeatedly join the smallest label not in the remaining sequence to the first entry; finally join the last two labels.
Each vertex appears deg(v) - 1 times in its Prufer code; trees with degrees d_i number (n - 2)! / product of (d_i - 1)!.
Unlabelled trees on 1 to 7 vertices: 1, 1, 1, 2, 3, 6, 11.
Matrix-tree theorem (Kirchhoff 1847): tau(G) equals the determinant of the Laplacian with any one row and its column deleted.
tau(C_n) = n, tau(K_n) = n^(n - 2), tau(K_(m,n)) = m^(n-1) n^(m-1), and tau(G) = tau(G - e) + tau(G / e).
lessons.tip: When you encode or decode a Prufer code in an exam, keep a small table with two columns: what is left and what you wrote. Most mistakes come from losing track of which leaves or labels are still available, and a table makes every step checkable.
lessons.task: Find the Prufer code of the tree with edges 1-2, 2-3, 2-4, 4-5, 4-6, 6-7. Then decode the sequence (3, 3, 1, 5) into a tree on 6 vertices. Finally, use the matrix-tree theorem to count the spanning trees of K_4 with one edge removed (the answer should be 8).

quiz.q: How many labelled trees are there on 6 vertices?
quiz.explain: Cayley's formula gives n^(n - 2) = 6^4 = 1296.

quiz.q: What is the Prufer code of the star with centre 1 and leaves 2, 3, 4, 5?
quiz.explain: Each time the smallest leaf (2, then 3, then 4) is removed and its neighbour 1 is written. The code has length n - 2 = 3.

quiz.q: A vertex appears 3 times in a tree's Prufer code. What is its degree?
quiz.explain: Every vertex appears deg(v) - 1 times, so deg(v) = 3 + 1 = 4.

quiz.q: How many unlabelled trees (different shapes) are there on 5 vertices?
quiz.explain: The path P_5, the star K_(1,4), and the shape with one degree-3 vertex and a path of length 2 attached: 3 shapes.

quiz.q: What does Kirchhoff's matrix-tree theorem compute?
options: The number of spanning trees, as a determinant of the Laplacian with one row and column removed
The length of the shortest cycle
quiz.explain: Deleting any one row and the same column of L = D - A and taking the determinant gives tau(G).

lessons.title: Spanning Trees, Cycles, Cuts and Minimum Spanning Trees
lessons.content:
Think of a fishing net. Pull out threads one by one, and as long as you only remove threads that are part of a loop, the net stays in one piece. At some point every remaining thread is essential, and the net has become a tree. How many threads did you remove? It turns out the answer does not depend on which threads you chose, only on the numbers of knots and threads. Today we look at the partnership between spanning trees, cycles and cuts. It explains why electrical circuits have a certain number of independent loop equations, why programmers measure code complexity with a graph formula, and why the famous minimum spanning tree algorithms of Kruskal, Prim and Boruvka are correct.

Spanning trees and cotrees: Let G be connected with n vertices and m edges, and let T be a spanning tree. T has n - 1 edges, called branches. The remaining m - n + 1 edges are called chords, and together they form the cotree. For the square with one diagonal (n = 4, m = 5), a spanning tree has 3 edges, and the other 2 edges are chords.

The cyclomatic number: The number m - n + 1 is called the cyclomatic number, or circuit rank, of a connected graph. If G has k components, it is m - n + k. It counts how many edges you must remove to destroy all cycles while keeping the graph connected. A tree has cyclomatic number 0. C_n has 1. K_4 has 6 - 4 + 1 = 3. The Petersen graph has 15 - 10 + 1 = 6. Notice that every spanning tree gives the same count, since every spanning tree has n - 1 edges.

Fundamental cycles: Adding a chord e to the spanning tree T creates exactly one cycle, because T already had a unique path between the ends of e (lesson 14). This cycle is called the fundamental cycle of e with respect to T. So there are m - n + 1 fundamental cycles, one per chord. Example: in K_4 with vertices 1, 2, 3, 4, take T to be the star with centre 1 (edges 12, 13, 14). The chords are 23, 24 and 34. Their fundamental cycles are 1 - 2 - 3 - 1, 1 - 2 - 4 - 1 and 1 - 3 - 4 - 1.

Combining cycles: Treat a cycle as its set of edges. The symmetric difference of two edge sets keeps the edges that are in exactly one of them. In K_4, the fundamental cycles for chords 23 and 34 are {12, 23, 13} and {13, 34, 14}. Their symmetric difference is {12, 23, 34, 14}: the edge 13 cancels out, and what remains is the 4-cycle 1 - 2 - 3 - 4 - 1. In general, every cycle of G can be built as a symmetric difference of fundamental cycles. In linear algebra language, the fundamental cycles form a basis of the cycle space, whose dimension is the cyclomatic number m - n + 1.

Why this matters in circuits: In an electrical circuit, Kirchhoff's voltage law says the voltages around any closed loop add to zero. There are many loops, but only m - n + 1 of the equations are independent; the rest are combinations, just like cycles. So an engineer writes one equation per fundamental cycle of a chosen spanning tree and has exactly enough. This is the setting in which Kirchhoff developed these ideas in 1847.

Cuts and bonds: For a set S of vertices, the edge cut [S, S-bar] is the set of edges with one end in S and the other end outside S. Removing it separates S from the rest. A bond is a minimal non-empty edge cut: removing it disconnects the graph, but removing any smaller part of it does not. In a connected graph, a bond splits the graph into exactly two pieces. A bridge is a bond with one edge.

Fundamental cuts: Removing a branch b of the spanning tree T splits T into two pieces. The edges of G that join these two pieces form a cut that contains b and no other branch. It is called the fundamental cut of b. There are n - 1 fundamental cuts, one per branch. They play the same role for cuts that fundamental cycles play for cycles.

Cycles meet cuts evenly: Every cycle and every edge cut share an even number of edges. Reason: walk around the cycle. Each time you cross the cut you switch from S to outside S or back, and you must end where you started, so you cross an even number of times. A neat consequence: a chord's fundamental cycle and a branch's fundamental cut share either 0 or exactly 2 edges. That is the hidden symmetry between cycles and cuts.

The exchange property: Let T be a spanning tree and e a chord. If you add e and remove any edge f on the fundamental cycle of e, the result T + e - f is again a spanning tree: it still has n - 1 edges, and it is still connected because f's job is now done by the rest of the cycle. This simple swap lets you walk from any spanning tree to any other, one edge at a time, and it is the engine behind the proofs of the MST algorithms.

Minimum spanning trees: In a connected weighted graph, a minimum spanning tree (MST) is a spanning tree whose total edge weight is as small as possible. You met the algorithms in the Algorithms course. Here we focus on two facts that explain why they work: the cut property and the cycle property.

The cut property: Take any cut of the graph. If an edge e is the unique lightest edge crossing that cut, then e belongs to every minimum spanning tree. Proof idea: suppose an MST T does not contain e. Adding e to T creates a cycle, and that cycle crosses the cut an even number of times, so it contains another crossing edge f, which is heavier than e. Swap: T + e - f is a spanning tree with smaller weight, contradicting that T was minimum. If several edges tie for lightest, the edge still belongs to some MST.

The cycle property: Take any cycle. If an edge e is the unique heaviest edge on that cycle, then e belongs to no minimum spanning tree. Proof idea: if an MST T contained e, removing e splits T into two pieces, and the cycle must cross between them using some other edge f, which is lighter. Swapping e for f gives a lighter spanning tree, a contradiction. So the heaviest edge of any cycle is always safe to throw away.

Uniqueness: If all edge weights are different, the MST is unique. Reason: if there were two different MSTs, take the lightest edge that is in one but not the other, and apply the exchange argument to get a spanning tree lighter than one of them. With ties, there can be several MSTs, all with the same total weight.

Kruskal, Prim and Boruvka in one breath: Kruskal's algorithm (1956) sorts the edges and adds each one unless it would make a cycle; every edge it skips is the heaviest on a cycle, so the cycle property says skipping is safe. Prim's algorithm (1957, found earlier by Vojtech Jarnik in 1930) grows one tree from a start vertex, always adding the lightest edge leaving the tree; that edge is the lightest across the cut between the tree and the rest, so the cut property says it is safe. Boruvka's algorithm (1926), designed for an electrical network in Moravia, lets every component pick its lightest outgoing edge at once, again safe by the cut property.

A worked example: Vertices A, B, C, D with edges AB = 1, BC = 2, CD = 3, DA = 4, AC = 5. Kruskal: take AB (1), take BC (2), take CD (3). Now DA (4) would close the cycle A - B - C - D - A, skip it. AC (5) would close A - B - C - A, skip it. The MST is {AB, BC, CD} with weight 6. Check with the cycle property: DA is the heaviest on A - B - C - D - A, and AC is the heaviest on A - B - C - A, so neither can be in any MST. Since all weights are distinct, this MST is unique.

Real-life example 1, laying water pipes: A pourashava (municipality) wants to connect 8 neighbourhoods with water pipes, and the cost of each possible pipe depends on distance and road conditions. The cheapest network that reaches everyone is a minimum spanning tree. The engineer can also read off the cyclomatic number of the full candidate graph: it tells how many extra pipes beyond the tree would be needed to give every neighbourhood a backup loop. Adding exactly the right chords gives redundancy where it is most needed.

Real-life example 2, code complexity: Software engineers draw a program's control-flow graph, with blocks of code as vertices and possible jumps as edges. Thomas McCabe's cyclomatic complexity, M = E - N + 2P for a graph with E edges, N vertices and P connected parts, is closely related to the cyclomatic number. It counts independent paths through the code, and testers often aim for at least that many test cases. A function with many if-else branches has a high number, a warning sign for bugs, and many coding teams in Dhaka's software firms set limits on it in code reviews.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Thinking the cyclomatic number depends on the spanning tree chosen. Forgetting the + k for disconnected graphs. Applying the cut property to a heaviest edge or the cycle property to a lightest one. Thinking ties in weights make the MST impossible; they only allow several MSTs. Exams ask: list the fundamental cycles and cuts for a given spanning tree; compute the cyclomatic number; express a cycle as a symmetric difference of fundamental cycles; prove the cut and cycle properties; run Kruskal or Prim and justify each step; prove MST uniqueness with distinct weights.

Recap: A spanning tree has n - 1 branches; the other m - n + 1 edges are chords, and m - n + 1 is the cyclomatic number. Each chord makes a fundamental cycle, each branch a fundamental cut, and every cycle meets every cut in an even number of edges. Swapping a chord for an edge of its fundamental cycle gives another spanning tree. The cut property (lightest edge across a cut is safe) and the cycle property (heaviest edge on a cycle is never needed) prove Kruskal, Prim and Boruvka correct, and distinct weights give a unique MST. Next lesson: directed graphs and tournaments.
key_points: A spanning tree has n - 1 branches; the m - n + 1 remaining edges are chords (the cotree).
The cyclomatic number of a graph is m - n + k (m - n + 1 if connected); it is the same for every spanning tree.
Each chord creates exactly one fundamental cycle; these m - n + 1 cycles form a basis of the cycle space under symmetric difference.
Each branch defines a fundamental cut; every cycle and every edge cut share an even number of edges.
Exchange property: T + e - f is a spanning tree whenever f lies on the fundamental cycle of the chord e.
Cut property: the unique lightest edge across any cut is in every MST; cycle property: the unique heaviest edge on any cycle is in no MST.
With all weights distinct, the MST is unique.
Kruskal (1956), Prim (1957, Jarnik 1930) and Boruvka (1926) are all justified by the cut and cycle properties.
lessons.tip: For any MST question, say which property justifies each step: 'this edge is the lightest across the cut between the tree and the rest' (cut property) or 'this edge is the heaviest on this cycle' (cycle property). Examiners give full marks for the reason, not just the final tree.
lessons.task: Take the graph with vertices 1 to 5 and edges 12, 13, 23, 24, 34, 35, 45. Choose the spanning tree {12, 23, 34, 45}. List all chords and their fundamental cycles, and check there are m - n + 1 = 3. Then give weights 12 = 4, 13 = 1, 23 = 3, 24 = 2, 34 = 5, 35 = 6, 45 = 7 and find the MST with Kruskal, naming the property behind each choice.

quiz.q: What is the cyclomatic number of a connected graph with 12 vertices and 20 edges?
quiz.explain: For a connected graph it is m - n + 1 = 20 - 12 + 1 = 9.

quiz.q: How many edges can an edge cut and a cycle have in common?
quiz.explain: Going around a cycle you cross the cut each time you switch sides, and you must return to the start, so the crossings come in pairs.

quiz.q: Edge e is the unique heaviest edge on some cycle of a weighted graph. What follows?
options: e is in no minimum spanning tree
e is in every minimum spanning tree
quiz.explain: This is the cycle property: swapping e for a lighter edge of the cycle would always give a lighter spanning tree.

quiz.q: Why is the edge Prim's algorithm adds at each step safe?
options: It is the heaviest edge on a cycle
It is the lightest edge crossing the cut between the current tree and the rest
It is always a bridge of the original graph
quiz.explain: Prim always picks the lightest edge leaving the tree, which is the lightest across that cut, so the cut property says it belongs to some MST.

quiz.q: In K_4 with spanning tree {12, 13, 14}, what is the symmetric difference of the fundamental cycles of chords 23 and 34?
quiz.explain: {12, 23, 13} and {13, 34, 14} share only 13, which cancels, leaving {12, 23, 34, 14}, the cycle 1-2-3-4-1.

lessons.title: Directed Graphs and Tournaments
lessons.content:
Five school houses play an inter-house cricket league where every house plays every other house exactly once, and there are no draws. At the end, the sports teacher wants to line the houses up so that each house beat the next one in the line. Is that always possible, no matter how crazy the results were? Surprisingly, yes. Today we study directed graphs more deeply: graphs with no directed cycles, which model tasks with prerequisites, strongly connected pieces, the clever theorem that tells a city when its streets can all be made one-way, and tournaments, which model exactly that cricket league.

Quick recap of digraph words: A digraph has arcs (u, v) going from tail u to head v. The out-degree of v counts arcs leaving v and the in-degree counts arcs entering v. A source has in-degree 0 and a sink has out-degree 0. A directed walk must follow the arrows; a directed path repeats no vertex and a directed cycle is a closed directed path. The underlying graph is what you get by ignoring the directions. An oriented graph is a digraph with no pair of opposite arcs (u, v) and (v, u), so it comes from giving each edge of a simple graph one direction.

Directed acyclic graphs: A DAG is a digraph with no directed cycle. Course prerequisites form a DAG: Structured Programming must come before Data Structures, Data Structures before Algorithms, and so on, and it would be absurd if some course were, through a chain, a prerequisite of itself. Task schedules, spreadsheet formula dependencies, and the versions in a git history are all DAGs.

Every DAG has a source and a sink: Take a longest directed path in a finite DAG, from u to v. If some arc entered u from a vertex w, then w is either on the path, which would close a directed cycle, or off it, which would make a longer path. Both are impossible, so u has in-degree 0: a source. By the same argument v is a sink. This is the directed version of 'every tree has two leaves'.

Topological ordering: A topological order lists the vertices so that every arc goes from an earlier vertex to a later one. Theorem: a digraph has a topological order if and only if it is a DAG. One direction: if there were a directed cycle, its first vertex in the list would need to come after its last, impossible. Other direction: a DAG has a source; put it first, delete it, and the rest is still a DAG, so repeat. This is Kahn's method, and the Algorithms course also showed the DFS method.

Topological order, worked: Courses: D (Discrete Math), P (Programming), S (Data Structures), A (Algorithms), G (Graph Theory). Arcs: P to S, S to A, D to A, D to G, A to G. Sources: P and D. Take P first, then delete it; now S and D are sources. Take D; then S; then A (its prerequisites S and D are done); then G. Order: P, D, S, A, G. Another valid order is D, P, S, A, G. A DAG can have many topological orders; it has exactly one only when there is a Hamilton path through it.

Strong components and the condensation: Recall from lesson 9 that a digraph splits into strongly connected components: groups where everyone can reach everyone along the arrows. If you shrink each component to a single vertex, keeping an arc between two components when some arc joins them, you get the condensation. The condensation is always a DAG: if there were a directed cycle among components, all the components on it could reach each other, so they would have been one component. So every digraph is a DAG of strongly connected pieces.

Robbins' theorem, one-way streets: When can a city make every street one-way and still let people drive from anywhere to anywhere? In graph language: when does an undirected graph have a strongly connected orientation? Herbert Robbins proved in 1939 that this is possible exactly when the graph is connected and has no bridge. If there is a bridge, giving it one direction traps everyone on one side. If there is no bridge, every edge lies on a cycle, and orienting cycles consistently works. So a planning office in Old Dhaka can convert a lane network to one-way only if no single lane is the only link between two areas.

Tournaments: A tournament is an orientation of a complete graph: between every two vertices there is exactly one arc. Think of a round-robin competition with no draws, where an arc from u to v means u beat v. A tournament on n vertices has n(n - 1)/2 arcs. The score of a vertex is its out-degree, the number of wins. Since every match gives exactly one win, the scores add up to n(n - 1)/2.

Score sequences: Which lists of numbers can be the scores of a tournament? Any k teams play k(k - 1)/2 matches among themselves, so together they must win at least that many. H. G. Landau proved in 1953 that this is also enough: a list s1 at most s2 at most ... at most sn is a score sequence exactly when, for every k, the sum of the k smallest scores is at least k(k - 1)/2, with equality for k = n. Example: (0, 2, 2, 2) works for 4 teams, total 6. But (0, 0, 3, 3) fails: the two lowest teams played each other, so one of them won at least once, yet their scores add to 0.

Redei's theorem: Every tournament has a Hamilton path. Laszlo Redei proved this in 1934. Proof by insertion: suppose v1 to v2 to ... to vk is a directed path through k of the vertices, and x is a new vertex. If x beats v1, put x at the front. If vk beats x, put x at the end. Otherwise v1 beats x and x beats vk, so as you move along the path there is a first place where vi beats x and x beats v(i+1); insert x between them. Repeat until all vertices are on the path. That answers the sports teacher: the houses can always be lined up so each beat the next.

Redei, worked: Houses A, B, C, D. Results: A beat B, B beat C, C beat A, D beat A, B beat D, C beat D. Start with path A to B. Insert C: C beat A, so it could go in front, and B beat C, so it could also go at the end; choose the end: A to B to C. Insert D: does D beat A? Yes, so put D at the front: D to A to B to C. Check: D beat A, A beat B, B beat C. A Hamilton path, even though the results contain the cycle A beat B, B beat C, C beat A.

Strong tournaments and Hamilton cycles: Paul Camion proved in 1959 that every strongly connected tournament with at least 3 vertices has a Hamilton cycle. So in a league where no group of teams beat all the others, the teams can be arranged in a ring where each beat the next. A tournament that is not strongly connected has a group at the top that beat everyone below.

Transitive tournaments: A tournament is transitive if whenever u beats v and v beats w, u also beats w. Then the teams can be ranked perfectly: the scores are exactly 0, 1, 2, ..., n - 1, and there is exactly one Hamilton path, which is the ranking. A tournament is transitive exactly when it has no directed 3-cycle. Real leagues are rarely transitive, which is why sports fans argue.

Counting upsets, the 3-cycles: In any tournament, the number of directed 3-cycles equals n(n - 1)(n - 2)/6 minus the sum over all vertices of s(s - 1)/2. Reason: a triple of teams is not a cycle exactly when one team beat both others, and a team with score s beats both members of s(s - 1)/2 pairs. Example: scores (1, 1, 1) on 3 teams give 1 - 0 - 0 - 0 = 1 cycle. Scores (0, 1, 2) give 1 - 0 - 0 - 1 = 0 cycles, the transitive case.

Kings: A king is a vertex that can reach every other vertex by a directed path of length at most 2: it beat you, or it beat someone who beat you. Landau showed that every tournament has a king; in fact any vertex with the highest score is one. Proof idea: if the top scorer x did not reach some y in two steps, then y beat x and also beat everyone x beat, so y would have a higher score than x. Contradiction.

Real-life example 1, the inter-house league: With 5 houses there are 10 matches. Suppose the scores are (4, 2, 2, 1, 1). Landau's check: the two lowest have 2, at least 1; the three lowest have 4, at least 3; the four lowest have 6, at least 6; all five have 10. Valid. The number of 3-cycles is 10 - (6 + 1 + 1 + 0 + 0) = 2. The champion with 4 wins is a king, and Redei guarantees a line-up where each house beat the next, which the teacher can use for the prize-giving photo.

Real-life example 2, a university course plan: The CSE department lists prerequisites as arcs. Before publishing the plan, the department can check it is a DAG by trying to build a topological order. If the method gets stuck with no source left, there is a directed cycle, meaning some prerequisites contradict each other, and the plan must be fixed. If it succeeds, the order is a valid sequence in which a student could take the courses.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Thinking a DAG's underlying graph has no cycles; it can, as long as the arrows do not go around. Forgetting the equality condition for the total in Landau's theorem. Confusing Redei (Hamilton path in every tournament) with Camion (Hamilton cycle only in strong tournaments). Exams ask: find a topological order or a directed cycle; prove every DAG has a source; find strong components and the condensation; state Robbins' theorem; test score sequences; find a Hamilton path by insertion; count 3-cycles; prove the top scorer is a king.

Recap: DAGs have no directed cycles, always have a source and a sink, and are exactly the digraphs with topological orders. Every digraph is a DAG of strong components. A graph has a strongly connected orientation exactly when it is connected and bridgeless (Robbins). Tournaments orient K_n; scores add to n(n - 1)/2 and satisfy Landau's conditions; every tournament has a Hamilton path (Redei), strong ones have a Hamilton cycle (Camion), and the top scorer is a king. Next lesson: matchings and Hall's marriage theorem.
key_points: A DAG has no directed cycle; every finite DAG has at least one source and one sink (longest path argument).
A digraph has a topological order if and only if it is a DAG; repeatedly removing a source builds one.
The condensation of a digraph (strong components shrunk to points) is always a DAG.
Robbins (1939): a graph has a strongly connected orientation iff it is connected and has no bridge.
A tournament orients K_n; its scores (out-degrees) add up to n(n - 1)/2, and Landau's conditions characterise score sequences.
Redei (1934): every tournament has a Hamilton path; Camion (1959): every strong tournament with n >= 3 has a Hamilton cycle.
A tournament is transitive iff it has no directed 3-cycle; the number of 3-cycles is C(n, 3) minus the sum of C(s_i, 2).
Every tournament has a king (reaches all others in at most 2 steps); any top scorer is a king.
lessons.tip: For tournament questions, write the score of every vertex first. Scores give you the number of arcs, the Landau check, the number of 3-cycles and the king, all without redrawing the whole tournament.
lessons.task: Make up results for a 5-team round robin (10 matches, no draws). Compute the scores, check Landau's conditions, count the directed 3-cycles with the formula, then find a Hamilton path using the insertion method and verify that a top scorer is a king.

quiz.q: Which digraphs have a topological ordering?
quiz.explain: A directed cycle makes an order impossible, and every DAG can be ordered by repeatedly removing a source.

quiz.q: When can every street of a connected city map be made one-way while keeping every place reachable from every other?
options: When the map has no bridge (Robbins' theorem)
When every junction has even degree
When the map is a tree
quiz.explain: Robbins (1939): a strongly connected orientation exists iff the graph is connected and bridgeless.

quiz.q: A tournament has 8 teams. What is the sum of all scores?
quiz.explain: There are 8 x 7 / 2 = 28 matches, each producing exactly one win.

quiz.q: Is (0, 0, 3, 3) a valid score sequence for 4 teams?
options: No, the two lowest teams played each other, so their scores cannot add to 0
No, because the sum is odd
quiz.explain: Landau's condition needs the 2 smallest scores to add to at least 1; here they add to 0.

quiz.q: What does Redei's theorem guarantee?
options: Every tournament has a Hamilton cycle
Every tournament has a Hamilton path
Every tournament has a unique king
quiz.explain: Redei (1934): every tournament has a directed Hamilton path, built by inserting vertices one at a time.

lessons.title: Matchings and Hall's Marriage Theorem
lessons.content:
Final year students in a CSE department must each get one thesis supervisor, and each teacher can supervise only one student in this round. Every student lists the teachers they are happy to work with. Can every student be placed? If one student is unhappy with everyone, obviously not. But sometimes the trouble is hidden: three students who are all willing to work with only the same two teachers. Today we learn the theory of pairing things up, called matching. We will see why some matchings cannot be improved, how to improve the others step by step, and Hall's famous marriage theorem, which tells exactly when everyone can be matched.

Matching: A matching in a graph is a set of edges where no two edges share an endpoint. Think of each edge as a pair, and nobody is in two pairs. A vertex touched by an edge of the matching is called matched or saturated; the others are unmatched or free. The number of edges in a largest matching of G is called the matching number, written nu(G) or alpha'(G).

Maximal versus maximum: A matching is maximal if you cannot add any more edges to it. It is maximum if no matching in the whole graph is larger. These are not the same. In the path a - b - c - d, the matching {bc} is maximal: every other edge touches b or c. But {ab, cd} is larger, with 2 edges, and that one is maximum. A greedy method that grabs edges until stuck gives a maximal matching, which can be as small as half of a maximum one.

Perfect matchings: A perfect matching matches every vertex. It has exactly n/2 edges, so n must be even. K_n has a perfect matching exactly when n is even. The cycle C_n has one exactly when n is even, and then it has exactly 2. The Petersen graph has one: the five spokes joining the outer pentagon to the inner star. A star K_(1,3) has none, since the centre can be matched to only one leaf.

Counting perfect matchings: In K_(n,n), match the first vertex on the left in n ways, the next in n - 1 ways, and so on, giving n! perfect matchings. In K_(2n), pick the partner of the first vertex in 2n - 1 ways, then the partner of the next free vertex in 2n - 3 ways, and so on, giving (2n - 1) x (2n - 3) x ... x 3 x 1. For K_6 that is 5 x 3 x 1 = 15. These counts appear in probability and chemistry problems.

Alternating and augmenting paths: Given a matching M, an M-alternating path is a path whose edges alternate between being outside M and inside M. An M-augmenting path is an alternating path that starts and ends at free vertices. Example: path a - b - c - d with M = {bc}. Then a - b - c - d is augmenting: ab is outside M, bc inside, cd outside, and both a and d are free. Flip it: remove bc from M and add ab and cd. The new matching {ab, cd} is one edge bigger. Every augmenting path works like this, because it has one more outside edge than inside edge.

Berge's theorem: A matching M is maximum if and only if there is no M-augmenting path. Claude Berge proved this in 1957. One direction is the flip above: an augmenting path makes M bigger, so M was not maximum. The other direction: suppose M is not maximum and M' is bigger. Look at the edges in exactly one of M and M'. Each vertex touches at most one edge of each, so these edges form paths and even cycles that alternate between M and M'. Since M' has more edges, some path has more M' edges than M edges, and that path is M-augmenting.

A longer augmenting path, worked: Path graph 1 - 2 - 3 - 4 - 5 - 6 with M = {23, 45}. Vertices 1 and 6 are free. The path 1 - 2 - 3 - 4 - 5 - 6 alternates: 12 out, 23 in, 34 out, 45 in, 56 out. Flip every edge: M becomes {12, 34, 56}, a perfect matching with 3 edges instead of 2. Notice that 2, 3, 4 and 5 stay matched; they just change partners. That is the whole trick of augmenting: nobody already matched loses out, and two free vertices gain partners.

The augmenting path algorithm: Berge's theorem gives an algorithm: start with any matching, even an empty one, and repeatedly search for an augmenting path; flip it; stop when none exists. In bipartite graphs the search is a simple BFS or DFS from the free vertices on one side, and the whole process runs in polynomial time. The Hopcroft-Karp algorithm (1973) speeds this up by flipping many shortest augmenting paths at once. For general graphs, Jack Edmonds found a polynomial algorithm in 1965, the blossom algorithm, which handles odd cycles cleverly.

Hall's condition: Now let G be bipartite with sides X and Y. We want a matching that saturates every vertex of X, like matching every student to a supervisor. For a set S of vertices in X, let N(S) be the set of all their neighbours in Y. If S has more vertices than N(S), there are not enough partners for S, and the job is impossible. So a necessary condition is: |N(S)| is at least |S| for every subset S of X. This is Hall's condition.

Hall's marriage theorem: Philip Hall proved in 1935 that this condition is also sufficient. A bipartite graph with sides X and Y has a matching that saturates X if and only if |N(S)| is at least |S| for every subset S of X. The name comes from the old picture of a group of people each with a list of acceptable partners; the theorem says everyone can be paired exactly when every group of k people, together, likes at least k partners.

Why Hall's condition is enough, the idea: Take a maximum matching M and suppose some vertex x in X is free. Collect all vertices reachable from x by M-alternating paths. There is no augmenting path, by Berge, so every vertex of Y we reach is matched, and its partner in X is also reached. So the reached part of Y is matched one-to-one with the reached part of X other than x. Let S be the reached part of X: then N(S) is exactly the reached part of Y, which has |S| - 1 vertices. That breaks Hall's condition. So if Hall's condition holds, no vertex of X stays free.

Hall, worked: Students A, B, C, D and supervisors 1, 2, 3, 4. A likes 1 and 2. B likes 1 and 2. C likes 1 and 2. D likes 2, 3 and 4. Take S = {A, B, C}: N(S) = {1, 2}, which has only 2 vertices, fewer than 3. Hall's condition fails, so not all four students can be placed; at most 3 can. The obstacle is precisely those three students with only two acceptable teachers. If C also likes 3, then every group passes the test and a full matching exists: A to 1, B to 2, C to 3, D to 4.

How far from perfect: There is a stronger form, sometimes credited to Konig and Ore. The deficiency of S is |S| - |N(S)|. The size of a maximum matching equals |X| minus the largest deficiency over all subsets S of X (taking the empty set into account, so the deficiency is never below 0). In the example above the largest deficiency is 3 - 2 = 1, so the maximum matching has 4 - 1 = 3 edges.

Regular bipartite graphs have perfect matchings: Let G be a k-regular bipartite graph with k at least 1. Take any S in X. The k|S| edges leaving S all land in N(S), and N(S) can receive at most k|N(S)| edges in total. So k|S| is at most k|N(S)|, which gives |S| at most |N(S)|. Hall's condition holds, so X can be saturated, and since |X| = |Y| for regular bipartite graphs (lesson 11), the matching is perfect. Removing it leaves a (k - 1)-regular bipartite graph, so repeating shows the edges split into k perfect matchings, a fact we use for edge colouring in lesson 24.

A card trick from Hall: Shuffle a standard deck of 52 cards and deal it into 13 piles of 4. Hall's theorem guarantees you can pick one card from each pile so that the 13 chosen cards are exactly one of each rank, ace to king. Make a bipartite multigraph with piles on one side and ranks on the other, with one edge per card. Every pile has 4 cards and every rank appears 4 times, so the graph is 4-regular, and the argument above gives a perfect matching. It works no matter how the cards were shuffled.

Real-life example 1, thesis supervisors: The CSE office can turn the students' preference lists into a bipartite graph and run an augmenting path algorithm. If it finds a matching that covers all students, done. If not, the algorithm's final search finds a set S of students whose combined list is too short, exactly Hall's obstacle, and the office knows which group to ask for wider preferences or which extra teacher to recruit. The theory does not just say 'no'; it points at the reason.

Real-life example 2, ride sharing: Ride-sharing services in Dhaka have, at any moment, a set of waiting riders and a set of free drivers, with an edge when a driver is close enough to a rider. Pairing as many riders as possible with drivers is a maximum bipartite matching problem. Real systems also weigh distances and waiting times, which turns it into a weighted matching problem, solved by methods like the Hungarian algorithm (Harold Kuhn, 1955). The augmenting path idea sits inside these methods.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Confusing maximal (cannot add) with maximum (largest possible). Checking Hall's condition only for single vertices; groups matter. Forgetting that a perfect matching needs an even number of vertices. Thinking Hall's theorem applies directly to non-bipartite graphs. Exams ask: find a maximal and a maximum matching; find an augmenting path and flip it; prove Berge's theorem; state and prove the easy direction of Hall's theorem; find a violating set S; prove regular bipartite graphs have perfect matchings; count perfect matchings of K_(n,n) and K_(2n).

Recap: A matching is a set of edges with no shared ends; maximal means it cannot be extended, maximum means largest, perfect means every vertex is matched. Berge: a matching is maximum exactly when no augmenting path exists, which gives the augmenting path algorithm. Hall: in a bipartite graph, X can be fully matched exactly when every set S in X has at least |S| neighbours. As a result every k-regular bipartite graph has a perfect matching, and its edges split into k perfect matchings. Next lesson: covers, independent sets and stable matchings.
key_points: A matching is a set of edges with no common endpoints; nu(G) is the size of a maximum matching.
Maximal (cannot be extended) is not the same as maximum (largest possible); a perfect matching covers all vertices.
K_(n,n) has n! perfect matchings and K_(2n) has (2n - 1)(2n - 3)...3 x 1.
An M-augmenting path alternates and joins two free vertices; flipping it increases the matching by one.
Berge (1957): M is maximum iff there is no M-augmenting path.
Hall (1935): a bipartite graph has a matching saturating X iff |N(S)| >= |S| for every subset S of X.
Maximum matching size = |X| minus the largest deficiency |S| - |N(S)|.
Every k-regular bipartite graph (k >= 1) has a perfect matching, and its edges split into k perfect matchings.
lessons.tip: To show a matching is maximum, you need a certificate: either show no augmenting path exists, or point to a set S that violates Hall's condition by exactly the right amount. Practise writing both kinds of certificate, because exams often ask 'prove this matching is maximum'.
lessons.task: Students A to E and projects 1 to 5. A likes 1, 2. B likes 1. C likes 2, 3. D likes 3, 4, 5. E likes 1, 2. Start with the matching A-1, C-2, D-3. Find augmenting paths and flip them until none remain. Then find a set S that shows why not all students can be matched.

quiz.q: In the path a - b - c - d, what is {bc}?
options: A maximal but not maximum matching
quiz.explain: No edge can be added to {bc}, so it is maximal, but {ab, cd} has 2 edges, so {bc} is not maximum.

quiz.q: What does Berge's theorem say?
options: A matching is maximum iff it has no augmenting path
Every graph has a perfect matching
A matching is maximum iff it covers X
quiz.explain: Berge (1957): an augmenting path would let you enlarge the matching, and if none exists the matching is already maximum.

quiz.q: How many perfect matchings does K_(4,4) have?
quiz.explain: K_(n,n) has n! perfect matchings, so 4! = 24.

quiz.q: Students A, B, C all accept only teachers 1 and 2. Which statement is true?
options: Hall's condition fails for S = {A, B, C}, so not all three can be matched
All three can be matched if teacher 3 exists
They can be matched only if the graph is regular
quiz.explain: N({A, B, C}) = {1, 2} has 2 vertices, fewer than 3, so no matching can cover all three.

quiz.q: Why does every 3-regular bipartite graph have a perfect matching?
options: Because it has an odd cycle
Because 3|S| edges leave any S and N(S) can take at most 3|N(S)|, so Hall's condition holds and the sides are equal
quiz.explain: Counting edges gives |N(S)| >= |S|, so Hall's theorem saturates X, and regular bipartite graphs have |X| = |Y|.

lessons.title: Covers, Independent Sets and Stable Matchings
lessons.content:
Dhaka's traffic police want to put CCTV cameras at road junctions so that every road segment can be watched from at least one of its two ends. Cameras are expensive, so they want as few as possible. Meanwhile, a cultural club wants to pick as many students as possible for a committee where no two members are already close friends, to avoid cliques. These two problems look unrelated, but they are mirror images of each other, and both are tied to matchings from last lesson. Today we meet vertex covers, independent sets and edge covers, the beautiful Konig-Egervary theorem, Tutte's condition for perfect matchings, and finally the Nobel-prize-winning idea of stable matchings.

Independent sets: A set of vertices is independent if no two of them are adjacent. The largest size of an independent set is the independence number, alpha(G). In the cycle C_5, any two non-neighbours like v1 and v3 form an independent set, but three vertices would always include a neighbouring pair, so alpha(C_5) = 2. In K_n, alpha = 1. In K_(m,n), alpha is the larger of m and n, by taking a whole side.

Vertex covers: A set of vertices is a vertex cover if every edge has at least one endpoint in the set. The smallest size of a vertex cover is written beta(G) (some books use tau). The camera problem asks for a minimum vertex cover of the road graph. In C_5 you need 3 vertices: with 2, at least one edge of the five would be missed. In a star, the centre alone is a cover, so beta = 1.

The mirror rule, alpha + beta = n: A set S is independent exactly when its complement V - S is a vertex cover. Reason: S independent means no edge has both ends in S, which means every edge has an end outside S. So a largest independent set is the complement of a smallest vertex cover, and alpha(G) + beta(G) = n for every graph. Check on C_5: 2 + 3 = 5. Check on a star with 4 leaves: alpha = 4 (the leaves), beta = 1, total 5 vertices.

Edge covers: An edge cover is a set of edges such that every vertex is an endpoint of at least one of them. It exists only if there are no isolated vertices. The smallest size is written beta'(G). A perfect matching is an edge cover with exactly n/2 edges, the best possible, since each edge covers at most 2 vertices.

Gallai's identity for edges: In a graph with no isolated vertices, the size of a maximum matching plus the size of a minimum edge cover equals n. Idea: from a maximum matching with k edges, n - 2k vertices are uncovered; add one extra edge for each of them, giving an edge cover of k + (n - 2k) = n - k edges. A careful argument shows you cannot do better. Example: the path a - b - c has a maximum matching of 1 edge and a minimum edge cover of 2 edges, and 1 + 2 = 3.

Matchings versus covers: In any graph, every matching is at most as big as every vertex cover. Reason: the edges of a matching share no endpoints, so a cover needs a different vertex for each matching edge. So max matching is at most min vertex cover. In a triangle, the maximum matching has 1 edge but a vertex cover needs 2 vertices. In C_5, it is 2 versus 3. In general graphs there can be a gap.

The Konig-Egervary theorem: In a bipartite graph, the size of a maximum matching equals the size of a minimum vertex cover. Denes Konig and Jeno Egervary proved this in 1931. So in bipartite graphs there is never a gap. This is closely related to Hall's theorem and to max-flow min-cut: all three say that the obvious obstacle is the only obstacle.

Konig-Egervary, worked: Sides X = {a, b, c} and Y = {1, 2, 3}, edges a1, a2, b1, c1. A maximum matching is {a2, b1}: c cannot also be matched, since its only neighbour 1 is taken, and no augmenting path exists. A vertex cover of size 2 is {a, 1}: a covers a1 and a2, and 1 covers b1 and c1. Matching 2, cover 2, exactly equal, as the theorem promises. The cover is a certificate that no matching can have 3 edges.

Consequences for bipartite graphs: Combining the results, in a bipartite graph alpha(G) = n - beta(G) = n minus the maximum matching size. So the largest independent set, which is NP-hard to find in general graphs, can be found quickly in bipartite graphs with a matching algorithm. For the club committee, if the friendship graph happens to be bipartite (say, friendships only form between two different batches), the best committee size is easy to compute.

Hard in general: In general graphs, finding a maximum independent set or a minimum vertex cover is NP-hard; vertex cover was on Karp's 1972 list. A quick approximation for vertex cover takes both ends of every edge in a maximal matching; this gives a cover at most twice the minimum, as you saw in the Algorithms course. For maximum matching itself, polynomial algorithms exist even in general graphs.

Tutte's theorem: When does a general graph have a perfect matching? For a set S of vertices, let odd(G - S) be the number of components of G - S with an odd number of vertices. Each odd component needs at least one of its vertices to be matched to a vertex of S, because it cannot match all its vertices internally. So we need odd(G - S) at most |S|. William Tutte proved in 1947 that this condition, for every S, is also sufficient. Example: in the star K_(1,3), take S = the centre. G - S has 3 odd components (three single leaves), and 3 is more than 1, so no perfect matching.

Petersen's theorem: As a consequence of Tutte's theorem (though Julius Petersen proved it earlier, in 1891), every 3-regular graph with no bridge has a perfect matching. The Petersen graph itself is an example: it is cubic and bridgeless, and its five spokes form a perfect matching.

Stable matchings, the problem: Now add preferences. There are n students and n hostel rooms (or n doctors and n hospitals), and each side ranks the other side. A perfect matching is unstable if there is a blocking pair: a student and a room who both prefer each other to the partner they got. In an unstable matching, the pair would break the rules and swap. A matching with no blocking pair is called stable.

The Gale-Shapley algorithm: David Gale and Lloyd Shapley showed in 1962 that a stable matching always exists, and found it with a simple algorithm. Each free proposer proposes to the highest-ranked receiver they have not yet proposed to. Each receiver keeps the best proposal received so far and rejects the others; a held proposal can be dropped later if a better one arrives. Repeat until everyone is matched. The algorithm always ends, because each proposer proposes to each receiver at most once, so there are at most n x n proposals.

Gale-Shapley, worked: Proposers A, B, C and receivers X, Y, Z. Preferences: A ranks X, Y, Z. B ranks X, Z, Y. C ranks Y, X, Z. X ranks B, A, C. Y ranks A, C, B. Z ranks A, B, C. Round 1: A and B propose to X, C to Y. X keeps B and rejects A; Y keeps C. Round 2: A proposes to Y, who prefers A to C, keeps A and rejects C. Round 3: C proposes to X, who prefers B, so C is rejected. Round 4: C proposes to Z, who is free and keeps C. Result: A with Y, B with X, C with Z. Check: A would rather have X, but X prefers B to A; C would rather have Y or X, but both prefer their partners. No blocking pair, so it is stable.

Who benefits: The Gale-Shapley matching is the best stable matching for every proposer and the worst stable matching for every receiver. So which side proposes matters. Alvin Roth applied these ideas to real markets, such as the system that matches new doctors to hospitals in the United States and school-choice systems in several cities, and in 2012 Shapley and Roth shared the Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences for this work.

Why stable matchings always exist, the idea: Once a receiver holds a proposal, she always holds one from then on, and each new one is better for her. Now suppose the final matching had a blocking pair, proposer p and receiver r who prefer each other. Since p prefers r to his final partner, p proposed to r earlier and was rejected at some point, which only happens when r held someone she liked more. From then on r only traded up, so she ends with someone she prefers to p. That contradicts r preferring p. So no blocking pair exists.

Real-life example 1, CCTV at junctions: Model a Dhaka neighbourhood with junctions as vertices and road segments as edges. A camera at a junction watches every segment touching it, so the cameras must form a vertex cover. If the road network were a grid of blocks, which is bipartite, the minimum number of cameras would equal the maximum matching, computable quickly. For an irregular network the problem is NP-hard, and planners use the 2-approximation or smarter heuristics, knowing the result is close to the best.

Real-life example 2, hostel seat allocation: A university assigns first-year students to hostel rooms using both students' preferences and the hostel's priority list (for example by merit or distance from home). Running Gale-Shapley with students proposing gives a stable outcome that is best possible for students: no student and room would both prefer to swap. Several real admission systems around the world use exactly this idea because it is fair and hard to game for the proposing side.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Mixing up vertex covers (cover edges with vertices) and edge covers (cover vertices with edges). Applying Konig-Egervary to non-bipartite graphs. Forgetting that the receiver keeps the best proposal so far, not the first one. Thinking stable means everyone gets their first choice. Exams ask: compute alpha, beta, alpha' and beta' for small graphs; prove alpha + beta = n; verify Konig-Egervary on a bipartite graph; use Tutte's condition to show no perfect matching; run Gale-Shapley and check for blocking pairs.

Recap: Independent sets have no edges inside; vertex covers touch every edge; the complement of one is the other, so alpha + beta = n. Edge covers touch every vertex, and max matching + min edge cover = n. Matchings are never bigger than vertex covers, and in bipartite graphs they are equal (Konig-Egervary). Tutte: a perfect matching exists iff odd(G - S) is at most |S| for every S. Gale-Shapley always finds a stable matching, best for the proposers. Next lesson: drawing graphs without crossings, planar graphs and Euler's formula.
key_points: An independent set has no two adjacent vertices (alpha); a vertex cover touches every edge (beta).
S is independent iff V - S is a vertex cover, so alpha(G) + beta(G) = n.
An edge cover touches every vertex; with no isolated vertices, max matching + min edge cover = n (Gallai).
In every graph, max matching <= min vertex cover; in bipartite graphs they are equal (Konig-Egervary, 1931).
In bipartite graphs, alpha = n - (max matching), so it can be found quickly; in general graphs it is NP-hard.
Tutte (1947): G has a perfect matching iff odd(G - S) <= |S| for every vertex set S.
Petersen (1891): every bridgeless 3-regular graph has a perfect matching.
Gale-Shapley (1962) always finds a stable matching (no blocking pair), best for the proposing side; Shapley and Roth won the 2012 economics Nobel.
lessons.tip: When you find a matching and a vertex cover of the same size in any graph, stop: both are optimal, because a matching can never beat a cover. Writing both side by side is the cleanest way to prove optimality in an exam.
lessons.task: Run Gale-Shapley twice on these preferences, once with A, B, C proposing and once with X, Y, Z proposing. A: Y, X, Z. B: X, Y, Z. C: X, Z, Y. X: A, C, B. Y: B, A, C. Z: A, B, C. Compare the two stable matchings and check each has no blocking pair.

quiz.q: A graph has 12 vertices and its largest independent set has 5 vertices. What is the size of its smallest vertex cover?
quiz.explain: The complement of a maximum independent set is a minimum vertex cover, so beta = n - alpha = 12 - 5 = 7.

quiz.q: In which graphs does the maximum matching always equal the minimum vertex cover?
quiz.explain: This is the Konig-Egervary theorem. In a triangle, for example, the maximum matching is 1 but the minimum cover is 2.

quiz.q: Why does K_(1,3) have no perfect matching according to Tutte's condition?
options: Removing the centre leaves 3 odd components, more than |S| = 1
quiz.explain: Tutte requires odd(G - S) <= |S| for all S; with S = {centre}, there are 3 single-vertex (odd) components.

quiz.q: In a stable matching problem, what is a blocking pair?
options: Two people matched to each other
A person matched to their last choice
Two receivers with the same preferences
A proposer and receiver who both prefer each other to their current partners
quiz.explain: A blocking pair would both gain by leaving their assigned partners for each other, which makes the matching unstable.

quiz.q: Which statement about the Gale-Shapley algorithm is true?
options: It always ends with a stable matching that is best for the proposing side
It gives everyone their first choice
It only works when preferences are identical
quiz.explain: Each proposer proposes to each receiver at most once, so it ends, and Gale and Shapley proved the result is stable and proposer-optimal.

lessons.title: Planar Graphs and Euler's Formula
lessons.content:
Here is an old puzzle. Three houses in a village each need a connection to three utilities: gas, water and electricity. The pipes and cables run along the ground and must not cross each other. Can you draw all nine connections without any crossing? People have tried for over a century, on paper, on napkins, on classroom boards. It cannot be done, and today we prove it with a formula that also tells us why a football has the pattern it has. The topic is planar graphs: graphs that can be drawn on a flat sheet with no edges crossing.

Planar graphs and plane graphs: A graph is planar if it can be drawn in the plane so that edges meet only at their shared endpoints, with no crossings. Such a crossing-free drawing is called a plane graph or a planar embedding. Careful: a graph drawn with crossings may still be planar, if some other drawing avoids them. K_4 is usually drawn as a square with both diagonals crossing, but you can move one vertex to the inside of the triangle formed by the other three, and the crossing disappears. So K_4 is planar.

Small examples: Every tree is planar: just draw it branching outward. Every cycle is planar. K_1 to K_4 are planar. The cube graph Q_3 is planar: draw a small square inside a big square and join matching corners. Every graph on 4 or fewer vertices is planar. The interesting questions start at K_5 and K_(3,3).

Faces: A plane drawing cuts the sheet into regions called faces. One of them is the unbounded outside region, called the outer face. A triangle drawn on paper has 2 faces: the inside and the outside. The square with one diagonal has 3: two triangles inside and the outside. A tree has only 1 face, the whole plane, because it has no cycle to enclose anything.

Euler's formula: For every connected plane graph with V vertices, E edges and F faces, V - E + F = 2. Euler noticed this for polyhedra in the 1750s. Check: a triangle has 3 - 3 + 2 = 2. The square with a diagonal has 4 - 5 + 3 = 2. The cube has 8 corners, 12 edges and 6 faces: 8 - 12 + 6 = 2.
